#5610. Joint Letter on the Revision of the CO₂ Emission Standards for Cars & Vans

Counting combustion vehicles as clean would blur the market signal and bring back the very uncertainty that carmakers, suppliers, and investors cannot afford. Manufacturers could meet their targets without selling a single electric car.

Dear Climate and Environment Ministers of the European Union,

We, a broad coalition representing non-governmental organizations, think tanks, energy providers, renewable and cleantech industries, and the e-mobility sector, are writing to express our concern over the current direction of EU discussions on the revision of the cars and vans CO₂ emission standards regulation.

Road transport remains the primary driver of Europe’s oil dependency. This structural vulnerability costs the EU hundreds of billions of euros annually, weakens our economy, and leaves citizens exposed to geopolitical shocks. The second fossil fuel crisis in just four years has already added more than €50 billion to Europe’s energy bill, hitting households and businesses hard.

Our continued reliance on fossil fuels also accelerates the climate crisis. This summer, Europeans paid the price as successive heatwaves brought record temperatures, devastating wildfires, and severe droughts across the continent. Transport remains the EU’s biggest emitter, with cars and vans alone accounting for 16% of total CO₂ emissions.

Yet while the market is moving rapidly, political discussions are falling out of touch with reality.

Europe already has a mature, increasingly affordable and readily available structural solution in electric vehicles – which are also the most effective way to shield consumers from volatile fuel prices. Electric vehicles are scaling fast, reaching a record 27% market share in the third quarter of 2026 in the EU.

Instead of building on this momentum, discussions in the Council on the car CO₂ regulation threaten to slow the EV trajectory and inject uncertainty for companies and consumers. Most concerning is the proposal to create a new category for combustion cars running on e-fuels and biofuels, so-called “vehicles running exclusively on eligible fuels” (VEEFs), and count them as zero-emission vehicles.

Too much attention is being paid to combustion-based technologies, distracting from the electric future. Cars running on these fuels still burn fuel in a combustion engine; treating them on par with battery electric vehicles would create a false and unfair equivalence. Under this proposal, manufacturers could meet their targets without selling a single electric car.

Counting combustion vehicles as clean would blur the market signal and bring back the very uncertainty that carmakers, suppliers, and investors cannot afford. It would penalize businesses that are scaling up today and jeopardize the €200 billion already invested in the battery-electric transition. Europe cannot compete globally on electric cars if targets are weakened and undue credit is given to e-fuels, biofuels and hybrids.

We must reset this narrative on vehicle electrification. Europe’s clean industry needs investment certainty and regulatory stability. We therefore call on Climate and Environment Ministers to safeguard the car and van CO₂ targets adopted just three years ago, reject any weakening of the 2030 and 2035 ambition, and remove the “vehicles running exclusively on eligible fuels” (VEEFs) category.

Now is the time for political leadership. Member States have the chance to ensure this fossil fuel crisis is Europe’s last, and to act decisively to build a clean, sovereign, and affordable mobility system supported by a strong EU clean industry.

Download the letter to see the full list of signatories.

Transport & Environment’s (T&E) vision is a zero-emission mobility system that is affordable and has minimal impacts on our health, climate and environment. Created over 30 years ago, we have shaped some of Europe’s most important environmental laws.

#5609. New Trump Tariffs — Nice

Following an election in which voters responded in historic fashion to rising prices — due mostly to Trump’s tariffs and Trump’s war on Iran — President Donald Trump has decided to jack up prices even further by launching a series of new tariffs. The new tariffs span 14 countries or other trading partners.

First of all, the big names here are China and the European Union. As if the prices of all kinds of goods haven’t gone up enough, Trump decided to raise the tariffs on Chinese products from about 20% to about 40%. Don’t expect importers and retailers to eat those costs. Those will certainly be passed on to consumers, even if not fully.

The tariff on products produced in the EU is 15%, which is exactly the maximum tariff agreed to in a 2025 negotiation between the US and the EU. I imagine the EU didn’t anticipate the US turning around and implementing the maximum tariff a year later….

In addition to China and Europe, Trump added tariffs onto products produced in Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam.

“The administration is now using section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 as the legal basis for the new rounds of tariffs. The law gives the executive branch power to respond to unfair foreign trade practices after conducting formal investigations,” The Guardian reports. “Though the White House did not give a timeline for the new tariffs, it said they could go into effect in January at the earliest. The US trade office said it would hold hearings on the new tariffs and its investigation into the unfair trade practices on 25 January.”

It looks like Trump and team are happy to keep jacking up prices on US consumer goods into 2027, even just after the total blue tsunami that just swept the nation. It seems that Trump just doesn’t care, and is stuck in a 1970s-era ideology around the economy, trade, and tariffs. And we’ll all pay the price for that.

#5604. Smarter Cooling, Stronger Reliability: Advancing Wind Turbine Gearbox Performance

As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs. Although major drivetrain components often receive the spotlight, one overlooked system can have an outsized impact on turbine reliability and performance: gearbox oil cooling.

Heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes. When cooling systems become clogged with airborne debris, dust, or organic material, oil temperatures rise, lubrication performance declines, and component stress increases. Over time, these conditions can contribute to reduced gearbox efficiency, elevated maintenance demands, and avoidable downtime.

“Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs. Technologies that improve cooling efficiency and reduce service exposure can have a meaningful impact on long-term turbine reliability and operational profitability,” according to Mike Erickson, HYDAC’s Market Manager for the Wind Industry.

Traditional “panel cut” heat exchanger designs have long been susceptible to clogging due to their tightly packed fin structures. In many wind environments — particularly agricultural, dusty, or high-pollen regions — debris accumulation can severely restrict airflow. Oil leaks can further compound the issue by trapping contaminants within the exchanger core, making cleaning more difficult and labor intensive.

This operational challenge has driven the need for more resilient cooling technologies designed specifically for real-world wind farm conditions.

HYDAC’s new “Square Wave” heat exchanger design represents a significant advancement in addressing these reliability concerns. Engineered to allow debris to pass more freely through the exchanger fins, the design minimizes clogging while improving cooling efficiency under demanding operating conditions.

The importance of effective cooling cannot be overstated. Wind turbine gearbox oil typically operates within an optimal temperature range of approximately 45°C to 65°C. Even modest temperature increases can significantly impact oil viscosity. According to field data, a 12°C rise in oil temperature can reduce viscosity by nearly 28 percent — affecting lubrication quality and accelerating wear on critical drivetrain components.

Field trials have demonstrated measurable operational benefits from the Square Wave design. During a one-year trial on GE 1.x turbines, the upgraded exchanger consistently reduced clogging and lowered maintenance requirements compared to traditional panel cut cores. Operators reported reduced up-tower cleaning time and fewer temperature-related cooling faults.

Field validation across multiple turbine platforms has further reinforced the operational advantages of the Square Wave design. In one case study involving legacy 1 MW-class turbines operating in the Pacific Northwest, a major renewable energy operator installed pilot sets of Square Wave heat exchangers as part of a cooling performance evaluation. Installation teams reported the upgraded exchangers integrated seamlessly into the existing platform with no retrofit complications.

After initial operating data demonstrated improved cooling consistency, the operator expanded the evaluation program with additional units. Long-term SCADA analysis later showed turbines equipped with Square Wave technology operate approximately 20 to 25 percent cooler than comparable turbines using conventional heat exchanger designs under similar operating conditions. The data also highlighted another important advantage: the Square Wave cores continued to maintain airflow and cooling efficiency in debris-heavy environments where traditional exchanger designs became increasingly restricted over time.

The successful deployment also generated interest from additional wind service organizations seeking retrofit-ready cooling upgrades that could improve turbine reliability while reducing maintenance burdens across aging fleets.

“What operators are increasingly recognizing is that small improvements in thermal management can create meaningful gains in turbine reliability, maintenance efficiency, and long-term asset performance,” said Erickson. “The field data we’re seeing continues to validate the value of designing cooling systems specifically for real-world wind operating environments.”

More recently, long-term SCADA data from Mitsubishi platforms further validated the technology’s performance. After two years of operation, turbines equipped with Square Wave heat exchangers operated approximately 19 to 25 percent cooler than reference turbines using standard exchanger designs under comparable operating conditions.

For wind asset owners and service providers, the implications are substantial: Improved thermal management supports healthier oil viscosity, more stable gearbox operation, and potentially longer component life. At the same time, reduced cleaning frequency and fewer cooling-related service events translate directly into lower operational expenditures and increased turbine availability.

As the industry continues to prioritize lifecycle optimization and energy production efficiency, innovative subsystem upgrades such as advanced heat exchanger technology are becoming increasingly valuable. Rather than waiting for costly failures or performance degradation, operators are seeking practical retrofit solutions that improve reliability without requiring major system redesigns.

“Effective thermal management is critical to protecting gearbox health and maintaining oil performance over time. By addressing one of the most common causes of cooling degradation — debris accumulation — operators can improve uptime while reducing unnecessary maintenance interventions,” said HYDAC’s Erickson.

For wind stakeholders evaluating ways to improve gearbox reliability, reduce maintenance exposure, and enhance turbine performance, cooling system optimization deserves greater attention. Proven retrofit technologies like advanced heat exchanger designs can offer a practical path toward improved uptime and operational efficiency without requiring major system overhauls.

As fleets age and performance expectations continue to rise, collaboration between operators, service providers, and technology partners will be essential to building more resilient wind assets for the future. Now is the time to evaluate whether existing cooling systems are supporting — or limiting — long-term turbine reliability goals.

“HYDAC’s goal is to help wind owners and service providers solve practical operational challenges in ways that create long-term value across the entire asset lifecycle. Innovations like the Square Wave heat exchanger are designed to improve reliability, simplify maintenance, and support greater energy production over time.”

Don’t let cooling system limitations impact turbine performance.

Proactive cooling optimization can help operators reduce maintenance exposure, protect critical drivetrain components, and maximize energy production across the asset lifecycle. #5603. Ianalumab Extension Study Confirms Benefit in Sjogren's, Though Still Modest

— Much will hinge on third phase III study now underway

For patients with Sjögren's disease, a second year of treatment with the investigational anti-B cell drug ianalumab boosted response totals, raising the likelihood that it could eventually win approval.

Research presented at the American College of Rheumatology's recent annual meeting showed further improvements in EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index (ESSDAI) scores after already improving significantly, relative to placebo, with an initial 48 weeks of treatment.

Ianalumab targets B-cell activating factor (BAFF) and is also lethal to B cells. The expectation is that this double whammy will make the drug more durably effective than other B-cell depleting agents like rituximab (Rituxan). It's also being tested in a range of other conditions marked by B-cell pathology, including lupus and systemic sclerosis.

As previously reported, participants in the so-called NEPTUNUS-1 and NEPTUNUS-2 randomized trials saw an average 6.5-point decrease from baseline in ESSDAI scores after the first 48 weeks of ianalumab treatment at 300 mg monthly. Continuing on that regimen in the open-label extension study for another 60 weeks brought an additional 1.0-point improvement, according to Thomas Dörner, MD, of Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin, and colleagues.

More impressively, responder totals also increased substantially in the extension. Whereas 58.9% of patients in the main trials had achieved at least 5-point reductions in ESSDAI scores, the proportion rose to 68.4% by week 108. Numbers for the fraction of patients achieving ESSDAI scores less than 5, indicating low disease activity, were identical -- 58.9% at week 48 and 68.4% at week 108.

As well, almost one-quarter of participants initially randomized to monthly ianalumab achieved clinical remission (ESSDAI=0) at week 108, up from 13% at week 48.

Patients randomized to placebo in the main trials were re-randomized in the extension to receive ianalumab, at doses of 300 mg given either monthly or every 3 months. Among those getting the drug monthly, they too saw substantial improvements. Basically, by week 108, they reached the same degree of symptom relief that the original ianalumab groups had achieved at week 48.

All this is good news for ianalumab's sponsor, Novartis, for which the original NEPTUNUS findings were somewhat disappointing. Yes, the primary endpoint of a significant advantage over placebo in change-from-baseline in ESSDAI score was met in both trials, but just barely (P=0.0496 in NEPTUNUS-1). And other outcomes either failed to show a significant difference from placebo or the effect sizes were too small to matter much.

Although safety did not look to be a substantial problem -- and the extension data appeared to confirm that -- the modest-at-best efficacy did not bode well for FDA approval. So Novartis is now sponsoring another placebo-controlled phase III trial focusing on patients with a high symptom burden, the better to see a clear difference between the drug and placebo in effectiveness.

Two ianalumab doses were tested in the NEPTUNUS trials, 300 mg monthly or every 3 months. Those patients continued on these doses, while the placebo groups were re-assigned between them. The latter got their first ianalumab dose at week 60, meaning they then were under active treatment for 48 weeks at data cut-off for the current report.

Of the original 666 patients in the two studies, 610 entered the extension and 551 remained through week 108. In total, the extension is slated to last 5 years beyond the initial 1-year, double-blind period. The current report focused on those patients receiving monthly dosing in the extension, a total of 358, of which about one-third were from the original placebo groups.

A key secondary outcome was change in salivary flow. Participants with a modicum of flow at baseline did better than those with only minimal flow in the primary results, and this remained true in the extension. Dörner and colleagues stratified participants according to whether baseline salivary flow was more or less than 0.4 mL/min. The low-flow group saw little benefit from ianalumab, a 0.1-mL/min increase by week 48, and it remained at about that level through week 108 among those receiving the drug throughout. Not much improvement was seen, either, in the original placebo group after switching to ianalumab.

It was quite different in the group with baseline flow >0.4 mL/min. Those patients saw a 0.2-unit boost in flow by week 48, with an additional jump of 0.2 mL/min at week 72, although the mean value with continuous ianalumab at week 108 fell back to the level seen at week 48. Flow levels actually fell with placebo during the main trials, but recovered back to baseline levels with ianalumab in the extension.

No new side-effect concerns arose in the extension. At the time of data cut-off this past June, some patients had already been on the drug for 4 years (mean 135 weeks); 3% had experienced a serious adverse event considered related to therapy, with 1% stopping the therapy because of such events. Systemic reactions to drug injections occurred in 12%-14% of patients; these appeared to wane as patients continued with treatment.

#5602. Europe’s Solar Problem Is No Longer Solar

Europe’s solar fleet is delivering. The rules, grids, and investment framework around it are struggling to keep up.

SolarPower Europe’s September mid-year assessment describes a familiar contradiction: solar is contributing more to energy security and affordability, yet weakening policy support, grid constraints, and insufficient flexibility threaten continued growth.

In its September newsletter, the association reported that solar became Europe’s largest electricity source in June and estimated that it avoided more than €30 billion in gas imports for power generation over six months of the Middle East conflict. At that point, it forecast a slight contraction in EU solar deployment in 2026.

Europe’s ambition to become an electrostate is stuck in a State of Confusion and will remain unconvincing unless its rules and networks catch up. The challenge is no longer simply building solar. It is connecting it, using it, and making participation easier.

Ukraine’s September auctions illustrate the shift.

Preliminary results showed that a 50 MW solar auction attracted three bids totalling 38.99 MW. A separate 100 MW solar-plus-storage auction attracted 26 bids totalling 385.9 MW.

The terms differed: price ceilings were €0.08/kWh for standalone solar and €0.12/kWh for solar-plus-storage. These were bids, not completed projects. The results demonstrate stronger participation in the hybrid auction—not proof that adding batteries is inherently more profitable.

Physical projects show the transition too. A September report described Romania’s 918 MWh battery under construction and a separate 120 MWh system commissioned at Teiuș. Bulgaria’s Devnya solar plant expanded from 5 MWp to 65 MWp, adding 60 MW/165 MWh of storage.

But batteries are only part of the equation. Schneider Electric Research Institute’s October system-cost analysis models 40,500 scenarios combining distributed solar and batteries with central generation and networks.

Under global-average cost assumptions, optimised scenarios put total electricity-system costs about 10% below the benchmark, rising to as much as 40% below under assumed 2030s technology costs. These are modelled outcomes, not forecasts of European household bills.

The lesson from this company-sponsored research is coordination: electrifying transport, heating, and industry can improve infrastructure utilisation alongside distributed generation.

Denmark is confronting another bottleneck: access to scarce connection capacity.

Denmark’s October connection-prioritisation reform replaces a simple first-come, first-served approach with categories reflecting societal functions, electrification, and other uses. Within categories, projects placing less strain on the grid can receive priority.

Battery treatment matters. Standalone storage falls in category 3, below renewable generation and electrification in category 2. Qualifying co-located batteries can also fall in category 2.

Storage can increase connection requirements or improve an existing connection’s utilisation. Rules should recognise operation, not merely technology labels.

Europe needs transparent queues, credible project-readiness tests and connection arrangements that reward flexibility—not just faster permitting.

Roofs, station canopies, car parks, and noise barriers already occupy space for another purpose. Adding PV can reduce additional land take, although it does not make generation footprint-free.

Belgium’s Solar Tunnel demonstrates the principle. A 2011 announcement records 16,000 modules installed on a covered section of the Paris–Amsterdam railway near Antwerp, designed to generate 3.3 GWh annually for railway infrastructure and trains.

At Uden in the Netherlands, bifacial PV forms part of an A50 motorway noise barrier. The EU LIFE project’s monitored results recorded 325.5 MWh over 18 months—approximately 220 MWh annually.

The assessment also reports lower-than-expected generation and higher-than-anticipated capital costs. Multifunctional infrastructure is promising, not automatically cheaper. Engineering, procurement, and maintenance determine whether combined benefits justify the premium.

The strongest projects preserve their original function while adding electricity: shade plus charging, noise protection plus generation, or water infrastructure plus power. They complement conventional rooftop and ground-mounted solar rather than replace them.

At the other end of the scale, plug-in solar challenges the assumption that participation requires an owned roof and a substantial installation budget.

Germany’s Federal Network Agency provides a simplified administrative route for qualifying systems, with module capacity up to 2,000 Wp and inverter output up to 800 VA.

Registration remains mandatory. Separate network-operator notification is waived under specified conditions, including the unpaid-export arrangement. These administrative thresholds do not override technical or installation-safety requirements.

Germany’s environment agency explains that qualifying devices within technical limits can be commissioned by non-specialists.

That matters because administrative and installation costs can be disproportionate for small systems. Balcony solar offers a route for people without access to a conventional rooftop installation, including some apartment residents.

It does not replace large-scale generation or remove mounting, electrical-safety, building-consent, and country-specific requirements. Its importance is accessibility: proportionate regulation makes small-scale participation possible.

Europe needs large projects, distributed generation, solar-equipped infrastructure, accessible household systems, batteries, and flexible demand.

Writing from Down Under, the parallel is clear. High rooftop-solar penetration is reshaping Australian daytime demand and electricity prices. The response is batteries, flexible demand, and market rules that reward them.

The choice is not between ambition and practicality. Practical rules are how ambition becomes deployment.

Prof Ray Wills is a Perth-based energy futurist and director of Future Smart Strategies, and Adjunct Professor at The University of Western Australia, who writes on renewables, electrification, and the energy transition.

#5599. Sjogren's Disease Brings a Lot More Misery Beyond Dryness

— Brain fog, fatigue, infections, death explored in new studies

Oral and ocular dryness are the hallmark features of Sjögren's disease, but understanding the full symptom burden is still an active area of investigation, with recent studies reported at the American College of Rheumatology's annual meeting shedding light on some of the condition's lesser-known aspects.

For example, one new study found that oral disease serious enough to cause tooth loss helps drive serious infections such as sepsis in Sjögren's patients, a risk that is worsened further with immunomodulators typically used to control the disease.

Another found that nonphysical symptoms including "brain fog" and fatigue are nearly as common as dryness in Sjögren's disease, and a third confirmed that patients face a significant risk for early mortality.

All in all, this research puts Sjögren's disease alongside conditions more famous for their broadly burdensome symptom spectrum, such as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and systemic sclerosis.

An analysis of U.S. commercial and Medicaid insurance claims led by Thomas Grader-Beck, MD, of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, looked at associations between oral disease indicators and infection rates among some 60,000 people with Sjögren's disease.

Those suffering tooth loss, typically the result of periodontal disease, were significantly more likely to also experience systemic infections -- modestly when five or fewer teeth were lost (OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.13-1.24), or more strongly with more extensive extractions (OR 1.69, 95% CI 1.36-2.11). Absolute risks were substantial too: whereas systemic infections were recorded for 36% of those with no tooth loss (itself an indicator of risk associated with Sjögren's disease), the percentage reached 43% in patients with up to five lost teeth and 54% among those with six or more lost.

Dental visits, too, tracked with systemic infection risk in a "dose-response" relationship. Odds ratios for infections rose with each additional visit in the previous year: 1.11 with one visit, 1.32 with two, 1.41 with three, and 1.60 for four or more (all P<0.001 relative to no dental visits).

Moreover, the researchers reported, use of immunomodulator therapy -- a category that spans virtually every drug used for Sjögren's disease including corticosteroids, antimalarials, biologics, and conventional immunosuppressants -- by itself raised the risk for infections by 49%.

Oral disease and immunosuppression are "independent, additive risk factors for systemic infection," the group concluded.

Lane Destro, PhD, and colleagues at the Sjögren's Foundation in Reston, Virginia, had the Harris Poll organization survey people with the condition last year, with a total of 6,360 responses. It found that so-called brain fog -- a feeling of mental sluggishness and inability to focus -- and fatigue were almost as common as salivary and ocular dryness (prevalences of 77% and 90%, respectively, versus 93% and 95%), and also in the same range as joint pain (81%).

Other nonphysical symptoms were common too, if less so than brain fog and fatigue. Some 73% of respondents complained of insomnia, 64% reported eye fatigue specifically, 56% said they suffered headaches, and 56% indicated feeling dizzy or faint.

Patients also complained of additional burdens. Close to 60% said Sjögren's disease had affected relations with their spouses or partners and two-thirds reported impacts on other family relationships. A large majority agreed that Sjögren's "adds an emotional burden to my life," while half said the disease made them feel lonely. Not surprisingly, most also reported difficulties with work and employment stemming from the diagnosis.

Furthermore, the problems arising from fatigue and brain fog were disproportionately burdensome for these quality-of-life (QoL) issues. Having relatively severe dry eyes and mouth, for example, raised the likelihood of experiencing negative QoL effects by factors of roughly 1.5 to 2; a high fatigue burden, on the other hand, raised the risk by factors of 4 to 10, and the negative impact of brain fog was nearly as great.

French researchers confirmed that patients with Sjögren's disease face increased mortality risk, in the same way as patients with other autoimmune inflammatory conditions such as lupus.

Led by Elodie Portier, MD, of Hôpital Bicêtre in Paris, the group examined vital statistics for a 395-member cohort of Sjögren's disease patients in France and compared them with the general national population. Followed from 2007 to 2025, the cohort saw 77 deaths. The rate was 41% higher than among similar-age French people (95% CI 11-76). The gap was even greater for a Sjögren's subgroup marked by high symptom burden (54%, 95% CI 10-110).

The researchers also identified several risk factors for early mortality in the Sjögren's cohort. In multivariate analysis, each year of older age added 13% to the risk, while being male nearly tripled the likelihood of death (HR 2.66, 95% CI 1.04-6.77).

Having more than mild disease was also a mortality risk. Multivariate analysis comparing patients with EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Activity Index (ESSDAI) scores of 6 or more to those with ESSDAI 5 or less yielded a hazard ratio of 2.16 (95% CI 1.29-3.60). Each ESSDAI point conferred a 15% extra risk for mortality.

Patient-reported overall symptom burden showed a similar pattern, the researchers noted, but it fell just short of statistical significance.

#5598. Ford Returns To The 24 Hours Of Le Mans With The 2027 GT41

Ford has a relatively short but lauded history with the 24 Hours of Le Mans. In the 1960s it won four years in a row with the GT40, and pop culture fell in love with the GT40 via the film "Le Mans," and then again decades later with "Ford V Ferrari." The Big Blue Oval returned to Le Mans in 2016 with the Ford GT, which came first in its class, and it continued to race through 2019. Now Ford is headed back to Le Mans in 2027 with its latest hypercar effort, the GT41. Its new FIA Endurance Championship racer was revealed Thanksgiving day on Ford Field, while a different heated rivalry plays out: the Detroit Lions vs. Chicago Bears game.

The LMDh car sports a livery featuring footballs, bald eagles, the Ford name, and the Spirit of Detroit, a statue that has sat downtown since 1958. The Ford family owns the Detroit Lions, as well as a controlling share in the auto manufacturer that bears their name. This is the kind of synergy newer oligarchs wish they could achieve.

Powering the new GT41 is a naturally aspirated 5.4-liter V8 that's based on the same Coyote engine any old Ford-head can get in Mustangs and F-150s. The Coyote in the GT41 has been, of course, lovingly and painstakingly modified and rebuilt over and over again to drill down to peak Ford performance. The company then worked hard to destroy these delicately crafted pieces of machinery to ensure longevity during 24 hours of continuous driving. Ford is doing all of the development and testing in-house to make sure this new racer is the manufacturer's most ambitious program yet, born out of lessons learned during F1 Red Bull racing development.

It was 60 years ago when Ford swept the race in 1966, taking positions 1, 2 and 3. The manufacturer's program ended in 1967, but the GT40 went on to three more consecutive races, just with other operators, until 1969. That car was called GT40 because it stood 40 inches from the ground to the air intake; the new GT41 has grown by a single inch.

There is a direct line from the sport of kings to the global dominance of the car, and Ford had its hand in both. It was developing and racing his own automobiles 125 years ago that got Henry Ford interested in cars in the first place. Racing awards turned into seed money for manufacturing, and the rest is history.

The Ford GT41 already has a full suite of drivers, so sorry if you were planning on putting your name into the hat. Taking the wheel will be Logan Sargeant, Tom Blomqvist, Matt Campbell, Sebastian Priaulx, Mike Rockenfeller and Nick Yelloly, plus Tom Dillmann, who was recently announced as reserve driver. Running a car for 24 hours is a lot to ask of a single driver, after all. To really cement things, Ford has a new ad campaign using Carroll Shelby's motto "Go Like Hell," with voiceover work from "Ford V Ferrari' actor Matt Damon, who portrayed Shelby in the film.

This time it's not just Ferrari that Ford is looking to beat, though Ferrari did win in 2023, 2024 and 2025, so Ford should definitely be looking over its shoulder. 2027 is proving to be a crowed year for the WEC, with 12 different factory prototypes going head-to-head at Le Mans, including this year's new kid on the block, Genesis. Next year's 24 Hours of Le Mans will be a race worth remembering, no matter who comes out on top.

#5597. Hybrids Are a Waypoint, Not the Destination

An earlier version of this article appeared in The Driven on 15 October 2026. This version has been revised and updated with the most recent registration data.

By Ray Wills, Raphael Wellmann, and Peter Newman

In January 2024, Toyota chairman Akio Toyoda said battery EVs would reach at most 30% market share, with the remainder going to hybrids, hydrogen, and combustion vehicles. Norway’s BEV share was already at about 89% that year. Norway alone cannot settle a prediction about the global market, but it shows that 30% is no inherent ceiling on BEV adoption.

PHEVs are conditional transition vehicles. They earn their environmental case through verified electric kilometres, not through the presence of a charging port.

Mature markets tell the more revealing story. Once battery-electric vehicles offer sufficient choice, charging confidence, and competitive economics, hybrids do not settle into a permanent share of the market. Hybrids may lead early, peak, and then retreat.

Norway. The year is 2015. Hybrid vehicles had gained material market share and plug-in hybrids were beginning to arrive in volume. In 2017, PHEVs accounted for about 18% of new registrations. BEV growth temporarily paused, while hybrids benefited from familiar factories, familiar supply chains, and familiar consumer expectation.

After another PHEV surge in 2020 and 2021, the direction changed. By October 2026, battery-electric vehicles accounted for 98.8% of Norway’s new passenger-car registrations. Petrol plug-in hybrids represented just 0.2%, and petrol full hybrids 0.3%. Across the first ten months of the year, BEVs held 98% of the market. Hybrids had not become a permanent destination: they had become marginal in new-car sales.

It would be easy to dismiss Norway as a special case: a small, affluent, and subsidy-supported market.

Singapore has a distinctive vehicle-ownership system, built around Certificates of Entitlement, high ownership costs, and tightly managed taxation. Yet its market also shows hybrids losing ground as BEVs expand. Conventional hybrids accounted for 28.3% of new registrations in October 2026, while BEVs held 59.6% and PHEVs 6.2%. The monthly figures fluctuate: hybrid share was higher than in August. The longer-term question is whether hybrids retain their earlier prominence as BEVs become mainstream—not whether their share falls every month.

Denmark provides another example. In October 2026, battery-electric vehicles accounted for 88.2% of all new passenger-car registrations and 97.4% of households’ new cars. The distinction matters: household purchases and the overall market do not electrify at precisely the same pace. But both now show BEVs becoming the dominant choice.

These three markets are not identical, and their policies are not interchangeable. But they show a repeating shape. In leading electrification markets, hybrid share has not settled into a stable plateau. It has risen, peaked and then declined.

For years, Norway was treated as the exception: small, rich, subsidy-heavy, and unrepresentative. But its basic market pattern is now appearing wherever electrification has advanced far enough.

Once the pattern is visible in several unrelated countries, the question becomes whether it is appearing more widely, including in markets still early in the transition.

Trailing-twelve-month registration data across the selected markets show not a world divided between “BEV countries” and “hybrid countries,” but markets at different stages of electrification and following different routes.

Some move relatively directly from combustion vehicles to BEVs. Others pass through a stronger hybrid phase, then a PHEV phase, before BEVs become dominant. In China, PHEVs and range-extended EVs have gained strength alongside BEVs, supported by rapid product cycles, intense domestic competition, expanding charging networks, regulatory settings, and strong domestic manufacturers.

This is not a claim that hybrids have already peaked everywhere. Across the European Union, BEVs accounted for 23.4% of new-car registrations in the first ten months of 2026, while hybrids remained a major part of the market. In Australia, the hybrid share is still close to its high, but in October 2026, BEVs overtook hybrids on a trailing-twelve-month basis for the first time (18.5% vs. 17.6%). The transition remains uneven across countries, buyer types, and vehicle segments.

The route differs. The starting point differs. The pace differs. The picture that comes out isn’t “some countries like BEVs, others like hybrids.” As BEVs meet more buyers’ needs at competitive cost, hybrids face increasing pressure on their share of new-car sales. Whether their absolute sales also fall depends on the size and growth of the market.

There is a practical implication for buyers. A hybrid purchased today in a market that has not yet reached its tipping point may face greater residual-value risk when it arrives on the used market. If new-car demand shifts rapidly towards BEVs while used supply reflects today’s hybrid-heavy sales, resale values may come under pressure.

Fuel prices, tax settings, used-BEV supply, charging access, and export markets will impact, but it is a risk buyers, fleets, and financiers should acknowledge.

If the pattern is visible in the data, why does public discussion so often present hybrids as a permanent pillar of the future vehicle market?

One reason is that the transition is uneven—the future is here, it’s just not well distributed yet. In many countries, people have only seen the rising half of the hybrid curve. The peak and decline have not yet arrived. It is easy to mistake “still growing” for “here to stay.”

Another is that manufacturers with decades of investment in combustion and hybrid platforms have commercial reasons to extend the life of those systems. That behaviour seems rational. Hybrid platforms preserve familiar engines, suppliers, dealer servicing, and factory investments.

But that commercial logic is not evidence that hybrid demand will remain durable once BEVs can do the same job more effectively. As with everything, the biggest cost may come not in going too fast, but in going too slow.

It is also important not to overstate the case against PHEVs. A PHEV that is routinely plugged in can cover much of its owner’s daily driving on electricity. The problem is that many of those PHEVs are not used that way.

European Commission data from 320,000 PHEVs first registered in 2021 found real-world CO₂ emissions averaging 3.5 times their official type-approval values. The Commission concluded that these vehicles were not being charged and driven electrically as frequently as assumed in laboratory testing.

Company vehicles are a particular problem. Petrol may be employer-paid, immediate, and simple to use, while home charging is paid by the employee, workplace charging is unavailable, and reimbursement is cumbersome. Under those conditions, the petrol engine becomes the default.

A PHEV is a bridge—but only if people use it to cross from the petrol side to the electricity side.

The registration data do not say that every hybrid buyer has made the wrong decision. Some households and fleets still need a transitional option. Some regional, towing, remote-area, and high-kilometre uses remain difficult for today’s BEV models and charging networks.

But those are specific use cases that are not representative of the mass market and thus not a reason to preserve combustion systems for everyone.

Conventional hybrids reduce petrol consumption, particularly in stop-start urban driving, but every kilometre still depends on fuel. PHEVs can replace a substantial share of petrol with electricity, but only if they are regularly charged, have enough real-world electric range, and do not unnecessarily run their engine.

BEVs eliminate routine petrol use and are the most energy-efficient option for the expanding share of households and fleets whose driving and charging conditions suit them.

The role of policy is not to pretend that all drivers are identical. It is to make electric driving easier: reliable charging at homes, apartments, workplaces, and regional routes; electricity reimbursement as straightforward as fuel reimbursement; and real-world reporting of petrol use and electric kilometres in PHEV fleets.

The market is not likely to move from combustion to BEV in exactly the same way everywhere. But as battery-electric vehicles become cheaper, more capable, and easier to charge, the addressable market for hybrids contracts.

Hybrids can help drivers transition from the combustion era into the battery electric era.

But that is all they are, a waypoint towards an electric future.

Ray Willis is a Perth-based energy futurist and director of Future Smart Strategies, and Adjunct Professor at The University of Western Australia, who writes on renewables, electrification, and the energy transition.

#5596. For A Game Known For Stealing Cars, GTA 6's Transit System Is Actually Useable And Unbelievably On Time

Ok, Jalopnik admittedly went really hard on enlightening you on everything from immediate upgrades to behind-the-scenes secrets related to "Grand Theft Auto VI" last week. Maybe a little too hard. I promise this one-off discovery was purely out of genuine interest and transportation nerdiness. It's all about Leonida's public transit system.

YouTuber Sonny Evans is not a page I've ever come across in my gaming watches until today, and from what I've seen on his page, he tends to look into the beyond of game play, or simply someone who the wild what-ifs in open world games. The best way to understand his vibes is reading his bio which said: "I walked a bowl of stew across the map in Red Dead Redemption 2 and millions of people actually watched it." My guy. His more recent posted videos include driving a mobility scooter across the entirety of Leonida in GTA 6, following NPCs to see where they go and what they do, and the latest: seeing if GTA 6's public transportation actually works.

Sonny inspected the game's public transit ventures, using the in-game maps to navigate from home base to Vice City using the Interstate Loop buses and the metro lines before landing at Vice City airport. He timed the transit moves, mentioning at about 3:28 in the 10-minute video that his commute into Vice City via the Loop bus was 5 hours of game time. This absolutely correlates with the idea that Leonida is a Florida-like state, likely size-wise as well.

Sonny did the same with Vice City's Metro system, using the in-game posted maps and timing boards to see if the trains really did run on time. They did! This unfortunately makes them a little unrealistic, because anyone who has ever taken any form of public transit knows that nothing will be on time. Ever.

He also found a real, tiny discrepancy. The signs at the stop showing the Northbound and Southbound routes (showing the stops like they do on the New York City subways) for the trains were identical, which actually makes no sense. This made it a little more challenging for Sonny to figure out which way to go. Luckily, he guessed right and continued on to Vice City's airport.

This is where the video went a little off of the rails. Sonny discovers a few hidden areas including the underneath room to the luggage carousels. Then there was the speed run of getting past TSA, causing a little chaos, and ended with Sonny (as Jason, the main character) stealing a commercial plane.

So, it looks like if you get stranded somewhere in Leonidas and have no car handy to steal or carjack, you might be able to depend on public transit. The care the creators took in making that entire system work, even if its on-time buses and trains are somewhat unrealistic, is mad impressive. Now to see if someone will do their entire gameplay using just the public transit. I can't be the only person who would watch that.

According to the companies, integrating advanced steel frame solutions into selected Thornova Solar module series addresses two increasingly important priorities in the U.S. solar market: maximizing domestic content and improving module resilience under demanding environmental conditions.

The combined solution offers several key benefits:

The solution is particularly relevant for projects in demanding U.S. environments, including high-wind regions across the Midwest and Southeast, where structural reliability and long-term module performance are critical considerations.

“The signing of this Master Supply Agreement represents an important step in strengthening our relationship with Nextpower and expanding the value we deliver to U.S. customers,” said Andrea Bodenhagen, global marketing director of Thornova Solar. “By bringing together U.S.-made solar modules and domestically manufactured steel frame technology, we are helping our customers increase domestic content while benefiting from stronger, more resilient module solutions. The MSA reflects the shared commitment of both companies to strengthening domestic manufacturing and delivering solutions that respond to the evolving technical and commercial requirements of the U.S. solar market.

#5594. Plug-in Solar UL Certification for US Safety Regs — What UL 3700 Does & Doesn’t Say

Millions of renters, apartment residents, and condo owners can’t put solar on a roof they don’t control. Plug-in solar, also called balcony solar or plug-in PV, offers a workaround: one or more panels connected through a microinverter to an ordinary wall outlet, with no roof work and, in a growing number of states, no utility interconnection application — though, this is only applicable in select states (users should refer to their state laws before installation). A new safety standard, UL 3700, is helping this market mature, and it comes with a lesson every buyer should learn: a compliant component is not the same thing as a certified system.

Rooftop solar assumes you own a roof, can afford a large upfront cost, and can wait through permits and installation. Plug-in solar flips that. States are responding. As of mid-October, ten states had enacted plug-in solar laws: Utah, Maine, Virginia, Colorado, Maryland, New Hampshire, Connecticut, Vermont, New Jersey, and California. Effective dates vary, with several laws not taking effect until 2027, and New York’s SUNNY Act is awaiting the governor’s signature. Several of these laws require kits to meet a recognized safety standard, and some name UL 3700.

UL 3700, the Outline of Investigation for Interactive Plug-In Photovoltaic Equipment and Systems, was published in December 2025, and UL Solutions began certifying products to it in January 2026. It exists because rooftop solar standards weren’t written for equipment that homeowners plug in themselves. The safety problems are specific:

Hoymiles says the HiFlow Pro was built around these challenges and shuts down in 135 milliseconds if it’s unplugged or the grid fails. For comparison, Maine’s law requires shutoff within 0.2 seconds.

Here is the part that matters most for buyers. UL 3700 evaluates a complete system: the microinverter, how it connects, relevant accessories, and the overall configuration, not the microinverter alone. That means compliance for one part doesn’t automatically establish that the whole kit has been certified.

The HiFlow Pro shows how this works in practice. Hoymiles describes the microinverter itself as UL 3700-compliant, and it has been widely reported as the first plug-in microinverter in the US to reach that point after its July 15, 2026 launch. The complete HiFlow Pro system has not yet finished certification. Hoymiles says it is pursuing it and expects the process to wrap up in December 2026.

The HiFlow Pro is a plug-in microinverter, so the panels are bought separately or as part of a kit. Per Hoymiles, up to four units can run on separate outlets for up to 1,200 watts, depending on state and local rules, and models range from 360 W to 500 W to fit different legal limits. The company lists a peak efficiency of 95.5%, a NEMA Type 6 enclosure, an operating range of -40°F to 149°F, a 12-year standard warranty, and monitoring through the S-Miles Home app. It also cites 250,000 hours of reliability testing, and says TIME named the product one of its Best Inventions of 2026.

Follow the manufacturer’s instructions. Plug the unit directly into a wall outlet, not a power strip or extension cord, and use a GFCI outlet if you’re running a larger system on one circuit.

Hoymiles estimates up to 721 kWh a year from a single 360 W unit, modeled at 5.6 peak sun hours a day and about 2,403 kWh from a four-unit system. At 38 cents per kWh, a rate found only in the highest-cost regions, the company estimates savings of up to about $247 per unit per year and a payback of roughly two years. By our math, that figure assumes about 90% of the power gets used inside the home. Actual savings depend on how much electricity you use during daylight hours, and surplus power may flow to the grid without credit unless your utility offers net metering.

For context, EnergySage puts typical savings from a plug-in kit at $13 to $20 a month at the national average rate of about 18 cents per kWh, and $40 to $50 a month in high-rate states like California, New York, and Hawaii. Two limits are worth knowing: the system reduces your bill but doesn’t replace the grid, and it won’t provide backup power in an outage. The federal homeowner solar tax credit also ended on December 31, 2025, so payback estimates shouldn’t assume one.

Rules vary by state, and sometimes by utility. Hawaii, with some of the country’s highest electricity prices, isn’t among the ten states with a plug-in solar law, so renters and condo owners here should check with Hawaiian Electric and their association before buying. Even in states with laws, utilities may ask for notice, and landlord and HOA protections differ.

#5593. At $17,000, Is This LS-Swapped 2001 BMW M3 A Black Friday Bargain?

Today's Nice Price or No Dice M3 has a built LS V8 under the hood and a driver's seat that shows the wear and tear of someone having enjoyed the car for its intended purpose. Let's see if it's priced to spread that joy.

Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been a New York City tradition for over 100 years, an unofficial kickoff to the holiday season. This year, for the first time in the event's history, the parade has been postponed from Thanksgiving Day to tomorrow, Saturday, because the forecast called for heavy rain and wind. That storm could turn the record 100 inflatable cartoon characters into ballistic balloons, potentially endangering parade-goers who already braved the inclement weather.

We had no such qualms about the weather in bringing you a slice of Thanksgiving cheer yesterday in the form of a tidy little classic 1973 Chevy Vega notchback. And it had a V8 under its hood! It also had a not-insubstantial $17,000 asking price, which didn't sit well with most of you. That price quickly racked up a massive 91% 'No Dice' loss in the voting.

Okay, I have to apologize to you all. We started this week with a BMW E46 M3, and now, here we are finishing it off with... a BMW E46 M3. Here's the thing, though: this car dovetails nicely, not only with Monday's near-stock coupe but also with yesterday's Chevy Vega, since both this 2001 BMW M3 convertible and the Vega have been recipients of a Chevy V8 engine swap and carry the exact same asking price. With its LS under the hood and a few other issues, this E46 is also over 20% cheaper than the Monday car.

Say what you will about engine swaps and sullying the purity of so excellent a car as an E46 M3, the reasons behind this particular car's heart transplant may actually make sense. After all, being a drop top, it's much less desirable as a track toy. Plus, it probably could be converted back to S54 status without much trouble should the LS prove too mortifying for the next owner.

For the moment, however, it has a 5.3-liter LS V8, an engine that likely started life in a pickup or SUV before finding a new home here in this black-over-gray leather M3. It's not an unusual conversion, and the LS fits in the BMW's engine bay without much fuss. According to the ad, the engine drives the original BMW power steering pump, but an A/C compressor wasn't in the cards. That might make the BMW climate controls a bit wonky and make the open top a welcome feature for airflow.

The ad notes numerous internal and external engine updates, including an aggressive cam, aluminum heads, hardened internals, and a DOD/AFM delete. It runs a special ECU tuned by PCM of Mooresville, North Carolina, a company that specializes in GM engine tweaking.

Other conversion updates include a new high-performance clutch ahead of a ZF five-speed manual gearbox and strengthened rear subframe mounts. It all appears tidy and well put together, but the ad lacks details on how the car runs and rides, or even whether the original instruments function.

As for the car's looks, there are some plusses and minuses. Overall, it looks to be in solid shape with no body damage evident, a seemingly intact top, and the same Style 163M Cross Spoke alloys as we saw on Monday's car. Looking a bit more closely, as you would when considering buying something like this, a few issues stand out. Notably, the clear coat on the top of the rear bumper cap is fading significantly, and the leather on the driver's seat is also starting to give up the ghost. The rest of the upholstery appears to be in decent shape, with only minor scuffing on the passenger seat. The rear seats look like they've never been used at all.

Other things to note: the center console now houses a pair of add-on gauges, canted toward the driver. Those monitor engine coolant temperature and oil pressure. Above that sits a big screen infotainment unit that, hysterically, still has its protective plastic film intact. Per the ad, the car comes with a clean title. It also notes the mileage at 460, but doesn't explain when that count began.

This being Black Friday, one might expect to find a total door-buster bargain on tap for our consideration and judgment. The thing is, the way this all works is that you decide what's a bargain or not. You're in control. You're the final arbitrator of value. Use this power wisely.

With that in mind, let's now consider this LS-equipped M3's $17,000 asking price. See? That is exactly the same as yesterday's also V8-powered Vega. Which car would you rather have instead of $17K in your bank account? And yes, "neither" is an acceptable answer. For anyone with a wild hair about this Bimmer, though, would $17,000 be a fair price to pay for the car as it's presented in its ad? Or do the demerits (and lack of originality) make this a Black Friday deal you would pass up?

#5592. How Certain Foods in Adolescence Are Linked to IBD Risk

— Study finds associations with fruit, fish, and salty snacks, but not always in the same direction

Eating certain foods during childhood and adolescence was associated with higher or lower risks of later inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), prospective data suggested.

In pooled analyses of three cohorts in Norway, Denmark, and Sweden, high versus low intake of fruit in childhood was associated with a reduced risk of Crohn's disease (CD; adjusted HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.47-0.94), as was high versus low intake of fish (aHR 0.65, 95% CI 0.44-0.97), reported Annie Guo, PhD, of the University of Gothenburg Institute of Medicine in Sweden, and colleagues in Gut.

On the other hand, high versus low fruit intake in childhood was associated with an increased risk of ulcerative colitis (UC; aHR 1.54, 95% CI 1.07-2.20).

During adolescence, high versus low fruit intake was associated with a reduced risk of CD (aHR 0.57, 95% CI 0.36-0.88), but no significant associations were observed between fruit consumption and UC.

Meanwhile, high versus low intake of salty snacks during adolescence was initially associated with an increased risk of IBD (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.11-1.86), but after multivariable adjustment, the risk was attenuated (aHR 1.32, 95% CI 0.99-1.77). The adjusted HR for UC with a high versus low intake of salty snacks in adolescence was 1.51 (95% CI 0.97-2.37).

"To our knowledge, this is the first prospective study to examine associations between food-group intake during both childhood and adolescence and the subsequent risk of IBD, CD, and UC," Guo and team wrote. "If our findings are confirmed in other cohorts and by other study designs, promoting healthy dietary habits could be a potential strategy for IBD prevention."

As to what explains the associations between fruit intake and reduced CD risk, the authors noted that the "dietary fiber content of fruit may partly contribute to the observed inverse association between fruit intake and CD risk by promoting a favorable gut microbial environment."

Conversely, they suggested that the association with an increased risk of UC "could potentially be explained by differences in the etiology between the subtypes, since CD has been suggested to be more related to dysbiosis and UC to mucosal immune dysregulation."

As for the link between higher intake of salty snacks and an increased risk of IBD, they pointed out that the salty snack food group across the three cohorts was mostly composed of items high in saturated fats, and saturated fatty acids "have been shown to promote proinflammatory immune responses."

For this study, Guo and colleagues pooled data from three prospective population-based birth cohorts in Norway, Denmark, and Sweden encompassing 111,999 participants born in 1996 through 2009, contributing a total of 1,541,247 person-years of follow-up.

Information on dietary intake in childhood (7-8 years) and adolescence (11-15 years) was obtained from food frequency questionnaires, and included intake of fruit, vegetables, dairy products, meat, fish, sugar-sweetened drinks, and sweet snacks. Questions on dietary intake of salty snacks, such as potato chips and popcorn, were only asked during the teen years.

Diagnoses of any IBD were captured in national patient registries by 2024.

During the observation period, 653 incident cases of IBD were identified, with country-specific incidence rates of 45, 39, and 62 per 100,000 person-years in Norway, Denmark, and Sweden, respectively.

Following dietary assessment in childhood, the median ages at diagnosis were 15.6 years, 18.3 years, and 25.7 years in Norway, Denmark, and Sweden, respectively.

While the authors observed associations between fruit, fish, and salty snack intake and IBD risk, there were no associations with other food groups such as vegetables and meats.

Guo and colleagues acknowledged that their study had limitations, particularly since it was observational, and thus unmeasured and residual confounding could not be excluded.

I want to know what new car you'd buy with a 40% off Black Friday deal. Yes, I know some automakers will run promotional events on Black Friday and through the holiday season, but the deals never come close to a 40% off doorbuster. That's why today we're daring to dream, daring to imagine, daring to bask in the light of American consumerism and the hunt for a good deal.

For me, the choice is a simple one. If I can have any new car for 40% off its MSRP, I'm heading to my local Acura dealership, waking up the salesperson and leaving with a new Integra Type S. #5590. Seabed Mining Has a Refinery Problem Worth Billions

The Metals Company wants to recover polymetallic nodules from the seabed and sell the nickel, copper, cobalt and manganese they contain. That business needs an industrial processing system before its revenue projections become sales. TMC’s November 2026 update exposed the timing problem. Its proposed refinery complex in Brownsville, Texas, may not be operating when offshore collection begins. An established Japanese smelter operated by Pacific Metals, or PAMCO, is the prospective initial route, but it needs modifications to accept commercial volumes of nodules.

That gap belongs in the mining economics. TMC’s 2025 prefeasibility study allocated $4.426 billion to two proposed US hydrometallurgical refineries, about 89% of the study’s $4.971 billion of initial project capital. The denominator has a particular financing structure: the offshore amount covers the first collection system after an Allseas capital credit, while later systems are to be supplied through contracts and paid for through operating costs. The newer Brownsville proposal also has a different industrial scope. The 2025 figure shows the size of the processing business TMC’s economics must support, not a completed financing commitment for Brownsville.

Offshore collection gets the attention. Refineries decide what saleable material a collection system produces and who captures its value. A nodule delivered to port is a complex mineral feedstock, not a sale of four finished metals. One processing route smelts nodules into a nickel-copper-cobalt alloy and manganese silicate, converts the alloy into matte and refines the matte into marketable metals or chemicals. The manganese product needs customers or additional treatment. Each step consumes capital, energy, reagents, skilled labor and working capital.

TMC has a meaningful metallurgical program. Its third-quarter 2026 SEC filing describes earlier North American tests of about 70 tons of nodules and a 2,000-ton industrial demonstration at PAMCO’s Hachinohe facility. Further work at SGS in Canada tested the refining of intermediate material into battery-grade products. PAMCO has completed feasibility work on treating roughly 1.3 million wet tons per year through a modified existing facility. That is a stronger starting point than a conceptual processing flowsheet.

The November 12 corporate update nevertheless put the industrial dependency in plain view. TMC’s preferred Brownsville facility will be difficult to complete before the first commercial nodules arrive, and the Japanese facility requires modifications and aligned schedules. Korea Zinc, Glencore, Hatch, Mariana Minerals and other partners provide useful expertise and commercial relationships. Those relationships still leave the construction, commissioning, financing and refining arrangements to complete.

The value gap matters as much as the capital bill. In our 2025 seabed mining techno-economic assessment, metallurgist Lyle Trytten and I calculated a $553-per-ton contained-component reference value for representative Clarion-Clipperton Zone nodules at fixed historical metal prices. Using estimated purchase terms informed by analogous mineral markets, the same assessment gave a modeled raw-feed value of $188–256 per ton, or about 34–46% of that contained reference value.

The gap pays for real industrial work. Processors bear metal recovery losses, treatment costs, plant capital, financing, product quality and operating risk, and they need a return. The values are estimates on a common reference basis, not bids from refineries or the profit a processor would pocket. Commercial nodule tonnage is often reported wet; TMC’s study assumes 28% moisture. Feed-price comparisons with wet-ton mine costs require the same mass basis.

The mining company has three main choices. It can sell the raw nodules at a price a processor can afford. It can keep title to the material and pay a plant to process it, provided the contract sets capacity, treatment charges, recoveries and risk allocation. Or it can finance and operate refining facilities and pursue a larger portion of the finished-metal revenue. None transfers the work, capital and risk out of the industrial system.

TMC’s own operating estimates reinforce that point. The 2025 study projected $13.622 billion of lifetime processing costs and $3.254 billion of refining costs, together about $103 per wet ton, or 42% of its modeled operating expenditure. Those costs sit alongside the proposed refinery capital. The production system may be offshore, but the economic center of gravity reaches well into the onshore industrial chain.

Impossible Metals has a different, less developed processing position. Its published strategy begins with outsourcing to modified plants in allied countries and envisions dedicated facilities later. Its economic model used approximately $791 per ton of contained-metal value under its selected prices and grades, deducted a $230 processing charge, and arrived at roughly $560 per ton delivered to port. Those numbers use different input assumptions from our assessment and cannot be treated as a direct comparison with the $188–256 estimate. The commercial question is whether a processor would accept the feedstock and the risks on the terms in Impossible Metals’ model.

Existing nickel-processing projects offer warning enough. Ravensthorpe, Goro and Ambatovy had familiar metallurgical technologies yet encountered expensive commissioning and operational difficulties. An unusual feedstock, high-volume throughput, uncertain manganese outlets and synchronized offshore and onshore ramp-up add challenges for nodule ventures. Demonstrating that the chemistry works settles only one part of the investment case.

TMC has considerably more testing and more developed partners than Impossible Metals. That distinction matters. Neither has demonstrated a fully operating processing chain that delivers the required metals at its intended scale, recovery, capital cost and commercial terms. Government financing could change who carries part of the risk, but not what must be built or operated.

A seabed mining company cannot book finished-metal economics while making the refinery somebody else’s problem. Investors, taxpayers and prospective processing partners need to know who provides the billions in capital, who carries the ramp-up risk and how much of the metal value the collector retains after every participant has been paid.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing article follows the processing alternatives, TMC’s Japanese and US plans, Impossible Metals’ outsourcing assumptions, and the resulting revenue and investment gaps. It is the third article in a five-part seabed mining assessment.

#5589. CDC Director Draws Doubts From Employees and Ire From Legislators

— "She has a tough job, at a tough time, and a tough boss," one expert says

Three months into her tenure as head of the CDC, Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, is being investigated by House Democrats, facing a call to resign, and drawing ire from both within and outside the agency.

What's been happening at the nation's top public health agency has alarmed outside health professionals. It also has alienated staff, leaving morale as bad as ever, employees say.

Schwartz, 54, took the helm of the CDC at a very challenging time: the worst U.S. measles epidemic in more than three decades, a large dengue fever outbreak in Florida, and the fastest-growing overseas Ebola outbreak in history.

She reports to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who is a longtime critic of vaccines and federal public health policy and who played a role in decimating CDC staffing last year.

"She has a tough job, at a tough time, and a tough boss," said Noel Brewer, PhD, a public health professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

In an interview with the Associated Press on Tuesday, Schwartz defended her work, saying she's trying to restore trust in the CDC -- including by changing how measles-associated deaths are being reported. She said some of the criticisms are based on misperceptions and argued she is making progress on her goals.

"I do understand why people have concerns," Schwartz told the AP from her home in Naples, Florida. "Have I made mistakes? Certainly. But I'm here to work on the behalf of the American people."

Some experts say she has made the situation worse. And critics are seizing on the Pan American Health Organization's declaration last week that measles is continuously spreading here, marking the re-establishment of a public health threat that was eliminated in the last century.

"I have no confidence that she will do what it takes to course-correct at the CDC, and she should resign immediately," said Sen. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.).

When President Donald Trump nominated Schwartz to be the next CDC director in April, he called her "a STAR!" on social media.

She holds both medical and law degrees. She was chief medical officer for the U.S. Coast Guard, where she oversaw 41 clinics and 150 sick bays. She served as deputy surgeon general in the U.S. Public Health Service, helping to lead uniformed medical and health professionals posted at the CDC and government health agencies.

Many public health leaders were cautiously optimistic, noting the CDC badly needed steady leadership after enduring more than a year of turmoil and months of being led by interim directors.

Schwartz was the third Trump nominee for CDC director in less than 18 months. The first was a former Florida congressman whose nomination was pulled an hour before a Senate confirmation hearing. The second was Susan Monarez, PhD, who won Senate approval but then was ousted less than a month into the job when Trump administration officials said she was not aligned with the president's agenda.

Under Kennedy, the agency has seen around 30% of its staff leave, mostly through layoffs, resignations, and retirements.

At her nomination hearing, Schwartz pledged "radical transparency" to rebuild public trust in the agency, which she noted declined during the COVID-19 pandemic and which has eroded further under Kennedy.

"I will always stand on science and speak the truth, even in difficult moments," she testified.

Meanwhile, public misperceptions about vaccines have persisted. A recent Annenberg Public Policy Center survey found that about one in six Americans said they believed that "vaccines given to children for diseases like measles, mumps, and rubella cause autism" -- even though dozens of studies have determined there's no causal link. Roughly another one in five said they didn't know whether it was true.

Schwartz started at the Atlanta-based agency in mid-August. A week later, she held her first "all hands" staff meeting, during which she promised to advocate for the agency and said she wouldn't hesitate to disagree with Kennedy -- but only privately.

Some say that's when their optimism for Schwartz began to fade.

"I don't have a clear sense of what is important to her, what are her red lines," one CDC health scientist told the AP. "If we're talking about radical transparency," it is appropriate to know on what issues and what messaging she will not compromise, the scientist added. The employee spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution.

Asked about that assessment, Schwartz said: "I would never do anything unethical or illegal. ... That is a red line."

Despite that transparency pledge, CDC and HHS officials for months would not release Schwartz's salary -- even though it is public information. Schwartz is paid about $375,000 a year, CDC officials finally told the AP this week, above the typical range for previous CDC directors.

So far she also has been less visible than some predecessors. She has not held any news conferences, and has not used her bully pulpit to try to persuade more Americans to get vaccinations -- including for measles, the flu, and COVID-19.

Schwartz told the AP that, concerning measles, she doesn't believe a federal health official on TV will sway most of the unvaccinated.

But with the nation experiencing its worst measles epidemic in decades, many public health and medical leaders say Schwartz should be strongly urging Americans to get vaccinated.

"I hope to see her display independence from the vaccine rhetoric and challenges that have been part of this administration," said Wendy Armstrong, MD, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. "I don't think we have seen that yet."

Congressional Democrats Are Launching Investigations

Some Democratic legislators accuse Schwartz and Kennedy of downplaying measles.

Kennedy has challenged health officials' accounts of measles deaths. And the CDC has stopped quickly relaying state reports of measles deaths. It adopted a new policy requiring the review of death certificates, which has resulted in CDC counting only about half the measles-associated deaths that states are reporting.

Schwartz said that was her decision, and stemmed from her desire to have a uniform definition of what counts as a measles death.

Democrats on the House Energy & Commerce Committee have questioned why CDC changed the policy.

"As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of deaths that CDC reports," said Reps. Frank Pallone Jr. of New Jersey, Diana DeGette of Colorado, and Yvette Clarke of New York in a statement.

"We are expanding our investigation to examine the threats your actions pose to Americans' health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required," they added.

The statement followed a briefing at which Schwartz was supposed to answer congressional staffers' questions about the measles data. The committee leaders described Schwartz as unresponsive and, at times, misleading.

Schwartz argued that she was "fully transparent. And I am really concerned that they think there is more to the story. There isn't."

CDC Employees See Little Sign of Progress

The AP interviewed eight current CDC workers about Schwartz's tenure. They all spoke on condition of anonymity, saying they feared retribution for speaking frankly about what's going on within the agency.

Some said they never had high expectations. Others said they initially were hopeful but lost confidence, some of them blaming her handling of the measles death count. One said it's still too early to judge her.

Several said they had hoped for more improvements and stability. Announcements about leadership appointees coming, going, and changing titles have continued in a blur, the employees told the AP.

Some mentioned Caroline DeBerry, a former vice president at a conservative think tank and author of independently published novels including one titled "Esther: The Woman Who Didn't Know Her Place."

DeBerry got a job as acting director of communications, starting in August. Employees said she gained notoriety within the agency when all CDC website updates ground to a halt while awaiting her approval.

Asked about it, Schwartz said: "There was a bit of clunkiness that happened one day." She also said DeBerry is on "terminal leave" and her last day will be in December, but did not immediately offer additional detail.

None of the agency veterans interviewed by the AP said they have spoken with Schwartz. But some said they had seen her around the CDC campus accompanied by a group of security guards.

Security has been a sensitive topic at CDC, especially since an August 2025 shooting outside the entrance of CDC's main campus. A Georgia man who had blamed the COVID-19 vaccine for making him depressed and suicidal opened fire, killing a police officer and spraying bullets into 150 windows.

(The slain officer, David Rose, is widely held up as a hero by CDC employees, and some expressed irritation that Schwartz referred to him as "Officer Stone" during a recent health summit appearance.)

Tom Frieden, MD, MPH, who served as CDC director in the Obama administration, said he occasionally had an escort outside the CDC campus after he received death threats. But Schwartz moves with a large security team inside CDC, and agency staffers said they don't recall seeing that before.

"It feels like they're afraid of us," one health scientist said.

Schwartz acknowledged that early in her time at CDC, she walked the halls accompanied by about a half dozen guards at the recommendation of security leadership. The security details have been reduced to one plainclothes guard, she said.

Confusion Over the Publication of Scientific Reports

A directive about research publications shows just how far apart CDC staff feel from the political leadership.

Two CDC scientists told the AP that they were directed in a recent meeting to stop submitting their research to journals run by organizations that have sued Kennedy. The prohibition would cover Pediatrics, one of the most-cited journals for doctors who specialize in children's medical care, and Clinical Infectious Diseases, a highly regarded publication for doctors focused on germs.

The scientists said the directive was clearly stated but not written down in a memo or email.

HHS and CDC officials are adamant that neither Kennedy nor any other HHS or CDC official ever issued such a directive.

At the health summit, Schwartz acknowledged that CDC employees have lost trust in the political appointees who have been put in charge of the agency, "and I'm trying to earn that trust every day."

She talked about work going on to stabilize the agency's leadership and develop a "strategic hiring plan" for 2027.

CDC employees look around and see burned-out colleagues.

"I think everyone is just exhausted," one health scientist said. "There's just a sense that we can't go on like this anymore."
