#5588. 2020 Shelby GT500KR With 21,000 Miles Is Ready To Terrify With 900-HP Supercharged 5.2-Liter Predator V8

When we first drove the Mustang Shelby GT500KR back in 2020, we called it a preposterous 760-horsepower daily drivable monster. The funny thing is, this currently listed monster on Bring a Trailer has been modified to produce an even more preposterous 900 horsepower.

Shelby American produced a limited-run of factory-made special-edition GT500KRs as part of Shelby American's 60th-anniversary celebration. Those cars got a 60th-anniversary badge and were dubbed King of the Road. — hence the KR tacked on to the model name.

The GT500KR received a number of modifications to differentiate it from the standard GT500, including the supercharger and intercooler, upgraded adjustable springs and revised sway bars, and big Brembo brakes – specifically, six- and four-piston (front and rear, respectively) stoppers with ventilated rotors. Shelby offers the body kit and tuning to owners of 2020-22 GT500KRs for $54,495. But it was only open to 60 cars for the 2020 model year (a total of 225 over a three-year period), making this a very rare Mustang indeed.

We don't know what this GT500KR will cost when the gavel finally drops on this auction, but the original pricer was $127,895 for the direct-from-Shelby version. So the final price likely won't be cheap — especially for a Mustang.

Thinking about this another way, though, it's a deeply modified, 900-horsepower machine that can likely keep up with expensive supercars from the likes of Porsche or Ferrari. And Shelby American didn't just bolt on parts. They claim that they worked closely with Whipple to develop a 3.8-liter capacity supercharger with a larger throttle body, cold air intake, and a revised pulley system, as well as a multi-core intercooler. Shelby also made certain the car would pass emissions across the U.S.

Shelby American also worked directly with Ford on the carbon fiber hood – the side vents suck heat from the exhaust manifold to prevent heat soak from robbing the V8 of power. Forged 6061-T6 aluminum wheels were specifically developed for this version of the Shelby GT500KR, too, and buyers could get them in either brushed silver or gloss black. The black looks sweet, but I think this car would look equally special with silver rims. As befits a street racer, this Mustang gets Recaro front buckets in red-and-black leather, with grippy Alcantara side bolsters.

There aren't very many comps for the GT500KR, so setting expectations for the price is a bit tough. A few older models from the 1968 run have sold for well over $200,000, as have a few low-mileage versions of the most modern KR. A 592-mile example of the 2022 KR was bid recently to $153,000, but it didn't sell. Maybe the KR's sibling, the Code Red, could lend a bit of perspective.

In 2022, Shelby also brought back the twin-turbo Code Red with 1,300 horsepower and made just 30 examples. That car cost $209,995 when it was new, and it wasn't street legal, so you'd need a very big wallet and track access to enjoy it. To make that much power, Shelby swapped the supercharger for twin turbochargers. It also gave the car a unique, dual-fuel feed so it can run on racing octane as well as E85. A Code Red was also up for auction on Bring a Trailer recently, and it was bid up to $282,500 — but that didn't meet the seller's reserve.

You want a 2020 GT500KR with 900 horsepower to drive, though, not to be parked in a collection like that 226-mile Code Red most likely has been. And you can't street drive the Code Red. This car hits the sweet spot for insane power that's still usable, and no matter what price it goes for, this GT500KR should be driven. With 21,000 miles already on the clock, that's the sort of treatment it deserves.

#5587. Happy Thanksgiving From Guangzhou, Visiting XPENG

While many in the US are celebrating Thanksgiving, I am seeing some of the most advanced technology and most impressive EVs in the world. XPENG offered to bring me to see AI day and Auto Guangzhou. I am thankful for the opportunity. Expect to hear more in depth in the days to come.

After renewing my Chinese driving permit, I was able to drive the sporty P7 again and use NGP with VLA 2.0 to and from XPENG’s increasingly automated and clean factory. That is simply a great car to drive. Acceleration is smooth and powerful. Despite the motor torque, the chassis can more than handle it. It feels both connected and comfortable in a balance that can be hard to find in many cars. And it looks great, especially in the dark green of the test car. I wish I had time to take it to some twisty backroads. However, the intelligent driving system makes dense urban traffic far more tolerable. At the times when you don’t want to drive, NGP drives the car flawlessly. Over the past year I have seen the system evolve, and it now offers even greater perception, smoothness, and efficiency. It is something you must experience to fully appreciate.

I also had the opportunity to ride in the YoYo Robotaxi with my friend Dan Caesar. Compared to some other robotaxi systems, it is a definite step up in comfort. More like limo service than a traditional taxi. The driving is extremely smooth, as is the ride, even in the congested and unpredictable roads in China. It drives much better than a typical human or some of the competitors I sampled. With the seat reclined, massage on and excellent entertainment system playing music or movies, I didn’t want to leave. I could have used another lap. I’ll have more details soon.

The following day, I attended XPENG AI Day. Over the course of the multi-hour event and Q&A, the amount of technological progress I was exposed to was expansive. Not only did I get to hear in depth about all the technological developments at XPENG, but I also was able to ask the IRON humanoid robot a question. With roughly half of the company dedicated to R&D, the speed of progress is impressive.

During the presentation, I heard about major developments in intelligent driving, including innovations that increase efficiency and range. I also heard about milestones being accomplished in flying cars, which took off in a demonstration the next day. However, the humanoid robot walking in to demonstrate the progress ahead of mass production clearly attracted the most attention.

I would like to think that I have a better understanding of these topics than many people, given the experience I have had so far. But the new helping of ideas and concepts was too much for me to process. My brain feels completely stuffed. Like that extra helping of Thanksgiving dinner, it will take a little bit for me to digest everything I have seen. Keep an eye out for more in-depth reports.

However, information was not the only thing I was gorging myself on. The food is exceptionally good in Guangzhou. While I have had great food at restaurants here, my favorite food is at the XPENG headquarters cafeteria at Mom’s Kitchen. This program lets the parents of employees set up shop to sell food at the cafeteria. As many employees come from different parts of the country, the program gives  them a taste of home. I am not sure what the dishes that I was eating were called, but there is something simply better about a home cooked meal. It may not look fancy, but the flavors were amazing. In addition, the hotel had turkey available for dinner, so I didn’t miss out on food.

I also was able to explore some Fall foliage. However, the leaves do not change color here in Guangzhou. Flowers are in bloom year-round, giving it the nickname “Flower City.” As I had done the standard headquarters tour before, I was able to split off with Tanya of XPENG to explore the grounds. Next to the headquarters building is a park with running trails, a pond and a river running through it, including a small waterfall. Throughout the year, there are events in the park, including concerts.

What is particularly impressive in the park is that much of this was bare dirt from the construction of XPENG’s headquarters when I visited in last November. Over the past year, grass, plants and trees were planted. The river was cleaned up to be clean and clear, with people fishing in its waters. Something that I would not imagine doing in most urban rivers. The planting is still in progress, but the environmental restoration is already impressive. And it is a reminder of how important it is to balance industry with nature.

On days that are not too hot, employees will often take their lunches outside or even take out mats to take a nap on the lawn. As the trees grow in further, the shade will increase and improve the comfort further. The park is also open to the public, and you can often see children playing. I heard the most difficult part is that people wish they had more time to enjoy the park. But XPENG has been remarkably busy.

Tomorrow, is Black Friday. A day dedicated to buying stuff. However, I will be at Auto Guangzhou looking at a wide range of exciting vehicles that I can’t buy in the United States. Better cars that are better because they are EVs. Cutting edge technology, premium amenities, and impressive build quality at affordable prices. Vehicles that give you new perspective on what’s possible.

I was able to see clear progress in the industry from the show last November to the Beijing show in April. Although XPENG is launching their models globally, many other brands launch in their home market first. Seeing the speed, progress and competition is invigorating having come from a market that often feels like it is stalling, but it can also be a bit overwhelming. I feel lucky to have the opportunity to see it firsthand and hope I can give people a glimpse of what’s happening.

Overall, I feel thankful for the opportunities to see and experience the some of the most advanced clean technology in the world over the past year with CleanTechnica. I am especially thankful to XPENG for being so open about their technology and the underlying thinking. It has been enlightening to see how the progress is being made in China and how that progress is being brought to Europe. I thank the PR teams for taking such good care of me and answering my questions. I am also thankful to Jackery for showing me innovations in energy storage and solar that create solutions for customer needs in both the US and Europe. And I am also thankful for BMW showing me something to be hopeful about regarding EVs and manufacturing in the US.

I am also thankful for all the great people I have met. From technology leaders to media legends, I have consistently been impressed. I now often feel like I am visiting friends. Business travel can feel lonely, but I have rarely felt that this year.

I am thankful for our readers, who make this possible. I often feel like I am learning from their comments as much as they are learning from what I write.

And I am thankful for my wife for putting up with all my nerdy conversations and trips away from home. And I am thankful for my cats, who are always happy to see me. I’ll be home soon.

Larry lives in Queens, NY, with his wife and cats. He believes in Green Free Trade and the potential for the application of engineering talent to create solutions to the world’s most challenging problems.

#5586. Steel solar panel frames hit the mainstream

Steel is considered the backbone of the American economy, critical for both national and economic security. It’s also the backbone of solar power construction, found commonly in the racking and mounting structures tilting solar panels toward the sun. And now, after years of tests and trials, an Ohio factory is roll-forming steel for a solar product that could use a stronger backbone — the solar panel.

A factory worker places a section of steel solar panel frames on a pallet in Welser Profile’s plant in Valley City, Ohio. Credit: Nextpower

Roll-form steel company Welser Profile began manufacturing Nextpower’s NX CoreFrame steel panel frames earlier this year at its facility in Valley City, Ohio, just 30 miles outside Cleveland, and Solar Power World was invited to view production of its first major orders before adding another line fully dedicated to the solar component before the end of the year. Module frame company Origami Solar originally had the idea that swapping aluminum frames with steel would not only save the solar industry money and cut back on carbon emissions, it would also provide more physical support to bigger and heavier solar panels.

Welser, an Austrian company with origins dating back to the 1660s, is a leader in roll-form steel profiles typically only seen in aluminum extrusions and helped produce a steel frame that’s easy for panel manufacturers to assemble and contractors to handle.

“What’s special about Welser Profile is we pre-notch features in the material before it gets formed,” said Bill Johnson, North America CEO of Welser Profile. “Everything about the solar industry is about how do we make it more efficient, cheaper, faster, better? You do that by all these little details to add value farther up the stream that minimizes labor, install cost. Our hole patterns and other features allow operators to snap things together, not bolt or weld things. Everyone is looking at how to make this work in a Lego setup, not a high-intense labor workforce installing all these panels.”

Welser is helping bring the Origami Solar idea to life, but the new owner of the tech, Nextpower, is delivering steel frames to the masses. Nextpower, a steel expert through its experience in producing tracking and mounting systems, acquired Origami in 2025 and will use its existing network of steel partners to convince more PV project developers to consider an alternative to aluminum.

“Nextpower has launched over 30 manufacturing facilities in the U.S. since 2020. Nextpower buys over 700,000 short tons of primary U.S. steel annually, which is more than a small car company,” said Jenya Meydbray, VP and general manager of Nextpower’s steel frames business. “Nextpower has had [the steel frame] for one year, building on the years of Origami’s engineering with Welser’s support. What we’re doing today is launching into high-scale, high-volume production here in Ohio.”

The solar industry defaulted to aluminum panel frames because the material is lightweight, easy to handle and less susceptible to corrosion. But as the solar industry matured, more environmental and practical issues became associated with the metal. Aluminum production on average has a five-times larger carbon footprint than steel production, a difficult point to ignore in the inherently green solar industry. Solar panels have also gotten larger in surface area and use less glass to cut weight. Aluminum might no longer be the ideal material to physically support these “big, floppy modules.”

A steel coil feeds into a roll-forming machine producing solar panel frames. Credit: Nextpower

“Steel provides a far better structural support for the [panel] than aluminum does. That was the initial observation that the Origami founders made,” Meydbray said. “They landed on this specific [roll-form] profile. Roll-forming is a precision process. We’re making millions of sticks of solar panel frames a month, and all of them have to be within sub-millimeter of precision across the full length. Welser is 100 years older than America, so Welser is definitely the most experienced in this art form of steel roll-forming.”

Welser set up North American operations in 2018 after acquiring an automotive roll-form operation in Valley City. The company established a second location in the same industrial park to accommodate its growing client base in the solar, storage and energy industries.

Welser was one of the first roll-form partners to validate Magnelis — a zinc magnesium coating that has “self-healing” properties is capable of lasting 25 years in the field — and found it a great steel coating for solar energy applications. It’s one of the features of NX CoreFrame, Nextpower’s steel solar module frame.

“Coming up with a new coating on steel, you don’t just throw it on the steel and sell it to the market. You have to trial it, validate it, make sure it works,” Johnson said. “Raw zinc — the coating has to be too thick for the longevity that the solar industry needs. Magnelis can go much lighter coating and still produce the same salt spray, same longevity, and it’s cheaper, faster, smarter.”

Wesler is the latest high-volume production facility for NX CoreFrame, and Nextpower plans to reach 6.5 GW of annual production through additional manufacturing partners across the country.

With an established steel frame design, the product just needs to find a place on panel manufacturer’s production lines. Origami Solar had been signing supply agreements with U.S. panel assemblers, an activity that has only increased with the Nextpower transition. Meydbray said the pitch for a domestic supply chain has become more attractive, especially with Nextpower’s established regional steel manufacturing network.

A machine treats steel coil as it travels along a factory line. Credit: Nextpower

“Steel strengthens the supply chain of domestic manufacturing facilities. When frames are bought overseas, they spend five, six weeks on the water before they actually arrive to the factory. [Panel companies] have about 2,000 pallets of frames in inventory when they source from overseas,” he said. “We’re able to provide actual just-in-time delivery to our factory clients. We can make deliveries every 48 hours. [They can save room] where they used to have pallets stacked up. There’s also the working capital of having stuff sit on the water for six weeks. Solar panel manufacturing is not a high-margin business, and working capital management is critical.”

Nextpower has inked supply agreements with many multi-gigawatt panel manufacturers in the United States, including Jinko, T1 and Thornova.

“This integration of Nextpower steel frames allows us to deliver high-performance modules tailored to the evolving U.S. market,” said Andrea Bodenhagen, global marketing director at Thornova Solar, which is establishing domestic solar cell manufacturing in Oklahoma. “By incorporating U.S.-made steel frames, we strengthen supply chain resilience while helping our customers maximize domestic content and improve project economics.”

With bonus incentives from the investment tax credit still in play when solar projects use domestic products, an American-made steel frame can make all the difference.

“When we see projects that have 100% domestic content on the tracker, we know that’s a perfect candidate for steel frames,” Meydbray said. “Steel frames get 6% domestic content credit. It’s the second cheapest percent after the tracker. A domestically made solar cell is a lot more expensive than an imported solar cell. The frame is the second-most cost-effective way to buy percentage points.”

The NX CoreFrame is universal and can be used with any brand’s mounting or tracking system, but there are advantages when the project can be designed more cohesively through one supplier. Nextpower has spent the last year expanding beyond mounting systems, now offering inverter, electrical balance of system and panel products.

“[Nextpower] is ambitious, but it’s not arrogant. It prioritizes the customer relationships it’s built over the years. We spent time with our customers asking where their pain points are and expanded the business accordingly …  the company that makes the thing the solar panel is mounted to is the same company that makes the frame that’s being mounted,” Meydbray said.

Kelly Pickerel was a long-time reporter with Solar Power World before leaving her post as editor in chief in 2026. You may find her on LinkedIn.

#5585. As GLP-1 Use Grows, Patients and Doctors Rethink Thanksgiving Dinner

— Navigating the holiday while taking weight-loss drugs

For many people, Thanksgiving can feel like a competitive eating event. But for Kim Dillard Davis, one of millions of American adults who take prescribed GLP-1 receptor agonists, it is a day like any other.

The 54-year-old Raleigh, North Carolina-based digital creator and wellness coach has lost around 80 pounds since 2023 using GLP-1 drugs. Thanksgiving on a GLP-1 means she doesn't participate in the part of the holiday associated with indulgence.

"I can't sit down and eat the amount of calories that I once could. I'll still be able to sample everything, but I just can't overdo it," said Dillard Davis, who said she plans to be on the drug for life so long as her insurance is covering it.

More and more Americans are using GLP-1 agonists, and as the medications become more popular, they could be changing some Americans' approach to food-centric holidays like Thanksgiving, altering how they eat, what they enjoy about food, and scrambling some social interactions surrounding food.

The jump in popularity comes as President Donald Trump's second administration has made expanding access to GLP-1 drugs part of its health policy, arguing that the drugs, if made more affordable, could help combat rising obesity rates and other related chronic illnesses, eventually lowering broader healthcare costs.

While GLP-1 drugs will likely cause major shifts in ways that are hard to predict, Ashley Gearhardt, PhD, a psychology professor at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, suggests the overindulgence associated with Thanksgiving could diminish over time.

"I anticipate that flavors and tastes that have been culturally linked with Thanksgiving will continue to be important. There just may be fewer turkey comas at the end of the day," she said.

Navigating the Holiday While Taking GLP-1 Agonists

Some people who use GLP-1 drugs feel full faster and stay full longer, meaning they tend to eat smaller portions. The drugs have been reported to change how people think about food, reducing cravings and emotional eating but also diminishing the sensory pleasure people get from food. Some users also avoid eating rich or heavy foods, because the drugs can cause nausea or bloating.

Doctors say people who are just starting their weight-loss journey this year with the drugs should be particularly mindful of potential side effects.

"Thanksgiving doesn't have to be off-limits," said John Horlander, MD, a gastroenterologist in Louisville, Kentucky. "The key is moderation, smaller portions, avoiding excessive fatty foods, staying hydrated, and recognizing warning signs."

"A little prevention can go a long way toward keeping someone out of the emergency room over the holiday," he added.

The Trump administration has framed its steps toward increasing access to and bringing down costs for GLP-1 drugs as "a historic opportunity to reverse the obesity epidemic." More than 100 million American adults have obesity, according to the latest CDC data.

In 2025, Trump, a Republican, signed a deal with drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk to expand coverage and reduce prices for the popular weight-loss drugs tirzepatide (Zepbound) and semaglutide (Wegovy).

And coverage of the drugs for obesity was expanded to Medicare patients this year when the federal government began offering a selection of the brand-name medications to certain Medicare and Medicare Advantage beneficiaries for $50 a month through a new trial called Medicare GLP-1 Bridge. The program is scheduled to sunset after Dec. 31, 2027.

A June analysis by healthcare research nonprofit KFF found that 3.8 million Medicare beneficiaries could be eligible for the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, based on claims data from 2023. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services does not provide projections of how many people will start taking GLP-1 agonists as a result of the Trump administration's actions. The agency wants to expand access to these treatments, said a spokesperson, who was not authorized to speak publicly and talked to the Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.

Those policy changes come as the share of people on GLP-1 medications for weight loss has risen in the past few years -- 11% of U.S. adults said they currently take the drugs for weight-loss purposes, according to a Gallup poll conducted in May and June. The poll found that 15% of Americans report having used the medicine for weight loss, an increase of 9 percentage points from 2 years ago.

That means Americans, even if they aren't taking the drugs, could find more people on the medication who are sitting across from them at the Thanksgiving table. That could change how people talk about eating.

Gearhardt said that dinner guests should be mindful about not pushing loved ones to eat or commenting on appearances.

"We all have a tendency to kind of monitor and police each other's eating behavior," said Gearhardt, who studies food marketing and how addictive processes shape eating behaviors and mental health.

Commenting on how little or how much someone is eating "usually isn't a great relationship strengthener," she said. GLP-1 users might be especially sensitive, she said, because Thanksgiving can evoke feelings of grief over losing the intense reward sensation of highly processed foods.

Dillard Davis advised family members not to ask, "Is that all you're going to eat?"

"Leave that phrase off the table. We've spent our whole lives overeating. Let us eat small portions and be happy," she said.

Babak Orandi, MD, PhD, an obesity medicine specialist at NYU Langone Health in New York City, said, "There's a social aspect of eating, especially around the holidays. We don't want to lose that."

Patients, Orandi said, should focus "a little bit less on weight loss and a little bit more on weight loss maintenance" during the holidays, so as to not lose the enjoyment of eating.

For Dillard Davis, Thanksgiving has changed in other ways. Because of the reduced appetite brought on by the medication and to avoid large quantities of leftovers at home, her family has spent the last 4 years celebrating Thanksgiving at restaurants.

But as someone who has been on a weight-loss journey since she was 8 years old, she has learned to accept the changes.

"We still have to eat," she said. "Just don't worry about it so much."

#5584. 1998 Family Sedans Get Pushed To Their Limits On Track In The Latest 'Best Motoring' Episode

We've been raving about the ridiculously entertaining on-track comparison tests performed by the Japanese video series Best Motoring for over a decade now, but I stumbled into a gaping rabbit hole over the weekend and binged as many episodes as possible, so it's fresh on my mind. If you're unfamiliar with the work of Best Motoring, it was a Japanese car magazine and video series that ran for 24 years between 1987 and 2011, most famous for its hardcore on-track comparison tests. These tests put professional racing drivers into a lineup of several different competing road cars and set them on a five-lap battle, consistently coming within millimeters of disaster while pushing the limits in cars that often would never otherwise be used on a track.

It's always great fun to watch, and the latest upload is no exception. It pits six 1998 midsize sporty family sedans against each other: the JDM Honda Accord SiR, Nissan Primera Camino Te-V, Mazda Capella Zi-R, Volkswagen Passat 1.8T, Audi A6 2.8 Quattro, and Mercedes-Benz E320. None of these cars are the first names that come to mind when it comes to track day heroes, but that doesn't stop the Best Motoring team from driving the snot out of them.

The domestic Japanese cars included in this test didn't directly compete with the Mercedes E-Class and Audi A6, but they were included as performance benchmarks. The JDM Honda Accord SiR only had a 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine with VTEC, and it sent its 177 horsepower to the front wheels through a five-speed automatic transmission.

The JDM Nissan Primera actually made its way to the United States in the form of the Infiniti G20, and it also only packed a naturally aspirated 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine that sent about 140 horsepower to the front wheels through a CVT automatic. The Mazda Capella also made its way to the United States in the form of the Mazda 626, and in this test the former is fitted with a 168 horsepower 2.0-liter four-cylinder that sends power to the front wheels through a four-speed automatic.

As far as imports go, the Passat competed closely with the JDM cars, but the A6 and E-Class were from a class above. I don't want to spoil the results, though, so you'll have to watch and see for yourself how things shake out. If you're looking for a way to fill your long weekend, the Best Motoring official YouTube channel has over 830 videos to binge, with new uploads on a pretty regular basis.

#5583. Celebrating Cultures And Equity On Thanksgiving Day

There is an important subtext to this Thanksgiving Day in the United States. A “blue tsunami” has occurred, so, come January, the Democratic party will control the House of Representatives and the Senate. While there are many important elements to this upheaval, one thread connects them all: Democrats can reimagine both how they govern and how they communicate.

Former White House communication director Dan Pfeiffer argues this is not only possible, it is necessary. The Democrats, he says, must “make sure voters know that we tried like hell and that Republicans are to blame for the lack of progress.” Part of a successful communication strategy would involve embracing others across the political aisle. And what better time is there than Thanksgiving Day and the long weekend that follows?

Thanksgiving has long been celebrated as a way to assimilate immigrants into our national melting pot. Why not use the US holiday as a jumping off point to acknowledge the various celebrations that draw upon commonality of white American traditions, like turkey and stuffing — but also invite individual expressions of food and traditions from the diaspora? If we all would be more open to new ideas and their origins, wouldn’t the next steps be to open up conversations and insights into sustainability and equity?

We use labels because there’s so much information in the world that we can’t process each piece of it individually. The tendency to resort to labels is part of the psychological shortcuts we take to make sense of the world. So we group things and people together, and we attach labels to them. Labels help us to limit our time and attention instead of analyzing small details.

Nonetheless, when we label a person, we simplify the way we represent them in our brains. Labeling can create misunderstandings and stereotypes. On this Thanksgiving Day, let’s consider how the labels we place easily and quickly on others diminish our potential for social awareness and awakenings. Instead of succumbing to labels, let’s give thanks for the vibrant palette of people and cultures that surround us. In doing so, we enrich our lives and, by extension, the lives of those around us.

In fact, disparate cultures with differing politics often find commonality when they sit down to eat. Food scholar and Williams College professor Darra Goldstein says, “Quite apart from sustaining us, food has the ability to unite us.” She spoke at gastronomical lectures hosted earlier this autumn at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

And there’s photographer Jeremy Dennis’s exhibition, “The Course of Liberty,” at a new alternative space in Salem, Massachusetts called Airtight Garage. The exhibition provides a corrective to years of simplified myth-making, and his staged photographic compositions feature Native Americans in traditional clothing and unexpected settings. It is as if they have broken through a time-space continuum.

Think back to the fabled tale of scraggly European Pilgrim outcasts arriving on the eastern Atlantic shore. As Florida columnist JC Bruce laughs, “If you were an indigenous person living on the North American continent in 1621 and a bunch of religious zealots showed up with pasty skin and ridiculous clothing, would you think they were any odder than beings from the stars?”

“The Course of Liberty” questions what happens when two people claim the same space. As Cate McQuaid describes in the Boston Globe, the artist points to ideas of inherited history and reconciliation as Native people attempt to recover Native land.

Yes, we may need a lot more communication breakthroughs and backdoor discussions of sustainability and equity in the lead up to the January shift of Congress. But it’s not the first time such a moment in time has occurred in the US.

In 1864 President Abraham Lincoln reflected on the civil war. He saw a nation now dedicated “to the cause of freedom and humanity, and to afford to us reasonable hopes of an ultimate and happy deliverance from all our dangers and afflictions.”

So let’s celebrate on this Thanksgiving Day 2026 the birthday of cartoonist Charles Shultz, who said, “The best theology is probably no theology; just love one another.” Let’s do our best to live up to his ideal; good things will surely result if we do.

Carolyn Fortuna, PhD, is a longtime journalist and researcher for CleanTechnica who frequently writes about climate science, renewable energy, and environmental communication. Since joining the publication in 2016, Fortuna has authored nearly 1,900 articles focusing on ecojustice, clean technology adoption, and the intersection of science and public policy. #5582. Antibiotic Paste Approved to Prevent Surgical Site Infections

— Bacfenssi becomes the first approved product for local application following colorectal surgery

The FDA approved doxycycline hyclate (Bacfenssi) to reduce the risk of surgical site infections (SSIs) in adults and kids undergoing colorectal surgery, the agency announced on Tuesday.

Sold as a powder to be reconstituted into an extended-release paste, the tetracycline product is indicated specifically for surgeries involving incisions larger than 20 cm, as efficacy for smaller incisions was not established in trials. Pediatric patients must weigh at least 45 kg, according to the agency.

It marks the first approved option for preventing SSIs that is applied locally, the FDA said. Before closing the incision, the paste is applied directly to the fascia and tissues of the abdominal wall along the incision.

Support for the approval came primarily from SHIELD II, a multinational double-blind phase III trial, which showed that adding the doxycycline hyclate paste to standard of care reduced the risk for SSIs, mortality, or surgical reintervention by 40% over the month after surgery. In the investigational arm, that composite outcome occurred in 10.9% of patients compared with 18.1% in the control arm (P=0.004).

When looking at SSIs specifically, a key secondary endpoint, the product reduced the risk by 60%, with infections recorded in 3.8% of the doxycycline hyclate arm and 9.5% of controls (P=0.001).

Commonly occurring following colorectal surgeries, SSIs "can lead to prolonged hospital stays, reoperation, and significant patient morbidity, including wound breakdown and systemic infection," the FDA noted. "Despite the administration of systemic antibacterial drugs prior to colorectal surgery to reduce SSIs, the infection rate remains substantial, underscoring the need for additional preventive strategies."

Adverse events observed in trials of doxycycline hyclate were mostly mild and included incision site reactions, procedural pain, anemia, and wound dehiscence.

Labeling for the antibiotic paste includes potential risks for tooth discoloration and inhibition of bone growth if used in pregnancy and in children, Clostridioides difficile infection, potential for microbial overgrowth, along with known class effects of tetracyclines -- photosensitivity, fixed drug eruption, pseudotumor cerebri, and anti-anabolic actions. Drug interactions are possible with concomitant use of anticoagulants.

Doxycycline hyclate can cause fetal harm, the FDA noted, and "breastfeeding is not recommended for 40 days after administration."

Launch of the product is expected in early 2027.

#5580. Over 70,000 km by Plane a Year: Travel Influencers Are Blowing Their Carbon Budgets and encouraging Europeans to Do the Same

Travel influencers have a disproportionate climate footprint, generating an average of 10.0t of CO₂e emissions each just from flights in 2025, according to a new report by T3 Transportation Think Tank, commissioned by T&E. This is 16.7 times higher than the average European’s four leisure round trips and around 0.6 t CO₂e per tourist each year across all modes of transport for the 95% of their trips taking place in the EU. This does not yet include the travel emissions of the people they influenced.

The study tracks 25 primarily European and US travel influencers representing millions of followers, and examines their role in the advertising strategy of airlines. Influencers took an average of 16 flights per year, visiting four times as many destinations as a standard European.

The study shows that influencers predominantly take long-haul flights (49%) over medium (24%) and short-haul (27%) journeys. Long-haul flying is the most polluting form of transport: an economy long-haul flight generates roughly three to four times more emissions than a short-haul flight.

In total, these influencers flew a total distance of 1.8 million kilometers in 2025, equivalent to approximately 45 trips around the globe. Individually, each influencer flew an average of 72,244 km, equivalent to 34 return holiday flights between Paris and Athens.

Travel influencers are frequent flyers, with a disproportionate climate footprint. They regularly post about luxury, comfort and aspirational destinations. Influencers play a significant role in shaping where people choose to travel, thereby driving demand for high polluting flying. Through travel influencers, frequent air travel is normalised and encouraged.

The study shows that European and Middle Eastern airlines are ranked among the top 30 carriers that advertise on social media and websites. These include easyJet, Emirates and KLM. Even though airlines are not currently obliged to disclose their advertising budgets, the analysis reveals that social media, including influencer marketing, likely accounts for the largest marketing expenditure, around one third, with the UK seeing the highest spend (€50.2 million).

The list is dominated by airlines headquartered in the respective country and those that hold the most slots at the major international airports in each country. For example Air France spends more on social media advertisements in France (€2 million) compared to Spain (€29,000). Other carriers spending a lot on social media are easyJet and Aer Lingus, spending almost €26 million and around €7 million respectively. EasyJet spends more than twice on social media and online advertising than the following airlines.

“Airlines have found a ridiculously cheap way of promoting climate intensive behaviour. They pay influencers to make very frequent and polluting long distance flights look normal and desirable. The average of 72,244 km shouldn’t be something to brag about… that would take an average European nearly 23 years to match” said Aiza Rodrigues Akhtar, T&E Aviation Campaigner. “The EU must enforce disclosure of airline-funded influencer promotions of harmful high-emission flights and enforce accountability of both parties.”

For airlines, partnering with travel influencers is remarkably cost-effective: it can cost just a few thousand euros¹ or just a free seat upgrade, yet it leads to significant results. Compared to traditional channels such as TV broadcasts or billboard displays, social media ads have a higher return on investment: posts that are liked, shared or reposted remain in the digital space for longer, significantly boosting visibility.

Yet, both influencers and airlines are not fully transparent when it comes to advertising. Influencers do not always clearly label their promotional content, and airlines do not publicly disclose how much they spend on digital advertising. Consumer organisations underline that any commercial promotion on social media should be clearly labelled so that consumers know what they are being marketed to and when. The EU Digital Fairness Act, currently under development, is key to tackling misleading influencer marketing and closing transparency loopholes. As travel influencers promote high-emission flights, any paid promotions must be clearly labelled as such.

“Transparency is a first step, but it is not enough to prevent the damage caused by influencer ads for flying”, says Rémi ter Haar, legal campaigner at Fossil Free Advertising. “Calling for more truthful advertising in the aviation sector is like playing a game of ‘whack-a-mole’. We must get ahead in the game and ban their advertising, for the sake of the climate and public health. We cannot expect people to behave more sustainably, only to then manipulate them through advertising into doing exactly the opposite.”

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) recognises that regulating advertising is key to changing the behaviours needed to limit global warming to 1.5°C. Marketing portrays luxury goods as necessities, and the IPCC cites long-distance holiday ads as an example of how the industry creates and normalises carbon-intensive desires. While the EU Audiovisual Media Services Directive prohibits promotions that encourage behavior harmful to the environment, this rule is often interpreted too narrowly. Airline advertising, which promotes carbon-intensive behaviour, should be included in its definition.

¹ Influencers get paid between €269 to €2,692 for their travel content by airlines depending on the format: a 24-hour post (story), a static post or a short video (reel). Read more.

#5579. Why The Chrysler 440 Big Block Is One Of The Most Reliable V8s Of The Muscle Car Era

Big-block V8s like the Chrysler 440 helped make the classic American muscle car era a thing to remember. Back then, the adage "There's no replacement for displacement" was revered, and automakers continuously tried to outdo each other with larger and larger mills. Chrysler's 440 first hit the market in 1966, and by 1970, it was flanked by other big-block V8s like the Buick 455 and the Ford 429 — the largest engine offered by a Ford-badged passenger vehicle until 1973.

Chrysler's 440 was not only big and powerful, it wound up being extremely reliable. Much of the secret lies in its engine block, which used Chrysler's RB architecture. Mopar fans will know the RB block motors as "wedge" engines, owing to their use of wedge-shaped combustion chambers. The 440's block is known to handle a huge amount of extra power, with some owners on the For B Bodies Only forum claiming it will withstand horsepower outputs in excess of 700 when modified. That's 310 ponies more than the most powerful stock 440 engine could muster.

The Chrysler 440 gained its reliable and easy-to-own reputation during the classic muscle car era, thanks to attributes that also included simplicity. The 440's reach extended outside the scope of muscle cars, too, as it became one of Chrysler's jack-of-all-trades engines over the course of its existence. By the end of its life in 1978, Chrysler had built over 750,000 440s.

The Chrysler RB-block was an evolution of the existing B-block. The "R" found in its name stood for "Raised block," as Chrysler designed it with a deck height that stood 10.725 inches tall — 0.745 inches taller than B-block decks. Within the 440's block, Chrysler engineered a series of ribs that stiffened it, letting the block withstand more torsional stress. However, Chrysler only began doing this in 1968, meaning 440 blocks built prior are slightly more susceptible to cracking under heavy load.

As many DIY mechanics know, the simpler in design an engine is, the easier it generally is to repair. The same sentiment goes for the Chrysler 440, especially when compared to its contemporary, the 426 Hemi. The latter requires expensive Hemi-specific components for repair, and also needs its valvetrain adjusted at more frequent intervals than the 440. And the cost of overhauling a 440 is about half that of a 426 Hemi.

Another aspect to the Chrysler 440's reliability is its low torque range and low rev limit. It produces a huge amount of peak torque — up to 480 lb-ft of it —  at just 2,800 rpm, making setting off from a standstill particularly easy. It also has a low rev limit, with its redline typically set at just 5,000 rpm. This lets the engine spin more slowly, reducing strain on its rotating assembly.

At its peak in 1970, the 440 could produce 390 horsepower and 490 pound-feet of torque when equipped with the "Six-Pack" option — three two-barrel carburetors. That year, the 440 could then be found in Chrysler Corporation-bred muscle cars ranging from the Dodge Charger and Super Bee to the Plymouth GTX. It even saw use in foreign models such as the English Jensen Interceptor, and began finding its way into Dodge pickup trucks beginning in 1974. Chrysler even started supplying 440s to recreational-vehicle manufacturers like Winnebago around the same time.

The 440 was dropped from Chrysler's lineup in 1978, having spent the better part of 12 years on the market. Its cause of death was due to factors like changing emissions laws and Chrysler's use of its unreliable "Lean Burn" ignition technology in the 440. The poor state of Chrysler's finances at the time contributed, as well, forcing the company to make cuts to its lineup to focus more of its capital on small-car production.

However, the 440's fate was sealed several years prior. Spiking insurance costs at the turn of the '70s helped to kill powerful, big-block V8s. It simply became too expensive to insure a powerful car, and the classic muscle car era — along with the engines that helped power it — began to disappear. The first gas crisis of 1973 and the high fuel prices that resulted further hamstrung the big-block V8s as a whole.

#5578. High-Flying Influencers

This briefing is based on the T3 Transportation Think Tank study commissioned by T&E. This study examines the environmental footprint of travel influencers, and the role they and social media play in the advertising strategy of airlines. The first part analyses travel influencers’ associated emissions, travel frequencies and routes. The second part focuses on airline digital advertising investments in five European markets: France, Germany, Netherlands, Spain and the United Kingdom.

Travel influencers are digital opinion leaders that travel frequently and who shape the destination’s image, attitudes and behavioural intentions of their audiences through personal narratives. Most often, air travel is their main mode of transportation and they cover large distances by taking long-haul journeys. They post content all year-round, meaning they travel a lot and generate a substantial climate footprint. Through their posts, they display luxury, comfort and aspirational locations.

This constant posting of glamorised photogenic locations shapes their audiences’ destination preferences and can incite them to fly long-distance, fuelling air travel demand and contributing to overtourism and crowding of tourism hotspots. However, influencers are confronted with transparency issues: research suggests that too much sponsored content can undermine an influencer’s credibility, and at the same time identifies a lack of hashtags, used to explicitly disclose sponsored content (#ad or #sponsored), in such content.

Airlines’ advertisements promote carbon-intensive behaviours through frequent and long-distance flying. Although airlines don’t publicly disclose their digital advertising expenditure, social media forms one of the largest portions of their digital budgets. Social media is a powerful driver for travel inspiration, destination promotion and direct bookings. It exerts a high level of influence on consumer choices. Partnering with travel influencers offers airlines high returns on investment. Likes, shares and reposts ensure airlines secure continuous, long-term exposure and significant quantifiable marketing value.

Currently, regulatory standards specifically targeting influencer content and brand collaborations remain underdeveloped. There is also no regulation asking airlines to disclose their advertisement budget spend. In addition, the EU lacks a unified and robust regulatory framework that taxes, restricts or prohibits advertising for carbon-intensive advertisements, such as airline ads. Finally, aviation taxation and carbon pricing, needed to curb excessive emissions such as those from long-haul flights, are weak. To effectively fill these gaps, existing policy mechanisms as well as those currently being developed must be strengthened and expanded.

Travel influencers often disregard the significant carbon footprint of their long-distance trips, and encourage environmentally damaging lifestyles and excessive travel among their audiences. Airlines publicly commit to sustainability while actively funding social media campaigns and influencer promotions that encourage frequent, long-haul flying.

Together they drive carbon-intensive behaviours and air travel demand, which also contributes to overtourism. Regulatory measures need to be robust, strengthened and unified across the EU to enforce accountability of both parties:

#5577. Two Army Truck Plants In Iran Assembled Studebakers For Red Army Drivers To Take North

Imagine a situation where the United States is supplying Russia with military trucks. Now, imagine those same trucks being assembled in Iran. Using today's geopolitical climate as a basis, such a scenario sounds ridiculous. However, during World War II, that actually happened.

The brand behind the multicultural program was Studebaker — one of America's most popular marques during the early 20th century. Studebaker began shipping complete knockdown kits of its then-new US6 2½-ton 6×6 truck to the Persian Corridor supply route, and assembly took place at both the Andimeshk and Khorramshahr plants in Iran. Once the trucks were built, they were promptly driven north to the Soviet Union's Red Army for deployment among its forces.

The Soviets loved the American Studebaker, as it could handle just about everything the brutal Eastern Front could throw at it. The US6 carried an old-school ladder-frame chassis with enough room for troops, gear, and anything in between. All told, it's reported that tens of thousands of them were assembled at the two Iranian plants, and even Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin took notice of the US6's prowess on the battlefield.

Around 1939, the U.S. was interested in developing a new 6x6 truck that could handle virtually anything the military could throw at it. Studebaker was one of three automakers that sent design proposals to the Army Ordnance Corps, and its design was accepted. Production of the US6 began in 1941. Almost immediately, the United States saw an opportunity to help with the war effort in Europe prior to U.S. involvement, while also making some much-needed cash along the way, thanks to the Lend-Lease Act of 1941.

As part of the new law, Studebaker began shipping complete knockdown kits of its US6 to two Iranian-based assembly plants. Andimeshk became the first, with assembly commencing in March 1942. Assembly began in Khorrmshahr in January 1943. The U.S. Military then assumed control of both plants from General Motors in July 1943, but retained most of the local employees.

Once assembled, the finished US6 models would be given to the Red Army and driven north across the border between Iran and the Soviet Union to join the fight against the Germans. Soviet troops quickly took a liking to the trucks, and began to affectionately refer to them as "Studer", or "Студер" in Cyrillic.

The Soviets found a slew of alternate uses for the US6 besides serving as a troop or cargo transport vehicle. One of its most popular unconventional assignments was serving as a mobile platform for the Red Army's Katyusha rocket launchers. It was also given the task of towing heavy anti-tank weaponry. In fact, the US6 made such a positive impact on the Red Army's war efforts that Stalin personally penned a letter to Studebaker, thanking the brand for designing such a rugged military vehicle.

As one could imagine, earning the favor of Stalin himself wasn't an easy task, meaning the US6 had to be tough. The truck took advantage of a 5.2-liter Hercules JXD inline-6 engine featuring an L-Head design. It produced 86 horsepower, 200 pound-feet of torque, and could run on extremely low-quality gasoline — an important attribute for the often-ill-supplied Red Army. Underneath the truck sat a simple ladder-frame chassis using semi- and quarter-elliptical leaf springs.

All Studebaker US6 trucks came with three axles: one in the front and two in the rear. These 6x6 vehicles could be optioned with either six-wheel drive (all three axles receive engine power) or four-wheel drive (only the rear two axles receive power. Several variations of the US6 were made available to the Red Army as well, ranging from short and long-wheelbase models to tankers, semi tractors, and dump trucks. A version of the US6 called "U-3" was preferred by the Red Army's Katyusha rocket division, as its long wheelbase fit a launch platform.

After its military service, the Studebaker US6 was quickly discontinued, and the final model rolled off the assembly line in August 1945— the same month World War II ended. However, the Soviets had other plans. Seeing as the US6 was such an integral part of the Red Army's war efforts, Soviet automakers GAZ and ZIS designed their own trucks based on Studebaker's original design. The Soviets weren't kidding when they called the Studebaker US6 "King of Roads," and they made sure to continue its legacy in their own way.

#5576. Novel ADC Could Be New Option in Recurrent Ovarian Cancer

— A phase III trial will test sofetabart mipitecan in platinum-sensitive and -resistant disease

Promising data from a phase I study presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology congress suggested encouraging activity with the investigational antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) sofetabart mipitecan (Sofe-M) combined with bevacizumab in patients with recurrent platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Roisin O'Cearbhaill, MD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, discusses the early findings and how the three-part FRAmework-01 study could expand treatment options for patients with platinum-sensitive and platinum-resistant ovarian cancer.

Following is a transcript of her remarks:

It was a very exciting phase I study. It was looking at a folate-targeting antibody-drug conjugate, and they were looking at the platinum-sensitive population, patients whose cancer had recurred more than 6 months after prior platinum-based therapy. The majority of patients had measurable disease and they treated the patients with Sofe-M plus bevacizumab. So it was phenomenal to see the waterfall plots with such great response rates, objective response rates, in the vast majority of patients and disease control rates in 100% of the patients.

Not only the efficacy data, but also the toxicity data was very exciting in terms of the thing that we always worry about with antibody-drug conjugates or eye toxicity or pneumonitis. So it was great to see that those really weren't a concern with this novel ADC.

And so based on this and other clinical data, we're actually participating in a global phase III study. There are three different subprotocols in that.

In part A, we're looking at the platinum-resistant population, and that is going to be looking at standard-of-care, single-agent chemotherapy versus the Sofe-M. And then in the other two cohorts, they're for patients who have platinum-sensitive disease. In part B, patients have received a prior PARP inhibitor. And in part C, patients have not received a prior PARP inhibitor. In both part B and C, patients are randomized to the standard of care, which would be carboplatin plus another chemotherapy agent with bevacizumab. And then the investigational arm is looking at Sofe-M in combination with bevacizumab.

I hope that we'll have a new treatment option for our patients with recurrent platinum-resistant and platinum-sensitive disease. It would be really great if we could move away from empiric platinum-based chemotherapy and have other options to offer our patients in the platinum-sensitive setting. And for the platinum-resistant, it would be great to have yet another effective treatment option.

#5575. The European Parliament Brings the EU One Step Closer to a Sound Investment Policy

Being locked-in a race for technological leadership with China and the US, the EU lacks focus, coordination and financial firepower to transform its industry, ensure long-term prosperity while reaching its climate objectives.

This could soon change thanks to the forthcoming European Competitiveness Fund that will become active from 2028. Yesterday, the European Parliament cemented its support to a robust fund. Today, EU leaders meet and need to secure an adequate budget for the ECF to deliver.

Since the launch of the US Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, Europe has developed several strategies, masterplans and policy initiatives to build a compelling industrial policy. Still, they largely failed to deliver on focus, coordination and financial firepower.

With the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF), the Commission proposed a new instrument to support Europe’s industry and deliver on its Clean Industrial Deal. Yesterday, the European Parliament voted on rules that would make the proposal even stronger.

MEPs raised the ECF’s overall budget by €30 billion to €264 billion. Crucially, they boosted the envelope for clean energy and industrial decarbonisation to €40 billion, with €4 billion earmarked specifically for clean-tech manufacturing.

MEPs backed a budget of €40 billion for InvestEU, including €15 billion specifically for clean energy and industrial decarbonisation. Through budgetary guarantees, debt and equity, InvestEU aims to collect private capital for higher-risk domestic manufacturing projects that would otherwise fail to reach a final investment decision. This extra €29 billion in additional guarantees compared to the Commission’s proposal could unlock over €300 billion in total mobilised investment.

The Parliament also earmarks €10 billion for the Critical Raw Materials Centre (CRM Centre). The Centre is poised to secure resilient and sustainable critical raw material supply chains for Europe by investing in strategic projects. Securing budgetary resources via the ECF is a crucial step for success.

Over the years, the EU has developed a broad range of funding instruments, but they still largely focus on supporting research and developments. Yet, every year the EU falls further behind China in terms of manufacturing of key technologies, such as batteries. This is because the existing funding programmes neglect the critical and capital intensive scale-up period. Many new market entrants do not survive due to technological risk, insufficient access to risk capital and foreign competition.

Europe does spend substantial money to support industry, both via European funds and at the national level under slow-moving state aid schemes. However, many of the support schemes are spread out widely across technologies without enough focus and clear priorities.

This makes sense for funding early research to steer innovation. For scaling this is different. Today, we know which technologies we need to produce in the next 5 to 10 years to cut emissions and retain leadership, starting with clean transport: the battery value chain, zero-emission vehicles, clean aviation and maritime technologies and e-fuels.

To deliver on the green transition, European funding must be decisively redirected toward the development of strategic clean industries and essential technology value chains. T&E estimates that manufacturing of clean transport technologies alone requires at least €39 billion public funding per year by 2030. Broader decarbonisation needs — industrial heat, buildings, and cleantech deployment — require significantly more.

European cleantech innovators too often stall in the “valley of death” between R&D and commercial production. The Parliament’s text tackles this directly by mandating “ramp up” support for projects that strengthen critical value chains and reduce foreign dependencies — backed by a dedicated €4 billion envelope for clean technologies like battery cell manufacturing. Finally, the EU will be able to deploy production aid — a model that has proven impactful in other jurisdictions like the US.

The Parliament has set out a far bolder industrial vision than EU governments who so far largely stuck to the Commission’s narrower draft.

One immediate test will decide whether the ECF will make a difference in the future. EU heads of states and governments who meet today for a special summit must reverse the heavy cuts inflicted on the ECF in recent Council negotiating drafts. They should listen to more than 75 businesses that also highlighted the importance of a well-resourced European Competitiveness Fund in the next EU budget.

Designing a smart new industrial investment tool means little if leaders starve it of cash. They must back a Competitiveness Fund with the budget to match its ambition.

Article from T&E. By Till Eichler, Public Investment Policy Manager, T&E and Nina Betz, Public Investment Policy Intern, T&E.

#5574. How Many Nuclear Submarines Does The US Navy Have (And Where Are They Built)?

At first, submarines employed propulsion systems that relied on fuels like compressed air, steam, and even human labor. Now, roughly 400 years after the first working submarine prototype was tested, modern ones are much more sophisticated, and have even inspired atomic-age concept cars. They've come a long way from their roots, although the basic principle has always remained the same: Sneak up on your target and execute the mission.

The U.S. Navy boasts the world's most high-tech submarine force in the world, largely because it employs an entirely nuclear fleet consisting of 65 active subs. The Navy is planning to build more, too, with another 14 nuclear subs in the works as part of a $77-billion contract signed this year. There are two companies currently involved in building nuclear subs for the U.S. Navy — General Dynamics' Electric Boat division (EB) based in Groton, Connecticut, and Huntington Ingalls Industries' Newport News Shipbuilding division (HII) based in Newport News, Virginia. Both EB and HII work for the Navy under contract, and both are involved in different aspects of each submarine constructed.

However, while EB and HII are based in Groton and Newport News respectively, both have other locations where other portions of the actual sub-building process takes place. For example, EB does engineering in New London, Connecticut and hull fabrication and outfitting at Quonset Point, Rhode Island on a retired naval base where the Quonset hut originated. HII houses most of its production at its Newport News location, but also has a location in Goose Creek, South Carolina primarily responsible for metal fabrication.

Nuclear subs have been around since the early 1950s, as the first to grace the world's oceans was the USS Nautilus, commissioned on September 30, 1954 and built by EB. Alongside the USS Nautilus, EB has pioneered a huge swath of submarine innovations, such as building the Navy's first welded-hull submarine and the first strategic-deterrent sub. EB has been involved in designing 15 nuclear sub classes since the USS Nautilus was first penned, and is currently responsible for the Virginia-class sub — a replacement for the Ohio-class vessel. EB is currently working on the Virginia payload module as well, which gives existing Virginia-class subs more firepower, as well as cargo capacity.

HII's prowess in the submarine field is no less impressive: The company has built over 60 of them. Today, it's involved in the construction of the Virginia-class submarines alongside EB, of which it's helped deliver a total of 26. It's also working with EB on the upcoming Columbia-class nuclear sub,  tentatively set to hit the seas sometime in 2028.

While EB and HII are the only two companies building nuclear subs for the Navy today, this wasn't always the case. Historically, five other shipbuilders have done so alongside the current two. These included Navy-owned shipyards in Kittery, Maine, and in Mare Island, California. Privately owned yards also took part, including the Fore River Shipbuilding Co. in Quincy, Massachusetts, the New York Shipbuilding Corp. in Camden, New Jersey, and the Ingalls Shipbuilding Corp. in Pascagoula, Mississippi — now part of HII.

The introduction of the nuclear submarine in 1954 was a major step forward in the world of naval warfare. For example, World War II-era diesel-electric submarines typically had to surface every few days. However, the USS Nautilus could stay submerged much longer, 14 days or more. Range was greatly increased, too, as the Nautilus managed to travel over 60,000 nautical miles by early 1957 on a single reactor core. Its third and final core lasted even longer, providing 150,000 nautical miles of naval patrol before entering retirement. For context, the WWII-era diesel-electric sub USS Balao could only travel about 11,000 nautical miles before needing to return for fuel.

The benefits extended outside the scope of range, too. Beginning in 1960 with the deployment of the USS George Washington nuclear sub, U.S. nuclear submarines gained the ability to launch intercontinental ballistic missiles while submerged. Speed is also on a nuclear sub's side, as many regularly cruise at roughly 20 knots while submerged, while modern diesel-electric subs only manage about 8 knots while cruising on battery power.

The nuclear submarine gave the United States Navy a large advantage across the seas over seven decades ago, and while seven companies once worked to build them, only EB and HII remain active in the endeavor. The Navy's current 65-strong fleet also enjoys some serious job security, as certain members of the fast-incoming Columbia-Class are expected to serve roughly into the 2080s.

#5573. New Biologics May Be Able to Change the Course of Sjogren's Disease

— Experts discuss promising dazodalibep and ianalumab data presented at ACR

In this exclusive roundtable video from MedPage Today, three rheumatology experts discuss promising new treatments for Sjögren's disease, highlighting emerging data presented at the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) annual meeting.

Moderator Hanna Zembrzuska, MD, of the University of Iowa in Iowa City, is joined by Nancy Carteron, MD, of the University of California Berkeley, and Thomas Grader-Beck, MD, of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. In this first of four episodes, they examine phase III OASIZ-301 results for dazodalibep and long-term NEPTUNUS extension findings for ianalumab, including whether improvements in salivary flow could signal the potential to preserve salivary gland function.

Following is a transcript of their remarks:

Zembrzuska: Hello, and welcome to MedPage Today Roundtable on the most recent American College of Rheumatology meeting. My name is Hanna Zembrzuska. I'm an adult rheumatologist in Iowa City, Iowa, and I'm joined by some colleagues here who I will have them introduce themselves. Go ahead.

Grader-Beck: Hi, my name is Thomas Grader-Beck. I'm an associate professor at Johns Hopkins Rheumatology. I'm a member of the interdisciplinary Sjögren's center and I'm very excited to be here.

Carteron: Hi, I'm Nancy Carteron. I'm a professor at University of California at Berkeley and UCSF [University of California San Francisco], and I'm based at a Sjögren's center in Berkeley, and I'm happy to be here.

Zembrzuska: Yeah, I'm so happy to be here with Dr. Carteron and Dr. Grader-Beck, and we are going to do a virtual roundtable covering Sjögren's news from the most recent ACR meeting.

This is the most promising era in the history of Sjögren's disease research. For decades, care was limited to managing symptoms like eye drops and saliva substitutes with zero FDA-approved targeted therapies. But over the past year, multiple late-stage clinical trials have succeeded, bringing the first disease-modifying drugs to the brink of approval. So very exciting.

At the recent American College of Rheumatology annual meeting, there was a late-breaking oral abstract session that discussed dazodalibep, which is a CD40 ligand antagonist, and the results from its phase III OASIZ-301 trial. What were your main takeaways from this trial?

Carteron: I'll jump in. I think seeing yet another product meet the endpoints in Sjögren's historically was terrific. I think the fact that it also targets an additional pathway in the disease pathogenesis is promising.

Grader-Beck: I will say one other thing, maybe. I think the side effect profile overall was good. There was a little bit of a signal of hypertension and there wasn't much additional information about that, but maybe that's something to just keep in the back of the mind to see if that is something to really be concerned about. But otherwise, I thought it looked great.

Carteron: I would also add that in their study, they included a pretty significant number of patients that also had another coexistent autoimmune disease. So both lupus and rheumatoid arthritis plus Sjögren's patients were allowed in the study. And I think it was maybe even up to 20%.

I don't think there was any data presented separating that out, but I think that will begin to give us a little more information about real-world use of this particular kind of product. And I think the other point really is it's not a monoclonal antibody, so it's a different technology of inhibition. So it's actually a fusion protein that's very targeted.

But to get to Thomas's point about safety profile, it really does look like the newer technologies have figured out a workaround against some of the thrombotic effects that we saw early on when that particular pathway was inhibited. But intriguing the point that he's making about the hypertension, so stay vigilant.

Zembrzuska: So at ACR, long-term results from the NEPTUNUS extension study for ianalumab were also presented. This study had high retention rates and it reported data on stimulated salivary flow with improvements maintained through week 96. What does this mean exactly? Does this mean that sustained stimulated salivary flow indicates gland preservation or is that too strong of a statement? What do we think this means?

Grader-Beck: Yeah, I mean, it's very, very interesting and it's exciting to see that we see a consistent longer-term signal. So in the extension study, of course, everyone is on the drug and then you have some patients from placebo switching over to drug and you can start to see similar effects in the placebo group in terms of improvement of disease activity. And then also there was a little bit of a signal of the salivary flow.

I think it's too early, it's too early to say. We really need some more dedicated studies to tease that out. But if you look at the more mechanistic studies -- and there was data also presented at ACR this year, and last year actually too -- where you measure, for example, the vascularity in the glands before and after treatment. And you can clearly see a decrease of inflammation if you measure it by vascularity, you can see improvement of infiltrates, you can see actually improvement of salivary flow, but those were not placebo controlled. These are mechanistic studies.

So certainly that all points towards a possible effect. And the way it looks like, it would be patients that are actually earlier in the disease course that have more residual saliva may be the ones that may benefit more.

Carteron: I think we have data showing a decrease in glandular infiltrates of lymphocytes, but predominantly B cells, with deep B-cell depletion from a number of different products looking at it when they have. And so I think the overwhelming evidence is that there can be improvement, and I think even a small amount of improvement in salivary function may translate into a significantly meaningful outcome for patients. Whether it then translates into decreased dental damage or other things, clearly we need more.

But I think that for quality of life, not even well established, but even early on for patients, I find it particularly exciting. And also anecdotally for patients that were within the study that elected to continue and go into the long-term extension study because of a number of factors, but one of them also was increased oral comfort.

#5572. Graph of the Day: The World Now Makes 7 Solar Panels for Every TV

In 2015, the world made six solar panels a second. In 2026, it’s on track to make ten times as many.

At an Australian clean-energy conference in 2015 hosted by Renew Economy Disruption and the Energy Industry conference, I posed a simple test for the solar boom. If the world was still making more panels that consumed electricity — TVs — than panels that generated it, I reckoned we hadn’t quite seen the real boom yet.

On the updated chart (Figure 1), solar overtook televisions in 2016.

By May 2018, when I spoke at Power Philippines in Manila, the crossover had become a line in journalist Lala Rimando’s live coverage of my talk: more solar panels were now being made than TV sets.

We are now making more solar panels than TV sets. Check out this slide by @ProfRayWills .#powerph18#solarph18https://t.co/UGjfZke4IM pic.twitter.com/Kkf6R41RHx

— Lala Rimando (@lalarimando) May 23, 2018

Passing televisions was an important milestone, but it’s really the least interesting part of the story.

In 2021, the world made an estimated 360 million solar panels. A year later, it made about 790 million. By 2025, annual production had reached about 1.4 billion panels, against just over 200 million televisions. The gap opened not because the world stopped making TVs, but because it started making solar panels on a much bigger scale.

Put another way, the world went from making about six solar panels a second in 2015 to about 45 in 2025, averaged across every second of the year. My full-year estimate for 2026 puts the rate at about 62 panels a second — nearly two billion panels in a year (Figure 2).

And the panel count tells only part of the story. The average module rating I used to estimate those counts rose from 150 watts in 2008 to 475 watts in 2025. At that 2025 rating, 1.4 billion panels represent roughly 665 gigawatts of rated generating capacity coming out of factories in a single year.

Televisions offered me a familiar yardstick for what mass production for a consumer market looked like. A decade later, the question isn’t whether solar can match that scale. It’s how quickly we can put all those panels to work. After all, it is the fastest shift in energy in human history.

Ray Willis is a Perth-based energy futurist and director of Future Smart Strategies, and Adjunct Professor at The University of Western Australia, who writes on renewables, electrification, and the energy transition.
