#5571. 2026 Land Rover Defender Octa Would Be Better With A Worse Engine

The Land Rover Defender has been on sale for more than half a decade now, and it has remained mostly unchanged since its introduction. Except for in 2024 when the British automaker brought out the hardcore Defender Octa, a desert-destroying high-speed off-roader based on the four-door 110 model with an absolute thumper of a V8 under the hood. When the Octa and its BMW-derived V8 hit the scene, we knew that time was likely up for the regular Defender 110 V8's supercharged 5.0-liter AJ V8, and even though it took a few years, Land Rover officially killed the motor over the summer.

In just about every way, the Octa is a better vehicle than the old 110 V8. It has tougher looks, a beefier suspension, bigger tires and, crucially that new V8 under the hood. The BMW twin-turbo engine is more powerful and more efficient than the old supercharged Jaguar AJ133S, but like the rest of the Octa, it's severely lacking in the charm factor when compared to what came before it.

Full Disclosure: Land Rover was kind enough to lend me this 2026 Defender Octa with a full tank of gas to do with as I pleased for a week.

The AJ V8 can trace its roots back to the mid-1990s, so clearly someone at Land Rover decided it was time for a switchup. Just as Land Rover did with the L460 Range Rover, the automaker ditched its own motor for a BMW-sourced one, in this case the twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter S68 V8. By no means is the S68 a bad engine. Hell, it's a lot more powerful than the old one, with 626 horsepower and 590 pound-feet of torque on tap besting the old Defender V8 by 108 hp and 129 lb-ft. That's enough to drop the Octa's 0-to-60-mph to 3.7 seconds according to Car and Driver's testing, an improvement of almost a full second. Here's the thing, though — none of that is really all that important in a car like the Defender Octa.

When I drove the 110 V8 back in 2023, I lauded its raucous supercharged V8, and said that every time I stepped on the accelerator, I was met with the sound of V8 thunder puncturing my eardrums. I compared the noise it produces while driving around town to that of a cigarette boat idling in a marina. You get the picture. It sounds awesome.

Unfortunately, the same can't be said of the S68 under the hood of the Octa. It sounds the way it does in all modern BMWs, which is a bit, well, clinical. It's certainly a better way of providing motivational power to this 5,975-pound beast, but the theatrics are all but gone. A lot of that, of course, has to do with the pair of turbochargers. They mute pretty much any noise coming out of this thing, leaving nothing but a semi-hollow bellow coming out of the quad exhaust pipes. It's a shame, too, because the Octa's chief competitor, the Mercedes-AMG G63 that also has a twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V8, sounds absolutely phenomenal. (Thank you, side pipes.)

There's also the issue of power delivery. I know that in an off-road-focused SUV, the driver wants all the power and torque to be down low for better rock crawling or whatever, but please bear in mind that 99% of the folks who buy these cars are afraid to drive down a dirt road, so that's completely pointless. There was a joy in wringing the absolute hell out of that supercharged 5.0-liter V8, since its horsepower peak was all the way up at 6,500 rpm, just 250 rpm short of redline. Sure, torque peaked at 2,500 rpm, but with just 461 lb-ft on tap, you'd still need to really push the tachometer to get going. Meanwhile, the Octa's massive amount of torque means that the peak comes on at just 1,800 rpm. That leads to a far lazier driving style, and lazy just isn't fun, folks. We all know that.

I'm a fan of progress, don't get me wrong. I think we should be moving toward a more environmentally friendly and fuel-efficient future, but if we're going to replace a forced-induction V8 with a forced-induction V8, I think it's okay to complain a little bit if the engine isn't as fun to use. From a pure fuel economy standpoint, there aren't many gains to be had either. Obviously, it's not a one-to-one comparison, as the Octa has a whole bunch of other crap bolted to it, like 2.7 inches worth of fender flares and bigger tires. It's also taller and weighs nearly 330 pounds more than the old 110 V8, so the improvements are meager, to say the least. At 15 mpg city, 19 mpg highway and 17 mpg combined, the Defender Octa only gets 1 mpg better in the city and combined cycles over the 110 V8, and highway fuel economy stays in lock-step with the old car. To be fair, none of that really matters to the folks buying this car anyway, as my tester's asking price came in at a slightly eye-watering $177,595, including destination.

Any Defender with a V8 under the hood is a silly car that deserves a silly engine, and the S68 is not a silly engine, especially when it comes to the noises it makes and how it delivers power. While a Defender Octa with a 30-year-old AJ V8 under the hood would undoubtedly be a worse overall vehicle than the one Land Rover actually produced, I can't help but think it would put a bigger smile on my face, and that's what cars like these are actually all about.

#5570. The Proof Is In The Lettuce: Perovskite Makes Things Grow Better

Last year’s sharp U-turn in energy policy came with catastrophic consequences for farmers who were counting on federal assistance for solar power on their land. Still, the pace of innovation in the solar industry never stopped, and farmers may ultimately benefit whenever the policy winds blow in a more positive direction. In one particularly interesting development, the US startup UbiQD has assembled more evidence that its “UbiGro” perovskite-enhanced glass can help hothouse farmers improve their yields while saving water, too.

For those of you new to the topic, perovskite refers to a new class of relatively inexpensive, easy-to-fabricate solar materials, characterized by a crystalline structure based on the naturally occurring mineral perovskite (see lots more background here).

Raw perovskite is too unstable to function as a solar material on its own, but it can be combined with more durable materials in a solar cell, or in a solar module. Silicon-perovskite combinations are already emerging in the market, for example.

UbiQD developed its UbiGro glass to incorporate sub-microscopic particles of perovskite. Particles of that size are known as “artificial atoms” or quantum dots, as capably explained by scientists at Los Alamos National Laboratory:

Quantum dots are ultra-small bits of semiconductor matter that can be synthesized with nearly atomic precision via modern methods of colloidal chemistry. Their emission color can be tuned by simply varying their dimensions. Color tunability is combined with high emission efficiencies approaching 100%.

As Los Alamos indicates, quantum dots initially appeared in the LED field of the lighting industry before moving into solar energy applications as a means of ramping up the efficiency of solar cells. By 2016 researchers were experimenting with quantum dots in a perovskite solar cell. The pioneering startup Blue Dot was among those pursuing the perovskite connection.

Activity began to accelerate in 2025 when UbiQD acquired BlueDot. In the meantime, UbiQD had previously hooked up with the US thin film solar manufacturer First Solar to develop quantum dots for solar panels. That project also ramped up in 2025 when UbiQD closed on a $20 million round of Series B funding. According to UbiQD, its enhancements could double the solar conversion efficiency of First Solar’s bifacial solar panels.

In 2025, UbiQD also announced the findings from a study of its UbiGro greenhouse glass. The glass is treated with quantum dots as a means of fine-tuning sunlight to improve crop yields. The study was published by researchers at the University of California – Davis in the journal Materials Today Sustainability under the title, “Spectrally selective quantum dot laminated glass for photonic modulation and climate regulation in greenhouses.”

— Fresh biomass increased by 37.8%. Plants were nearly 40% heavier, indicating significantly more edible yield.

— Leaf area was increased by 38.0%. Larger leaf area means higher photosynthetic surface.

— Root length increased by 38.0%. Deeper roots improve water and nutrient uptake, resilience, and shelf life.

— Light-use efficiency was increased by 41.0%. The plants used sunlight more effectively, with more biomass per photon.

— Nutrient concentrations (N, P, K, Mg, Zn, Cu) were significantly elevated. The crops were more nutritious, with higher levels of essential nutrients.

— Spectral red:blue ratio increased by 61.0%, with no significant PAR losses. More red light was delivered without sacrificing total usable light levels.

“The findings highlight a promising pathway toward climate-smart greenhouse envelopes that integrate photonics with sustainable food and energy strategies,” the research team concluded.

In a series of followup trials last Spring, UC-Davis focused on the impact of UbiGro on water consumption by greenhouse-grown lettuce. The results were similarly encouraging.

“Water use efficiency improved by approximately 9%. Lettuce grown under QD glass produced 101 grams of fresh biomass per liter of water compared 93 grams per liter under conventional glass,” UbiQD noted.

“Unlike technologies that require additional energy inputs or changes to irrigation infrastructure, UbiGro glass works passively by optimizing the sunlight already entering the greenhouse while optimizing water use efficiency,” UbiD emphasized in a press statement.

UbiQD’s VP of Sales and Marketing, Eric Moody, also chipped in his two cents. “It’s an important new area of validation for UbiGro as we continue exploring how our technology can help growers get more from the resources they already use,”said Moody.

Want more details? Check out the study, “Crop Water Use and Evapotranspiration Estimation in Deep Water Culture Hydroponic System under Quantum Dot Glazed Greenhouse,” presented by UC-Davis Ph.D. candidate Mala Parvin at the 2026 American Society of Agricultural and Biological Engineers Annual International Meeting in Indianapolis last July.

First Solar has also been making some moves of its own. The iconic US firm is of particular interest for its focus on CdTe (cadmium-telluride) solar film instead of the silicon formula commonly used around the world. Here in the US, the Department of Energy has been promoting CdTe since the early 1990’s as a domestically sourced alternative to silicon, and it has become particularly popular in utility-scale applications.

First Solar has been embroiled in patent disputes of late, but the dust appeared to be settling last month when the company announced a non-exclusive patent licensing agreement with the US firm CubicPV Inc.

Among other, undisclosed terms of the agreement, First Solar will have access to CubicPV patents covering perovskite solar technology in the US. “The license further clears the path for First Solar to continue its development of photovoltaic (PV) devices built with a perovskite semiconductor for the US utility-scale, commercial and industrial, and residential markets, and applies to sales and distribution of those products domestically,” First Solar explains.

Somewhat ironically, if US President Donald Trump were to lend his full support to the domestic solar industry, First Solar would be a feather in his cap. First Solar bills itself as the largest producer of thin film solar in the world, and the largest solar manufacturer of any kind in the Western Hemisphere.

First Solar is also among the solar stakeholders contributing to the President’s oft-stated ambition of bringing more manufacturing back to the US during his time in office. “The Company’s investments include a new perovskite development line at its Perrysburg, Ohio, campus that produces small form-factor modules featuring a perovskite semiconductor, allowing First Solar to meet key internal milestones in its perovskite development program, including initial-stage efficiency, stability, and manufacturability objectives,” First Solar notes.

That’s just for starters. By the middle of next year, First Solar expects to have a pilot line up and running at a facility in Ohio, which will apply the technology to its existing Series 6 solar modules.

In addition, last month First Solar announced the start of Phase I of operations at its sixth facility in the US. Located in Gaffney, South Carolina, the new factory represents another step in First Solar’s onshoring plan for Series 6 production.

“The second phase is forecast to be completed by mid-2027, at which time the approximately $330 million facility is expected to double its annual nameplate capacity to 3.4 gigawatts (GW) and produce the Company’s CuRe technology, while supporting nearly 700 jobs. Approximately 500 of those jobs have already been filled,” First Solar explains.

For the record, the Gaffney facility expands First Solar’s existing footprint in South Carolina. The company also operates in Alabama, Louisiana, and Ohio. All together, First Solar anticipates to have a total of 17 gigawatts’ worth of domestic solar module manufacturing under its belt by the end of this year, which is just around the corner.

Photo: Greenhouse lettuce thrives under natural sunlight filtered through specialized glass from the perovskite solar startup UbiQD, while conserving water resources, too (cropped, courtesy of UbiQD).

#5569. Inside RFK Jr.'s Day-to-Day; 'Not Dying Fast Enough'; Peddling Unproven Cures

— A weekly roundup of how public health policy is shaping practice

The release of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s calendar for his time as HHS secretary shows meetings with the CEOs of Eli Lilly, Chipotle, Tylenol-maker Kenvue, and Philip Morris, along with the hours prepping for Joe Rogan's podcast and time to film videos with Kid Rock. (Politico, STAT)

Medicare's cap on hospice payments penalizes patients who are "not dying fast enough," as one nurse described it. (New York Times)

A Harvard professor who studies the link between diet and health -- a favorite topic of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. -- had his grants cut anyway. (New York Times)

The fight over ultraprocessed food caused some big divisions inside the White House. (The Atlantic)

Kristine Blanche, wife of Attorney General Todd Blanche, runs a website that sells unproven dietary supplements and medical treatments. (The Guardian)

A proposed rule from the Labor Department would end fast-tracking of green cards for nurses and physical therapists. (Fierce Healthcare)

NIH officials are wondering whether Anthony Fauci, MD, former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, clandestinely wrote a major paper debunking the "lab leak" theory of COVID. (Politico)

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force had its first meeting in a year and a half, newly stocked with Kennedy appointees. Reporting describes it as "tumultuous." (New York Times)

CVS's decision to break up into two separate companies would "continue to enable the company to drive up prices and crush competition," Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) wrote in a letter to the company's CEO. (The Hill)

Nearly 60% of Americans think the U.S. could have prevented the loss of its measles elimination status if the federal government had done a better job of encouraging vaccination and responding to outbreak, according to a new Ipsos poll.

A dozen Democratic members of Congress wrote to President Trump to ask how creation of a Women's Health Task Force is not duplicative of the NIH's Office of Research on Women's Health.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, MD (D-Mich.), said he'd be fine with putting President Trump's name on a "Medicare for All" plan, if that's what it would take to get it done. (The Hill)

A group has formed to draft Sen. Rand Paul, MD (R-Ky.), to run for president in 2028. (The Hill)

Federal scientists are increasingly concerned about the health effects of glyphosate. (Washington Post)

HHS and CMS need to better manage the risk of Medicare fraud, according to a report from the Government Accountability Office.

HHS awarded $47 million to 15 organizations to test new approaches to chronic disease prevention and management.

The FDA said it will now include information about accelerated approvals to patient labeling for drugs.

#5568. 9 Boring Normal Cars With Surprisingly Bad Fuel Economy

Most people are fine with sacrificing horsepower, cornering grip, and any semblance of driving fun if their daily commuter is cheap and economical. Of course, it doesn't have to be like that — fun commuter cars for enthusiasts who live in the city do exist. Still, we get it — the average car buyer isn't an enthusiast. But what happens when the econobox betrays you? You chose a practical commuter thinking you'd save money on gas, only to encounter lower mpg figures than those of larger, more engaging cars.

As it turns out, there have been many mundane cars sold in the U.S. that possess a staggering talent for burning fuel and your desire to sit behind the wheel. But how does this happen? Usually, it comes down to wrong powertrain choices, but the 2000s in particular marked a dark age for fuel economy, with the average new-vehicle rating dipping to a low of 19.3 mpg in 2004.

In this piece, we're lining up nine of these deceptively thirsty commuters, comparing them with often larger, more powerful alternatives from their time to expose their surprisingly bad fuel economy. We ranked these cars based on their EPA-estimated combined ratings, descending from the merely disappointing down to the truly abysmal.

Aiming to attract younger, budget-constrained buyers, Ford launched the Fiesta-based EcoSport in the U.S. for the 2018 model year. A subcompact crossover that had been on sale in Europe since 2014, the EcoSport should've offered fun-to-drive characteristics in a small, fuel-efficient package. Unfortunately, its name proved to be misleading — there was nothing economical or sporty about the EcoSport.

In Europe, the EcoSport was also criticized for being uninteresting to drive — hardly surprising given its tall and narrow stature. However, it could at least be economical. Most notably, Ford offered it with a 1.5-liter four-cylinder turbodiesel engine with 123 horsepower and a useful 221 lb-ft of torque.

In America, though, the EcoSport was available with a 1.0-liter turbocharged three-cylinder with 123 hp and front-wheel drive, or a 2.0-liter four-cylinder with 166 hp and all-wheel drive. The smaller engine earned an EPA-estimated rating of 28 mpg combined, too low a figure for what was essentially a 161.3-inch-long, three-cylinder city car. The 2.0-liter AWD version was even worse, earning an abysmal 25-mpg combined rating from the EPA. To put that into perspective, the larger and heavier 2019 Toyota RAV4 equipped with a 2.5-liter four-cylinder with 203 hp and AWD was rated at up to 30 mpg combined.

The EcoSport nailed the boring part, too. It was only available with a six-speed automatic, lacked grip and agility, and was glacially slow, with the 2.0-liter AWD model reaching 60 in 9.8 seconds in Car and Driver's test runs. On top of that, due to its diminutive size, the EcoSport's interior wasn't very practical, and practicality is something that American buyers expect from an SUV.

Rowing your own gears in a small, urban-friendly package brings joy to driving, but you'd also expect good fuel economy in return. Well, the 2008 Scion xB was relatively compact at 167.3 inches long and was available with a manual transmission. However, instead of giving it a smaller, fuel-efficient engine, Scion equipped it with the four-cylinder engine from the sporty Scion tC and Toyota's midsize sedan, the Camry.

Producing 158 horsepower and 162 lb-ft of torque, the 2.4-liter unit was decently potent for the small xB, bringing it to 60 in 7.8 seconds, according to Car and Driver. Unfortunately, this meant the compact Scion was also very thirsty for fuel, earning a 24-mpg combined rating from the EPA throughout its run. What's more, the xB earned a dreadful 22-mpg city rating — a tough pill to swallow for a compact commuter box. To illustrate the absurdity, the 2008 Honda Fit manual was rated at 31 mpg combined, thanks to its fit-for-purpose 1.5-liter engine with 109 hp. Heck, even the significantly bigger Camry earned a 25-mpg combined rating with the same engine.

Perhaps Scion should've also offered the 1.8-liter engine from the smaller xD. With 128 hp and 125 lb-ft of torque, the smaller four-cylinder is potent enough for the city, while also helping the xD earn a 29-mpg combined EPA rating with the manual. Oh, and despite packing a larger engine than its predecessor's 1.5-liter unit, the 2008 xB is a relatively boring, uninspiring car to drive. Not to mention, Scion gave up on the funky, fridge-like aesthetics of the predecessor for a smoothed-out design that lacks any personality.

Like any other transmission type, CVTs have many pros and cons, with their biggest advantage being higher efficiency than a regular automatic. However, the CVT in the 2007 to 2008 Dodge Caliber was anything but efficient. While the manual-equipped Caliber with the 2.4-liter engine was rated at 25 mpg combined, the CVT could only muster 23 mpg, with 21 mpg in the city and 25 mpg on the highway. With AWD, the efficiency dropped to an even lower 22 mpg. Dodge also offered a smaller 1.8-liter engine with 148 horsepower and a manual transmission, alongside a 2.0-liter engine with 158 hp and a CVT. These models were more efficient, but their 26-mpg and 24-mpg combined figures weren't particularly impressive, either.

While one could argue that the hate for CVTs is mostly overblown, these transmissions have never been engaging or sporty. So, although the 2.4-liter engine wasn't underpowered, producing a solid 172 horsepower and 165 lb-ft of torque, the regular Caliber has never been a driver's car. Fortunately, Dodge rectified that with the Caliber SRT4, which came with a 2.4-liter turbo-four, producing 285 hp and 265 lb-ft of torque. The SRT4 was available exclusively with a six-speed manual and front-wheel drive, and, according to Dodge, accelerated to 60 mph in 6 seconds. Thanks to its lowered suspension with Sachs twin-tube dampers, the Caliber SRT4 was also sharper and more interesting to drive than the regular variant.

The fuel economy penalty for choosing the SRT4? Just 1 mpg on the combined cycle when compared to a CVT-equipped 2.4-liter model. Heck, the SRT4 even earned a higher 27-mpg rating on the highway — impressive, considering the 100-plus-horsepower delta between the two.

Suzuki is usually associated with producing fun-to-drive, economical urban runabouts, but back in 2004, its compact car, the Reno, was anything but. That's because, if you look beyond the Suzuki badge, you'll learn that this car is actually a rebadged version of the Daewoo Lacetti.

Being from Europe, I drove a Lacetti extensively back in the day, and still remember how cheap it felt compared to the Golfs, Focuses, and Corollas of its time. And it's not only the cheap interior, but the whole driving experience. Yes, the car had a manual, but it was so imprecise, you'd be better off with an automatic. The steering left a lot to be desired, too. Because Suzuki did little beyond slapping its badge on it, the same applies to the Reno.

Perhaps the worst aspect of the Suzuki Reno, however, is its engine. The Daewoo-sourced 2.0-liter four-cylinder produced only 127 horsepower and 131 lb-ft of torque, enough for a 0-60 sprint of 9.5 seconds, per Car and Driver. That's slow, especially when you are also paying a fuel penalty. The manual-equipped Reno was rated at a terrible 23 mpg combined by the EPA from 2006 on, with the automatic getting an even lower 22-mpg rating.

For context, the 2006 Toyota Corolla came with a 1.8-liter engine with 126 hp and 122 lb-ft of torque, yet it was rated at 31 mpg combined when paired with the five-speed manual. Suzuki's own Aerio compact sedan/wagon was also more efficient at up to 24 mpg combined while packing a larger 2.3-liter engine with 155 hp and 152 lb-ft of torque.

Back in the 1990s, Volkswagen brought its TDI turbodiesel engines to the U.S., aiming to lure buyers with outstanding efficiency. The 1.9 TDI engine was a true fuel-sipper, helping the 2002 to 2003 Jetta Wagon earn an outstanding 39-mpg combined rating from the EPA. The fact that the ALH unit is a reliable diesel engine that just won't quit further cemented its status as a legend, so much so that these pre-Dieselgate Volkswagen TDI cars are becoming collector's items.

Unfortunately, the base gas-powered Jetta wasn't nearly as efficient. It came with a 2.0-liter four-cylinder good for 115 horsepower — more than the diesel's measly 90 hp. However, it also produced less torque at 122 lb-ft against the turbodiesel's 155 lb-ft. Crucially, it was significantly less fuel efficient. The manual-equipped Jetta 2.0 was rated at 24 mpg combined, with the automatic earning an even lower 22-mpg rating from 1999 to 2001, and a slightly better 23 mpg from 2002 to 2003. That's not only low compared to the diesel version, but also compared to the 2002 Corolla, which came with a more potent 1.8-liter engine with 125 hp and 125 lb-ft of torque that returned 30 mpg combined.

Worse yet, the Jetta was also available with more powerful gas engines that offered no better fuel economy than the base one. The 1.8-liter turbo-four produced 150 hp and 155 lb-ft of torque, while returning 24 mpg with the manual, or 22 mpg with the automatic. The top-end Jetta with the 2.8-liter VR6 engine produced 174 hp and 181 lb-ft of torque, returning 20 mpg combined. What's more, these engines were bumped to 180 hp and 200 hp, respectively, for 2002, while the base 2.0-liter engine remained unchanged.

When you're torn between the base and high-performance engines, settling for the base model only makes sense if it saves you real money upfront and at the pump. Well, the base 2008 Impreza only saved you money on the purchase, as it had similar fuel economy to the more powerful WRX model.

Packing a 2.5-liter four-cylinder boxer engine, the base Impreza was rated at a solid 170 horsepower and 170 lb-ft of torque. Equipped with standard AWD and a five-speed manual or four-speed automatic transmission, the Impreza was rated at 22 mpg combined, 20 mpg city, and 27 mpg highway by the EPA, hardly impressive for a compact car. Making matters worse, the sporty WRX was rated at 21 mpg combined, 19 mpg city, and 25 mpg highway with the manual, while producing 224 hp and 226 lb-ft of torque from its 2.5-liter turbocharged engine.

You might argue that this isn't a fair comparison, so here is an even better one: the newly introduced 2010 Legacy, which used the same engine, was more economical than the Impreza. The Impreza had still not been updated by that point, carrying its 22-mpg rating into the 2011 model year. The Legacy carried the same rating with the six-speed manual, but thanks to its CVT, the automatic model was rated at 26 mpg combined.

The Impreza didn't fare well against rivals, either. The 2008 Toyota Camry V6 had a 3.5-liter engine with 268 hp and 248 lb-ft of torque, yet it was also rated at 22 mpg combined. Even the more practical 2008 Honda CR-V SUV with the 2.4-liter engine (166 hp and 161 lb-ft) was rated at 22 mpg combined with AWD.

The midsize Suzuki Verona looked promising when it came out — on paper. It had one of the most comfortable interiors in the midsize sedan category, a standard 2.5-liter inline-6 engine, and a lower price than its rivals.

Unfortunately, the Daewoo mechanicals again exposed Suzuki's midsize car. A badge-engineered Daewoo Magnus, the Verona was one of the most boring cars to drive in its class. That would've been fine if it had been refined, but its soft suspension couldn't make up for the noisy cabin and cheap interior plastics that ruined any illusion of luxury.

Hey, at least it had a smooth inline-6 engine! Apart from that, though, the 2.5-liter unit was underpowered compared to its peers, producing 155 horsepower and 177 lb-ft of torque. Even worse, it was only offered with a four-speed automatic, so it needed a glacial 10.7 seconds to reach 60 in Car and Driver testing. And apart from being slow and dull to drive, the Verona also earned a 20-mpg combined rating from the EPA in 2004 and 2006, and 21 mpg in 2005.

To put that into perspective, the 2006 Honda Accord was rated at 26 mpg combined when paired with the 2.4-liter, 166-hp four-cylinder engine and five-speed manual. Even with the 3.0-liter V6, good for 244 hp and 211 lb-ft of torque, the Accord was rated at a higher 21 mpg. Not to mention, the Accord V6 was also available with a six-speed manual for higher engagement. Heck, the Mazdaspeed6, introduced for the 2006 model year, was a real performance sedan with 274 hp and AWD, yet it gave up just 1 mpg to the lethargic Verona.

You can't have a serious conversation about slow, thirsty commuters without mentioning the PT Cruiser. Chrysler's retro-looking car is cool, sure, and the automaker did a great job with the chassis, striking a good balance between handling and comfort. Thanks to the minivan-like, upright body, the PT Cruiser was also spacious and practical inside.

Still, with a drag coefficient of 0.38, the retro body was also as aerodynamic as a brick. So, despite producing only 150 horsepower, the entry-level 2.4-liter four-cylinder engine was rated at 20 mpg combined with the four-speed auto in 2003. By comparison, the base 2006 Chrysler 300 had a 2.7-liter V6 with 190 hp under the hood and returned 21 mpg combined. Even the model with the 3.5-liter V6 was as economical as the base 2003 PT Cruiser (20 mpg), all while packing 250 hp. The PT Cruiser's rating was improved to 21 mpg from 2004 to 2006, still a poor return from such modest power.

Adding insult to injury, the PT Cruiser received a turbocharged 2.4-liter engine for 2003, producing 215 hp, and it was rated at 21 mpg combined when paired with a five-speed manual. Chrysler increased the turbocharged engine's output to 220 hp for 2004, with the EPA fuel economy rating remaining the same. The four-speed auto version was rated at 19 mpg, just 2 mpg below the base automatic, but had 70 more horses to play with.

A midsize sedan with a 3.0-liter V6 that returns 19 mpg combined? That doesn't sound too bad, but bear with us. Introduced for the 2000 model year, the fourth-gen Taurus arrived with a sharper design and two upgraded 3.0-liter V6 engines. However, while one of these was a 24-valve twin-cam engine, the other one was a Vulcan pushrod unit.

Today, pushrod engines are mostly used in trucks because they are torquey at low rpm, but high-revving horsepower has never been their strong suit. So, the base 3.0-liter V6 in the fourth-gen Taurus produced only 155 horsepower at 4,900 rpm and a good 185 lb-ft of torque at 3,950 rpm. In 2001, the Vulcan-powered Taurus was rated at 19 mpg combined by the EPA. For comparison, the twin-cam Duratec unit earned a 20-mpg combined rating, while producing 200 hp and 200 lb-ft of torque.

Still, the Japanese rivals of the time were even more impressive. Debuting for 2002, the then-brand-new Toyota Camry arrived with a 2.4-liter four-cylinder engine. Although it was short on cylinders, it produced 157 hp and 162 lb-ft of torque while returning 24 mpg on the combined cycle regardless of the transmission. The 3.0-liter V6 Camry was also more economical at 21 mpg combined, while producing 192 hp and 209 lb-ft of torque.

The fact that the Taurus was lifeless behind the wheel only made the base engine's poor fuel economy harder to forgive. Not only that, but Ford's midsize sedan wasn't as refined as its rivals by the end of its run, both in terms of the driving experience and interior quality.

#5567. Musk Space Based Data Center Idea Is A Betrayal Of Humanity

Despite copious evidence that Elon Musk is little more than a snake oil salesman and carnival barker like P. T. Barnum, the world continues to believe the man is somehow smarter than the rest of us. Few seem to realize his empire is built on nothing more than wildly inflated boasts and  OPM — other people’s money.

Take away the billions Tesla received over the years from other automakers by selling emissions credits and the company likely would have failed early on. Musk recognized the opportunity those emissions credits offered and seized it with both hands. The existence of SpaceX depends almost entirely on the contracts it has secured from the US government.

People (including some here at CleanTechnica) get all weak in the knees when Musk makes his outlandish claims about robotaxis and Cybercabs, but the truth is that, after a decade, we are still waiting for that Model S to leave California, drive across the country, and park itself in a garage in Manhattan without a human driver ever touching the wheel.

Tesla, the car company, has shrunk its model lineup rather than expanding it. The Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck are now out of production, with no replacements in sight. The Roadster 2.0 is a party trick with a very limited potential market. The $25,000 Tesla is completely off the table.

Are the Model Y and Model 3 pretty good cars? Yes, they are. Yet the competition is bringing dozens of new models to market every month and introducing electric cars to world markets where their lack of exhaust emissions and lower operating costs can be a real benefit to the local population. The fact that Tesla ignores those markets is proof the company is little more than a niche player in the global automotive marketplace.

Musk’s penchant for issuing pie in the sky predictions and boldly going where no one has gone before is now fully underway in the AI madness. In a recent report by the New York Times by Grace Kay and Ryan Mac, the pair detail the same Muskian passion for making bold claims and then bullying his employees to make them a reality.

Musk has used his connections to the White House to construct a sprawling (and rapidly expanding) data center — which Musk, with his usual modesty, calls Colossus — in a predominantly minority neighborhood in Memphis, Tennessee. That enterprise has now spread to nearby Mississippi. The local utilities could not possible supply all the electrical power those enormous facilities consume, and so Musk is powering them with portable methane fired generators that spew far more emissions into the air than a modern combined cycle generating station would.

Musk cannot wait for environmental reviews and other government restrictions, so he has blanketed the neighborhoods around his data centers with effluvia from those portable generators and used his political clout to suppress opposition to  his plans. AI is too important to be delayed by such trivial concerns as people’s health or a massive influx of carbon emissions.

Colossus is home — assuming their is such a thing — to Grok, Musk’s AI invention that features the ability to undress virtually anyone for the amusement of pre-pubescent boys. We hear a lot today about Claude, the AI wizard from Anthropic, and ChatGPT from OpenAI, but Grok is hardly ever mentioned in the same breath as those AI tools.

That has placed Musk in a familiar bind. His dreams are far removed from reality, and so he has been forced to rent out computing power (now known simple as “compute”) to his competitors in order to pay the bills. The Times report says he has told employees that “SpaceX is falling behind in AI development, making it more lucrative to rent the company’s computing power out to rivals than use it to improve its own products,” three people told the Times reporters.

In August, Musk temporarily changed the group chat name for his AI team to “Sell compute because we can’t compete,” the Times was told. Then he did what Musk does so well — he tried motivating his people by threatening them. “Anyone wasting GPUs on bullshit while we are failing to compete will be asked to leave immediately, as this constitutes a betrayal of your team.” This type of bullying is typical of Musk, whose motto seems to be, “The beatings will continue until morale improves.”

Part of the problem is that SpaceX — the nominal owner of Musk’s AI ambitions — is now a public company, after its blockbuster IPO earlier this year. Before, it was a private company with no need to disclose its finances to the outside world. Now, it must justify is lofty valuation with real world results, and the pressure on Musk to justify his bet on AI is intense.

“SpaceX makes way more money right now renting out compute than from Grok,” said Nicolas Owens, an analyst who covers SpaceX for Morningstar Research, told the New York Times. “Grok is not the premier model in town, so I think it’s more doubtful that they would be able to tip the scale to where serving up A.I. off of their own servers is more lucrative than branching it out to Anthropic.”

Musk told his engineers in August, “At the end of the day, the only thing that matters for competitiveness is revenue per GPU, not benchmarks. If you can’t pay for your GPUs, then you either go bankrupt or you become a computer rental company. Move the needle on revenue.”

And yet, despite such blandishments, the company has shifted resources away from internal AI projects. The Times reports that Mike Nicolls, the president of the AI unit, disbanded the 60 member team behind Grok Imagine, an image and video generation tool that was once a top priority. He told the workers involved the cuts would “better align our structure and resources with critical business priorities.”

Those priorities now appear to be focused on renting out as much “compute” as possible to competitors such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and anyone else who needs extra computing power to drive the AI revolution forward.

In another attempt to distract the world of finance away from SpaceX’s financial struggles here on Earth, Musk now says he has received permission from the Federal Communications Commission to place up to one million data centers into sun-synchronous orbit around the Earth. That means they will be powered by sunlight nearly 24 hours a day, and their cooling needs will be minimized by the low temperatures in space.

SpaceX will build the 98 foot (30 m) long satellites at its Gigasat Factory in Bastrop, Texas, using AI chips manufactured at the 100 million square foot (ten times the size of the Texas Gigafactory) Terafab manufacturing facility in Grimes County, Texas.

On its website, Terafab modestly announces, “We aspire to be a galactic civilization.” To make that happen, first it intends to “Harness all the energy on a planet,” then “Harness all the energy from a star,” and finally “Harness all of the energy in a galaxy.” Some readers may find all this hype and hysteria reminds them of a phrase made popular during Barry Goldwater’s presidential campaign: “In your heart, you know he’s nuts.”

In a press release, the FCC said it had approved the request to place one million satellites in orbit subject to certain conditions. According to Reuters, SpaceX must begin deployment no ​later than November 2033, deploy 10 percent of the maximum number no later ⁠than November of 2035, and deploy 50 percent by November 2038. Approving the application ​will permit SpaceX “to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence,” the ​FCC said.

The enormity of this plan is illustrated by the fact that, at present, there are only a total of 17,000 satellites orbiting the Earth (not counting the moon). SpaceX originally asked for permission to launch 42,000 Starlink satellites, yet today only 11,000 have been deployed.

The satellites will be placed in Earth orbit by Starship, a reusable rocket developed by SpaceX. Those rockets are powered by methane, which has led environmental advocates to question the wisdom of the entire data centers in space project. But Elon has demonstrated by his actions with Colossus in Memphis and Mississippi he doesn’t care a flying fig leaf about the harm burning methane can do.

“Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people’s everyday lives as well as the future of our planet,” said Jan Hasselman, senior attorney at Earthjustice. “Agencies that authorize companies looking to space as the next frontier still must operate within the law, and the law requires the FCC to consider all the risks and impacts of these proposals. It is dismaying that the FCC has ignored the law so blatantly and tried to mask the fact with a holiday filing.”

The approval by the FCC seems to be in violation of the National Environmental Protection Act (NEPA). Sharp eyed readers will notice that NEPA will be gutted by the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) that may slip through a lame duck Congress before the end of this year.

“This approval to deploy a million data centers in space without any thought to the impacts on Earth is just a glimpse of what we’ll see during the next two years of Trump,” said Sam Sankar, senior vice president at Earthjustice. “This is great example of why Congress should not pass a flawed bill like BAAJA that would lock in terrible projects like this one. Donald Trump is going to do a lot more dirty and lawless deals over the next years, and BAAJA prevents future presidents from reconsidering them.”

Does human civilization need Musk’s Starmind? It seems clear Musk is hellbent on exporting humanity to the moon, Mars, and beyond because he knows for dead solid certain that he and his tech bro cronies will make the Earth uninhabitable in the not too distant future. If you think about what Musk did to Ukraine recently when he unilaterally restricted its access to Starlink, the prospect of him running the world, if not the entire galaxy, should fill you with dread.

A certifiable lunatic with the power to play God? Be afraid; be very afraid.

I have a history of giving my animals names that both fit their sentiments and that somehow relate to my automotive exploits. I also love to blend the two together, going for drives and bringing the pooches along. I'm curious if anyone else in the Jalopnik readership is the same way. Do you have any pets with a car-related name? If so, let's hear them!

I lived on a farm as a youngster, and we always had at least one dog around. We had a gaggle of mutts when I was still in school, with boring non-car-related names picked by my folks; Sydney, Rags, White Dog (a stray who stuck around), and a barn cat named Pita. Ever since I had the ability to name my own animals (which began with a sheep I raised named after NASCAR driver Kevin Harvick), they all had car-related names. When my wife and I first moved in together, we got a rescue basset hound we named Alois, after the German supercar maker himself, Mr. Ruf. A second basset already came with the name Henry, so we retroactively associated him with Mr. Ford. Though he wasn't nearly as racist, the basset did also love to eat weeds.

With both basset hounds having lived full lives and passed into memory, we were dog-free for over a year before we decided to look for our next family member a couple of weeks ago. Very quickly, we found this little monster you see here, a two-year-old English bulldog with a ridiculously flat face. Because of her copper coloring, she was given the name Penny. Sticking with that name, we decided her official government name would be Penelope Pitstop, the character from the old 1968 cartoon television series Hanna-Barbera's Wacky Races. Not only does our little Miss Penelope love to go in the car, but she rather dislikes walking long distances and takes frequent pit stops, as shown in the image above.

If you don't have a pet with a car name, or you want to figure out a good name for a pet you're going to be adopting soon (adopt, don't shop!), I'm going to list a few good ones here for you. If you really want, you can drop a picture or description of your pet in the comments below, and I'll provide some good suggestions. Here are a few of my favorite car-related pet names:

Whatever you choose, there are plenty of cool names out there for you to pick. Cat, dog, rabbit, lizard, whatever. You can pick a name and call them whatever you want. Maybe you want an iguana named carburetor, that's your prerogative.

So, sound off in the comments below with your pets' names, or cool car-related pet names that you might suggest for someone in the community. Let's chat about it. Give us your thoughts on pet names, and we'll discuss them. Then, I'll pick a few of my favorite responses to recap for everyone else next week. Sound good? Good.

#5565. Hepatitis B Shot at Birth Dips Among Babies of Infected Moms

— "Birth dose vaccination serves as a critical safety net," researchers say

Fewer newborns are receiving the birth dose of the hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccine, including those born to infected mothers, according to a national retrospective review.

For over 1.3 million U.S. infants born between January 2018 and June 2026, vaccination rates were 76.4% in 2018 and 79.8% in 2022 before beginning to fall in mid-2023, landing at 65.6% in June of this year, reported Nina Masters, PhD, MPH, of Truveta in Bellevue, Washington, and colleagues in NEJM Evidence.

From 2018 through 2025, a positive maternal HBV test led to vaccination in 97%-98% of newborns born to those mothers -- but that percentage dropped to 93.9% during January through June 2026.

Overall, as newborn HBV vaccination rates fell, maternal HBV screening rates rose. Over the study period, 90.5% of mothers had evidence of an HBV test, with 0.18% testing positive for the virus. The proportion of moms who had no recorded HBV test during pregnancy dropped from 15.6% in 2018 to 7.6% in 2026.

"Hepatitis B birth dose vaccination serves as a critical safety net against gaps in protection against perinatal HBV infection," Masters and team wrote.

"Applying the 90% screening rate found in this study to the approximately 3.6 million births per year, mothers without evidence of HBV screening during pregnancy may give birth to an estimated 360,000 infants per year," they noted. "Applying the 0.18% ... positivity rate in this study could translate to more than 640 infants a year born to mothers with HBV infection who are untested."

Universal HBV vaccination of newborns at birth has been shown to be safe and effective. However, the CDC's revamped Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices last December abandoned more than three decades of U.S. vaccine policy and voted to stop recommending a universal birth dose.

The panel recommended instead a shared clinical decision-making process for babies born to mothers who test negative for HBV. Under that approach, parents and clinicians would decide "when or if" to administer the vaccine. For families that opt to not give the birth dose, the panel suggested delaying the first dose until a child is 2 months old. The CDC's proposed childhood immunization schedule would move HBV vaccination to shared clinical decision-making except in high-risk groups.

The steady declines in newborn HBV vaccination rates across all maternal groups "potentially indicate distrust of medical interventions even beyond recommendations," Masters and team cautioned. "These results reinforce previous reports, likely reflecting continuing vaccine hesitancy and confusion among parents after recent changes in recommendations for newborn HBV guidelines."

The trends seen in this study could lead to more chronic HBV infections in the years ahead, according to a recent modeling study. That research predicted that moving from a universal birth dose to deferred vaccination or a shared decision-making approach could increase chronic HBV infections by 19% with delayed vaccination and 83% with shared decision-making. Other research has suggested that unvaccinated infants may face unexpected HBV household exposure risks even when moms test negative.

For this study, Masters and colleagues reviewed electronic health records from the nationwide Truveta Data database. The analysis included 1,338,961 infants born to 1,075,767 mothers who were ages 15-49 years at delivery.

Over the study period, 75.9% of newborns received HBV vaccination within 1 day of birth.

Vaccination rates were highest among babies born to moms who tested positive for HBV, at 96.9%. Vaccination rates were 75.9% among those with mothers who tested negative, 76.8% among those with moms with unknown infection status, and 75.4% among those with moms who had no evidence of a test in the database.

Among the 2,231 mothers who tested positive for HBV infection during pregnancy, 92.8% received both hepatitis B immunoglobulin and HBV vaccination.

#5564. Loblaw’s Hydrogen Truck Crossed the Rockies. Another Truck Brought Its Fuel.

Loblaw’s Hyundai XCIENT hydrogen fuel-cell truck crossed the Canadian Rockies from Vancouver to Calgary on November 18. The 1,046 km journey attracted enthusiastic coverage as a Canadian heavy-freight milestone. It also illustrated an infrastructure problem that gets much less attention than a successful crossing: the hydrogen had to be brought to the truck.

The Edmonton Region Hydrogen Hub announcement describes three fuelling occasions. The truck started with a fill at HTEC’s Vancouver hydrogen station, then refuelled at Sicamous and Golden from a mobile tube trailer supplied by Powertech. Other project partners arranged the trailer’s transportation and logistics. The tractor hauling the mobile fuel was almost certainly diesel-powered. The public account did not include that support truck’s fuel consumption, emissions or cost.

The hydrogen truck completed the trip, and the project partners demonstrated that a mobile hydrogen supply operation could support a freight vehicle across the mountains. Those are achievements, albeit not novel ones. A fleet operator considering hydrogen needs a more demanding result: dependable places to refuel on repeated journeys, delivered hydrogen prices, vehicle availability, maintenance requirements and the complete cost of the support system. Moving a fuel trailer between planned stops is not the same thing as operating a commercial refuelling corridor.

The three fills also complicate the familiar argument that hydrogen offers heavy trucks a decisive range advantage. Hyundai’s fuel-cell truck has marketed range specifications, but the crossing did not establish that range advantage against battery-electric heavy trucks. Battery trucks had completed demanding Alpine journeys years earlier, and commercial electric freight operations have progressed since then. The comparative distances, energy stops and subsequent operating evidence are important when evaluating what this latest event contributed.

There is a second question about what happened after the official announcement. In the TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment, I reviewed a bounded sample of news reports and social posts from the week after the journey. The press generally included the mobile refills. The promotional accounts circulating on social media were much more likely to celebrate the distance and mountains while leaving out the operation that supplied the fuel.

That difference matters. A photograph of a truck crossing a mountain pass makes an effective announcement. Refuelling arrangements, energy costs and repeatability are harder to compress into a congratulatory post. As the story travels, a demonstration can start to resemble a commercially proven transport system even when the fundamental business questions remain unanswered.

Loblaw also operates battery-electric freight vehicles. Those trucks are making commercial deliveries and accumulating service kilometres rather than appearing in a single supported trial. Comparing the deployment record within the same company with the attention lavished on its hydrogen journey is a useful way to test how publicity can distort perceptions of technological maturity.

The earlier TFIE analysis, Hydrogen Has Narrative Density. Electrification Has Deployment Density, identified that mismatch across several energy and transport markets. The Loblaw event shows the mechanism: an attractive milestone generates attention while the surrounding operating system receives less attention, and routine electric deployment barely enters the story.

The project partners have said operational results will follow. The decisive questions concern delivered fuel, support logistics and recurring freight service, rather than whether a fuel-cell truck can make one successful trip with dedicated logistical support. Fleet investment requires operating evidence, not publicity counts.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing quantifies the media-versus-social disclosure gap, compares the driving legs with an earlier battery-electric mountain crossing, and sets the demonstration against Loblaw’s existing electric-fleet deployment. A free subscription opens the complete assessment and its two analytical graphics.

The broader narrative-density assessment traces the same gap between announcements and deployments across energy sectors.

#5563. Oldsmobile Once Let You Buy The Same Police Package It Sold To The Cops

Most cop cars today are produced as standalone models. Ford, for example, offers pursuit-rated models like the Police Interceptor Utility and F-150 Police Responder. Civilians can't typically buy a pursuit-rated vehicle straight from the factory or dealer without special permission, either. At the dawn of the classic American muscle car era, though, Oldsmobile offered its 1964 F-85 Cutlass with the B09 Police Apprehender Pursuit package — and regular folks could actually buy it for just $285.

"B09" may sound like a boring options-list slot filler, but the package offered much more than some police-themed wheels. With it, buyers were treated to over 300 horsepower, a stiffened suspension, and a whole host of other goodies that transformed the F-85 Cutlass into a formidable performance machine. You may know it as the 442.

The thought behind Oldsmobile's B09 package was a competitive one. Prior to its release, Pontiac put its Le Mans GTO on the market for the first time — a model that's largely credited with kicking off the classic American muscle era. Oldsmobile felt it needed to get the new B09 F-85 Cutlass on the market quickly to meet the ultra-hot GTO. Once it arrived on the scene, it managed to carve out Oldsmobile's muscle car image going forward.

Oldsmobile already had a couple of police packages for its F-85 Cutlass, one of which was called the B07 Highway Patrol package. With the B07 option selected, Cutlasses would come equipped with a 310-horsepower V8 and a beefier suspension setup. Using the B07 as a baseline, the B09 package took shape.

Right off the bat, Oldsmobile's B09/442 Cutlass ran into some issues. Pontiac's then-general manager, Pete Estes, had been more than happy to bend the engine displacement limits in place at the time to further the division's GTO project. Jack Wolfram, Oldsmobile's boss, was less enthusiastic about rule-breaking. Regardless, he greenlit the B09 project.

It came with a 330-cubic-inch V8 — 59 cubes smaller than the GTO's — and offered just 310 horsepower, as opposed to the Pontiac's maximum of 348 hp. At the time, Oldsmobile had a 345-horsepower, 394-cubic-inch V8 on hand, but opted not to use it for the B09 Cutlass. The Olds also used a single four-barrel carburetor, whereas the GTO offered a Tri-Power setup consisting of three two-barrel carbs.

Despite some performance shortcomings compared to its rival, the B09-optioned F-85 Cutlass was well-regarded for its performance and handling prowess. Period reviews praised its handling characteristics thanks to its addition of rear sway bars, stiffer springs and shocks, and wider wheels than the standard F-85 Cutlass. Plus, its 310 horses could rocket it from 0-60 mph in roughly 7.5 seconds, though this was about a half-second slower than the '64 GTO.

It wasn't long before Oldsmobile had the idea to exchange the not-so-exciting B09 name for something better. The package was renamed 442, which originally stood for 4-barrel carburetor, 4 on the floor, dual exhausts. By the end of 1964, Oldsmobile had sold 2,999 Cutlass 442s. The model entered 1965 with a few big changes — the largest being an all-new 400-cubic-inch V8, pumping out 345 GTO-fighting horsepower  and 440 pound-feet of torque.

Come 1968, GM's A-Body platform — upon which the Cutlass was based — was given a redesign. At the same time, the 442 shifted from being an option package to a standalone model based on the Cutlass. In 1970, the 442 saw its most powerful iteration yet, with up to 370 horsepower on tap courtesy of a 455-cubic-inch V8. From there, horsepower figures began to drop as new emissions standards took effect, with the 442 moniker being relegated to something reminiscent of an appearance package beginning in 1975.

The 442's final swan song took place in 1991 as an option package for the front-wheel drive Oldsmobile Cutlass Calais. From there, Oldsmobile would only survive as a brand for another 13 years before its final model would roll off the assembly line. Had it not been for the B09 package, Olds may have never been able to break into the muscle car game, and may never have made a name for the 442 as the comfortable car with an attitude.

#5562. GRIDSERVE Secures £420 Million Financing to Strengthen Leadership Position in EV Charging & Support Next Phase of Growth

London, UK — GRIDSERVE, the UK’s most-used electric vehicle (EV) charging network, has secured a £420 million financing package, marking a significant milestone in the company’s financial development and providing a strengthened funding platform for its next phase of growth.

One of the largest financing packages of its kind in the EV charging sector, the deal comprises a £240 million loan to refinance existing debt, a £165 million capital expenditure facility to fund future investment in the network and a £15 million revolving credit facility to support working capital and liquidity.

Structured as green senior debt under GRIDSERVE’s Green Finance Framework, the financing was anchored by the National Wealth Fund, Crédit Agricole CIB, NatWest and Rabobank as cornerstone lenders, each acting as Mandated Lead Arranger alongside MUFG, with MUFG also acting as Sole Financial Advisor. The package strengthens the company’s long-term funding position, providing greater financial flexibility and dedicated capital to support its ongoing investment in critical UK EV charging infrastructure.

The refinancing also reflects the significant financial progress GRIDSERVE has made under CEO Daniel Kunkel. In 2025, the company reported positive EBITDA for the first time in its history, following a renewed focus on disciplined investment, utilisation-led growth and capital efficiency. The new financing structure builds on this progress, providing a robust foundation for sustainable growth and continued investment in the business.

Since opening its first EV charging station in Braintree in 2020, GRIDSERVE has established itself as a leading force in the transition to electric mobility. Its nationwide network now supports an average of 350,000 charging sessions every month across more than 200 locations. GRIDSERVE also remains the only UK charging operator to have invested in a dedicated interoperability testing facility, helping to underpin its 99% availability record and ensure that new electric vehicle models, regardless of manufacturer, can charge seamlessly across its network.

Alongside continued investment in its existing network, the new capital expenditure facility will support GRIDSERVE’s next phase of expansion, including the development of ultra-rapid EV charging provision beyond the motorway network.

Daniel Kunkel, CEO of GRIDSERVE, said: “Securing this refinancing package is a significant milestone for GRIDSERVE and reflects the progress we have made over the last year. We have demonstrated that our network can grow sustainably, supported by a disciplined approach to investment, utilisation and capital efficiency.

“The strength of this financing package, and the confidence shown in us by our lending partners, puts GRIDSERVE in a strong position for the future. It reinforces our long-term commitment to the UK and gives us the funding platform to continue investing in the infrastructure needed to decarbonise road transport. We look forward to building on this momentum as we enter the next phase of our growth.”

Oliver Holbourn, National Wealth Fund CEO, said: “Drivers need confidence that reliable charging will be available where they need it before making the switch to electric. By lending alongside commercial banks, the National Wealth Fund is supporting GRIDSERVE’s continued investment in its network, including plans to expand ultra-rapid charging beyond motorways. This is about backing the infrastructure that makes cleaner transport a practical choice for more people.”

Priya Veerapen, Managing Director, Infracapital, said, “GRIDSERVE has made significant progress since our investment in 2022, and this £420 million refinancing marks an important next step in its growth. Alongside TPG, we have invested more than £300 million in the business, reflecting our conviction in the long-term need for high-quality EV charging infrastructure and the important role GRIDSERVE can play in delivering it across the UK.”

Jamie Gilbert, Business Unit Partner at TPG Rise Climate, said: “The strength of this refinancing reflects the quality of GRIDSERVE’s business and the progress the company has made in establishing itself as a leader in UK EV charging. It also underscores the importance of continued investment in the infrastructure needed to support the UK’s transition to electric mobility.”

#5560. What Chinese Designers Say Will Sell With Americans

You might rightly think you already know the answer to this question: Nothing. Because the Chinese and American markets are profoundly different. Just consider EV adoption. So far in 2026, 53% of all new cars sold in China are EVs. In the U.S., that number is just 6.4%.

But Michael Tropper, one of the co-founders of the London- and Amsterdam-based design house forpeople, has spent the past two decades studying the Chinese market and living in China. Part of his work has focused on a partnership with the carmaker, Nio, a brand you've perhaps never heard of, but which took in over $13.1 billion in 2025 and sold 326,028 cars. Just to contextualize that sales figure, it's about 55% of the 589,160 Teslas sold in the U.S. in 2025, but almost eight times the 42,247 Rivians sold in the U.S. last year.

Tropper says forpeople has worked with Nio across all of its branding, from logo design through its massive, 4,236-station battery-swapping network. Tropper cites this as one aspect American carmakers could learn from: the struggle of public charging, and carmakers not making charging integral to ownership. Nio's swaps take a mere three minutes. Pause and think — you can't fill a gas car that quickly. Nio's network conducts 110,000 battery swaps every day, completing a battery swap every 0.77 seconds.

"Rather than starting with the car and its features," Tropper explained in an interview with Jalopnik, "Nio looked at the entire EV ownership experience and the frustrations users faced. That thinking led to services like ... battery swapping [and] battery-as-a-service ... all designed to make ownership easier and build a closer relationship with customers."

Here are several more innovations from Chinese brands that Tropper thinks will translate for U.S. customers — and a few that may not.

The Nio Firefly was originally designed for a European buyer. Once Europe decided to put tariffs on some Chinese car brands, though, the carmaker shifted, Tropper said, putting the car on sale in China first. It later got to Europe, though, and Tropper said this speaks well to its broad appeal. Part of what they were aiming for, he said, was "a spirited ... simple, characterful design." Another way to put this, Tropper said, is that the Firefly's look has "optimism and isn't kind of boring, but still appeals to really a wide variety of audiences."

Asked why that works, he said it depends. For instance, when it was first shown we wrote that the Rivian R3X is a rally EV you want to buy. But what, specifically, grabbed the public's imagination? Tropper answered that the R3X "borrows the character of classic rally cars without being tied to that history. It feels familiar but still genuinely new."

By contrast, he added, looking at other EV makers, "Scout is drawing on genuine heritage. Slate is taking a different approach, bringing back simplicity, a non-automotive, more product-design approach with a focus on tactile interactions. Lucid, meanwhile, are taking a more future-facing approach."

Tropper sees all these approaches as positive, because they're not monolithic. "I think that's healthy. As EV technology becomes increasingly similar, design becomes more important in giving brands distinction. There's room for different approaches, as long as they're authentic to the brand."

Tropper said one facet that's hugely important in design is trust, so one reason a Rivian might borrow rally overtones even without its own brand history is to give our brains an iconography we can identify. "Chinese brands are looking to the future. Western brands are increasingly looking to their past. In a market full of futuristic EVs, a familiar design can be a powerful way to stand out."

But to put a finer point on trust, he said, a car can't feel cheap. "On a product level, it's ... precision in the way that the product's put together, the feeling of even small interactions like opening the door handle or lifting the hood. ... It's those kind of micro details that can often also trigger the sense of trust ... and those more tactile interactions that you have with the product."

Forpeople studied this kind of interaction for Nio, Tropper said, and these tiny instances amount to "a, like, psychological neurological level, right? In terms of the way you perceive those interactions and that kind of engineering, and how it makes you feel. Whether you have a sense of peace of mind or whether you feel kind of on edge."

He explained that consumers don't build brand trust — or brand mistrust — in ways we can necessarily articulate, or from only looking at a product or touching it. It's "not necessarily .... just what you see, but also kind of from sound to lighting to ... even scent."

While Slate is obviously not a Chinese brand, the carmaker calls to mind something for Tropper that he thinks will matter increasingly in a digitized space: redefining ownership around the ease of customization. The Slate comes as a kind of skateboard you can convert from a truck into an SUV (though there are costs for the Slate Truck SUV conversion kit). The point for Tropper is that it allows customization and bedazzling that too many products are closed to.

"Owners can convert their pickup into an SUV after purchase, while collaborations with brands like Crayola open up new forms of personalization. The interesting shift is from buying a finished product to owning something that can evolve with you. That creates a very different relationship between customers and brands." He said Slate is smart to partner with Crayola, and such collabs are no accident. "They borrow credibility quite quickly from the other brands that they partner with ... and that can be quite powerful."

In terms of modularity, forpeople works with a Portuguese startup called Amble whose first vehicle, the Amble One, is like a highly customizable mashup between a golf cart and a Jeep. "Car design historically, all the focus has been on sort of changing colors and materials. But I think actually allowing you to tailor the vehicle to different use cases, like Amble, it's kind of allowing you to transition between the passenger vehicle to a cargo vehicle, to a pickup and a utility vehicle."

He said that interactivity with a car that's like a set of Legos has huge branding upside. "For me, the brands that succeed will give people more control over their space, their experience. That could become a more meaningful definition of luxury."

Tropper sees both a challenge and great design upside within the realms of AI and autonomous driving. On the former, he imagines much more than the voice control of the present, where you can use an assistant to change satellite radio stations. For instance, he said, "Rather than choosing from fixed apps, imagine cars generating applications and experiences in real time, from personalized games for children to interactive travel guides."

He also thinks that while proximity features already automate some aspects of our lives, where "getting into your car can automatically switch off appliances at home ... AI will take this much further. Rather than relying on preset routines or explicit commands, these systems will increasingly learn our habits, understand context, and anticipate needs we haven't even expressed."

For Nio, forpeople helped develop the character of an AI assistant called Nomi. It looks like a face on the car's dashboard, and Tropper said his team thought a great deal about making the AI understand that it's operating where your attention is divided. "You're not at a computer. You're not able to focus as deeply. So how do you interface with it in a different way?"

And that relationship gets deeper when the car is driving you, he said. "As people start to use robotaxis, we're now at this building-trust moment ... You want to really understand what the machine is is thinking, what it's perceiving, and have a different kind of way of communicating with the vehicle and it being able to give you little signals about what its intentions are. I think there's a really interesting space for design there, to help with that."

Forpeople's work has gone well beyond AI. For instance, Tropper said, with Nio's new ES9 SUV flagship the design house wanted to explore "how sound, light, scent, and the physical environment could be orchestrated to create more immersive experiences." This led to a system of "coordinating over 100 vehicle functions into a connected sensory experience." If non-drivers want to be entertained while in transit, or the vehicle is parked and the driver wants to take part, occupants can watch a film or TV show. During it, "lighting responds to the visuals, spatial audio surrounds passengers, and seats and suspension move with the action. Even airflow and scent can reinforce what's happening on screen."

That's compared to, say, just the audio system playing the soundtrack in theater mode. "The shift is from adding isolated sensory features to orchestrating the entire cabin as one responsive experience." It's integrated with the car's AI, too. "The ES9's Nomi AI assistant understands natural conversation and responds to passengers' requests," Tropper said. "Its five-zone climate system adjusts to individual preferences, even directing airflow based on seat position and sunlight."

Tropper said that car dealers are an issue when it comes to making a lot of innovations stick, because they're about sales, not the brand. For Nio, forpeople created a kind of clubhouse model that's similar to Rivian's non-dealership Spaces, because Rivian doesn't have dealerships.

"The real opportunity is creating places people genuinely want to spend time. That's what we explored with Nio House ... We helped develop the original concept and spatial experience, bringing together a café, forum, library and kids' club."

What works, he explained, is not faking it. "Authenticity is key. These spaces need to be genuinely useful and credible, rather than brands stretching into areas where they don't belong. Much of Nio House's activity is driven by users themselves, organizing events and sharing interests. You can't manufacture community, but you can create the conditions for it."

But Tropper said a clubhouse and community are kind of gravy; you're not going to get that to work without everything else. "Quality comes back to the fundamentals: safety, build quality, durability and reliability. People want cars that feel well made, deliver the range they promise, and work properly years down the line. That now extends to software, too — it should work seamlessly, updates should improve the experience, and problems should be resolved quickly."

None of which sounds particularly Chinese. It sounds like an honest bargain. And being able to mod your car your way sounds profoundly American. The AI part? You tell us. But, you know, getting rid of car dealers? Where do we sign!

Monta, the global EV charging software platform, and ChargeHub, operator of Passport Hub, North America’s leading EV roaming platform, today announced a partnership that connects Monta’s charging station management system (CSMS) to Passport Hub. Through this single integration, charge point operators (CPOs) running on Monta’s software, including established U.S. networks such as EnviroSpark, FLASH, and Get Charged, will become discoverable and payable for drivers across dozens of automakers, charging apps, fleets, and other eMSPs already connected to Passport Hub.

Monta’s CPO customers will be connected to Passport Hub automatically, at no additional cost. As the integration rolls out, operators will gain real-time visibility of their stations’ location, availability and pricing across the Passport Hub network. Drivers will also be able to activate stations remotely from partner apps, including the ChargeHub app, used by more than 1 million drivers annually.

Monta opened its U.S. headquarters in Miami in 2024 after achieving a leading position in the European charging software space. The agreement will accelerate its North American growth by giving its customers access to the continent’s roaming demand, without having to negotiate and maintain dozens of bilateral OCPI connections. That’s the standard we aim to bring to the North American market,” said Casper Rasmussen, CEO of Monta. “Connecting to Passport Hub lets every North American operator on Monta reach the continent’s major driver apps and automakers through one integration, with the roaming revenue deposited immediately in their operator wallet, so they can focus on running excellent—and busy—charging networks.”

“Every time a world-class CSMS like Monta joins Passport Hub, the whole ecosystem levels up,” said Simon Ouellette, CEO of ChargeHub. “Monta brings deep operational know-how from some of the most mature charging markets in the world, and with one connection, entire networks open up to roaming.
