#5558. Consumer Reports' Best Compact SUVs Ranked By Interior Space (And What That Will Fit)

The compact crossover market is absolutely stacked with options these days, with practically every manufacturer pushing one of these lifted hatchbacks into production. Some are better than others, though, which is where Consumer Reports comes in. Our pals at CR have gathered their impressions of every compact SUV and ranked them by road test data, comfort, safety, predicted reliability, and predicted customer satisfaction. Since they've already done the hard work, we thought it would be fun to pick out the six top-rated machines and see how they compare on just one metric: cargo capacity. And we're going to do it with a twist.

It's nice to know which vehicles in the class come highly rated, but maybe you have some practicality questions a ranking just can't answer. Consumer Reports will tell you that a Lexus NX Hybrid (photo above) is a better car than a Ford Escape, but you already knew that. So we're going to give you some weird real-world cargo space applications.

What kinds of things do you really want to carry in your compact crossover? Maybe you have a trio of Belgian Malinois that hate each other and need to be crated and separated. Could you haul a minibike? Do you need to deliver cases of beer across state lines because the boys are thirsty in Atlanta and there's beer in Texarcana? Maybe you're a tennis instructor, or you're hauling pizzas for a birthday party. Here are the facts on which of these cars is best for you, and why.

Based solely on Consumer Reports' scoring metrics, the best compact SUV on the market today is the powerful, efficient Subaru Forester Hybrid. It scored better than the standard Forester, because the hybrid is quieter and more pleasant taking off from a stop. And it had a higher score than the much more expensive Lexus NX Hybrid or Porsche's popular Macan. By the time you get to its own tax bracket, the Forester Hybrid trounces the better-than-its-gas-version Toyota Corolla Cross Hybrid, the Nissan Kicks, and the tariff-hampered Mazda CX-30. There are over a dozen other players in the class, but we're going to keep to these six for our comparison.

Because we want to know the maximum amount of something each of these vehicles can carry, we're going to only concern ourselves with the cargo volume with the rear passenger seats folded. Standard EPA cargo volume is typically measured from the front sliding seat in its rearmost position, and vertical measurement taken from a horizontal tangent to the top of the seatback.

How do these six machines compare if you're rating them only on the size of their cargo areas? The Corolla Cross is the smallest of the six at just 44 cubic feet, just shy of the Mazda's 45.2 cubic feet, and the Lexus NX Hybrid's 46.9 cubic feet. From there it's a pretty big jump to the other three, with the Macan coming in at 53.1 cubic feet, the Nissan Kicks jumping up to 60 cubic feet, and the Subaru Forester Hybrid winning again at 70.7 cubic feet.

To provide some context as to the sizes of the cargo areas in these vehicles, we'll start with some normal everyday items you might want to haul with your small crossover. Because of the varying shapes of these cars, we're going to work with large quantities of small items that can conform to the specified box.

Let's begin with tennis balls. Everyone carries around a car full of unpackaged tennis balls at least once a year, right? It's good to know just which car will carry the quantity of tennis balls you need to haul. Obviously spheres can't fill 100% of the space, so we have to assume a 74% efficiency rate when dense packing equal spheres. The volume of a tennis ball is about 9.15 cubic inches, and a cubic foot is 1,728 cubic inches, meaning we can fit 139.75 tennis balls in each cubic foot. The Corolla Cross, with its cargo area filled to the brim, could carry 6,149 tennis balls, while the Forester Hybrid could haul 9,880 of them.

Or let's say you're hosting a birthday party and you need to carry a bunch of Costco pizzas. These pizzas come in boxes measuring 18.5 x 18.5 x 2 inches. The Nissan Kicks measures 55.7 inches from the back of the front seats to the hatch, meaning you should just barely be able to get three Costco pizzas deep in the back. According to Edmunds' cargo capacity test, the Kicks is at least 38 inches wide, so you could go two pizzas wide. Let's not get too hectic here and say we're stacking pizzas about 2½ feet high, meaning we can get stacks up to 15 pizzas tall. That's 90 pizzas!

Porsche touts the standard gasoline-powered Macan as "easily accomodating" two full-size golf bags or four roller suitcases, even with the rear seats up. Due to the car's sloping roofline, it might be difficult to get three large dogs in the back, but Porsche does sell three different-sized zip-up inflatable dog transport boxes for the Macan's back hatch.

The largest of these is made for dogs sized up to about 90 pounds, while you could fit two of the smallest ones side-by-side if you had a pair of Pekinese or something. All of them allow for the dog to be crated behind the rearmost seat, so you could still have rear-seat passengers. If you're picking a smaller SUV like this, you'll have to be wise about what kind of dog fits your car.

Here's a nice theoretical for you. You're out traveling the neighborhoods at yard sales next summer and you come across a small minibike and exchange a crisp $20 bill for it. It'll make a nice little project for you and your kid to bond over, and they'll have some fun ripping around the neighborhood, annoying Carol from the homeowners' association down the street, which you see as an added bonus. Can you get it home in your Lexus NX?

Something like the Rascal 212 Off-Road mini bike measures about 45 inches long, and 37 inches tall at the handlebars. Obviously you'll want the fuel tank to be empty so as not to spill, but as Autoblog's test shows the NX cargo area is at least 44 inches wide and NX owners on lexusnsforum indicate the height of the opening is just a smidge over 37 inches, it should fit without issue, assuming you fold at least one chunk of the 60/40 rear seats.

Now we've reached the answer to the question everyone wants to know: Just how much beer can you fit in the back of a Mazda CX-30? According to a CX-30 owner's measurements at cx30talk, with the seats folded the rear cargo area measures about 59 inches deep, 39.5 inches wide at the narrowest, and 29.5 inches in height at the rear opening. A standard 24-pack of 12-fluid-ounce cans of beer is 5.4 inches long, 10.15 inches high, and 15.07 inches wide. As with the pizzas in our earlier example, we'll just math it out.

The CX-30 should fit 10 packs laying down flat, which can theoretically be stacked five cases high. That alone is 50 full cases of beer, or 1,200 cans. There's still room for a few to be added handle-side up around the perimeter, two high. By my estimation, there's space for 12 more cases around the edge, for a grand total of 62 cases, or 1,488 cans. If you get creative you might be able to Tetris in another case or two, but we'll call it there for now.

There's just one problem here. The Mazda CX-30's maximum payload capacity, including the combined weight of all passengers and cargo, is just 850 pounds. With a case of beer weighing in at 18 pounds, those 62 cases add up to 1,116 pounds! The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says the average American man weighs 199 pounds, leaving you just 651 pounds of beer to work with if you're a guy driving to pick them up alone. You can reasonably only haul 36 cases of beer, so you'll either have to make a second trip, or cut some people from the guest list for this weekend's rager.

#5557. New Obesity Definition Flags More Adults at Dementia Risk

— Dementia risk shifts as obesity definition expands

A new definition of obesity identified more adults with an increased risk of dementia compared with defining obesity by body mass index (BMI) alone, pooled data from two cohorts showed.

Using the European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO) definition, more than 80% of adults classified as overweight were reclassified as having obesity, according to Rui Zhou, PhD, of Guangdong Pharmaceutical University in Guangzhou, China, and co-authors.

Compared with people of normal weight without comorbidities, those with EASO-defined obesity had a significantly higher risk of dementia (pooled HR 1.93, 95% CI 1.50-2.48), Zhou and colleagues reported in Neurology.

Those with EASO-defined overweight, on the other hand, had a lower risk of dementia than those with normal weight (pooled HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.45-0.81).

The EASO framework incorporates BMI, body fat distribution (waist-to-height ratio), and medical, functional, or psychological comorbidities.

"These findings underscore the inadequacy of using BMI alone to define obesity," Zhou said in a statement. "The results support the integration of body fat distribution and other health conditions into classifying obesity."

Obesity is linked with dementia, with midlife obesity having an especially high risk. Evidence from both animal and human studies suggests that obesity negatively affects the brain through multiple mechanisms, including hypothalamic dysregulation and metabolic, inflammatory, and vascular disruptions that target the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex.

The BMI definition of obesity has drawn criticism in recent years, leading to alternative frameworks from groups like EASO and the Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology global commission.

The implications of the new obesity definitions for dementia risk have been unclear, Zhou and co-authors noted. To help clarify this, they compared the prevalence of obesity under the EASO framework versus traditional BMI criteria and examined how obesity was associated with incident dementia and all-cause mortality.

The study used data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA; 6,542 people) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS; 12,402 people).

The researchers defined dementia using algorithmic criteria or self-reported physician diagnoses, and determined all-cause mortality from death registries, medical records, or interviews with relatives. They included 17,617 participants in the dementia analysis and 18,197 in the mortality analysis.

The mean baseline age in the ELSA group was 65.9 years and 54.3% were women. In CHARLS, the mean baseline age was 58.2 and 53.2% were women. The median follow-up was 11.5 years in ELSA and 8.2 years in CHARLS.

Under the EASO framework, 85.8% of ELSA participants and 80.2% of CHARLS participants who were previously classified as overweight by BMI shifted to the obesity category.

Overall, 37.7% of ELSA participants and 24.9% of CHARLS participants had obesity using the EASO definition. The most common comorbidities in the newly defined obesity group were high blood pressure (42.6%) and diabetes (35.1%).

Compared with people with normal weight and no comorbidities, people with EASO-defined obesity had higher dementia risk in both cohorts. They had higher mortality risk only in the CHARLS cohort, but the pooled mortality estimate was significant (pooled HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.01-1.68).

EASO-defined overweight was associated with lower dementia risk in both cohorts and with lower mortality (pooled HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.13-0.81).

The so-called "obesity paradox" seen in earlier studies may stem from failures to account for obesity-related comorbidities or to exclude unhealthy individuals from comparison groups, the researchers suggested.

When normal weight without morbidity was the reference in this study, both EASO-defined and BMI-defined obesity were consistently associated with increased dementia risk, they noted. "However, when all normal weight individuals (including those with comorbidities) were used as the reference, these harmful associations were masked," Zhou and colleagues pointed out.

Obesity was measured only at baseline, and changes over time were not captured, the researchers acknowledged. Despite adjusting for multiple variables, residual confounding cannot be excluded.

#5555. Why European Households Are Rushing to Buy Solar Panels Ahead of a Dark, Cold Winter

Changes to solar incentives and long installation processes mean European homeowners could benefit from planning now.

Winter is cold, dark, and grey. Yet for many Europeans, it’s a great time to switch to solar power.

While many are focused on the holiday season, industry experts are urging homeowners considering a switch to solar to contact suppliers before Christmas — although not to take advantage of the winter sun.

Several European countries are making changes to solar energy subsidies and tax breaks in 2027, meaning homeowners might want to fast-track their plans to enjoy the financial benefits.

But even without changes to government incentives, there are good reasons to get ahead of the spring sunshine.

Although a typical rooftop solar installation takes just one or two days, getting building permits and, in some cases, approval to connect to electricity grids can take weeks. Sometimes months.

Last year, an OECD report citing earlier research found that permit times for rooftop solar projects ranged from six weeks in Malta to as many as 10 months in Bulgaria.

The country has since made it easier for homeowners, scrapping permit requirements for solar systems up to 20 kilowatts intended for personal use, but delays are still common across Europe.

In Germany, a consumer watchdog warned last year that homeowners in Saxony were waiting months to have their solar panels connected to the grid — and, in extreme cases, more than a year.

And Edward Gurney, the founding director of the UK-based Solar and Battery Company, says getting approval from electricity providers can take four to five weeks even under normal circumstances.

“A lot of solar equipment is manufactured in China, and getting replacement stock delivered can take around six weeks,” he says.

Winter weather can also disrupt installation schedules, as icy roofs make working conditions unsafe.

“When you’ve already got a busy installation schedule, losing even a few days to bad weather can push subsequent installations back,” Gurney says.

Waiting until the weather warms up could mean missing out on a prime period for solar production, too.

Solar power generated less than five per cent of the EU’s electricity in January last year, but by May, it was supplying more than 20 percent, according to the European Environment Agency.

In Germany alone, 74 per cent of the solar electricity fed into the grid last year was generated between April and September.

The sooner homeowners have their panels installed, the sooner they can start benefitting from this springtime bump.

In the meantime, Gurney recommends using winter to assess how much electricity you might use and compare quotations from different installers.

“The number of panels, battery capacity and how much electricity your household uses will all affect the long-term value of the installation,” he says.

Homeowners in several European countries could face changes to the cost of installing solar panels in 2027. Since April 2022, homeowners in England, Scotland and Wales have been able to have solar panels installed without paying value-added tax. From 1 April 2027, the tax rate will return to five per cent.

In Germany, people who install solar panels from January onward could miss out on government support unless new energy laws are approved before the end of the year, the German Solar Industry Association warns.

Although German lawmakers have tentatively agreed to continue paying homeowners for surplus electricity they sell to the grid from solar systems up to 25 kilowatts, they have yet to strike a final deal.

And in Austria, the government plans to stop offering grants for solar panels in 2027 and instead help homeowners buy batteries to store the electricity they generate.

Source: Euronews via EIN PRESSWIRE. By Craig Sauers

#5552. Europe’s Industrial Future Does Not Depend on Making Every Ton of Hydrogen

An industrial policy that starts with domestic hydrogen production targets can end up making European manufacturing more expensive. Chemical plants need ammonia. Steelmakers need suitable iron inputs. Neither necessarily needs to produce the hydrogen used to manufacture those materials within the European Union.

The difference is already visible in industrial trade. In September 2025, Trafigura loaded 23,500 tons of certified lower-carbon ammonia from CF Industries’ Donaldsonville plant in Louisiana for Envalior in Antwerp. Envalior intended to use the ammonia to produce caprolactam, an input for engineering materials. The American ammonia was manufactured from natural gas with carbon capture. It was a lower-carbon shipment, not an example of renewable hydrogen production.

The chemical division of labor matters. Producing ammonia requires hydrogen, but buying ammonia for chemical production does not require a separate supply of hydrogen. Its hydrogen is already incorporated into the ammonia molecule. The European plant buys the chemical it needs and continues its manufacturing operations. The upstream hydrogen plant is located where the ammonia is made.

Many proposed hydrogen import corridors take a longer route. Ammonia is manufactured abroad, shipped to Europe, then cracked back into hydrogen for domestic users. Cracking adds industrial equipment and energy consumption. A refinery buying hydrogen and a chemical plant buying ammonia have different requirements. Infrastructure serving one should not be assumed necessary for the other.

Primary iron offers another example. Hot-briquetted iron, or HBI, is a transportable form of direct-reduced iron. Voestalpine is constructing an HBI supply system in Linz to feed its planned electric arc furnace. Much of the HBI will arrive from Texas through the port of Koper in Slovenia and travel onward by rail. Iron reduction takes place abroad while steelmaking and finishing remain in Austria.

The Texas route uses natural gas for iron reduction. Its significance is that ironmaking and steelmaking can take place in different countries. A future supply chain using qualified low-emissions iron could build on the same commercial separation, subject to product quality, carbon accounting and delivered price.

Europe’s energy and industrial planners should begin with the products its factories need. For ammonia, that means chemical grade, carbon intensity, contracted supply and price at the plant gate. For iron, it means grade, metallic yield, emissions performance and dependable deliveries. These requirements determine which domestic and imported production routes deserve investment.

The location of upstream production still has consequences. Domestic ammonia and primary iron plants provide skilled jobs, technical capabilities and some insulation from international disruption. Imports can reduce costs for downstream manufacturers but increase exposure to overseas suppliers. Europe should price those benefits and risks rather than using them as reasons to assume domestic hydrogen production in every industrial pathway.

The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism adds another factor: imports must be assessed against the applicable embedded-emissions rules and product coverage. It does not require the same production technology on both sides of the border.

That is the sequence I used in TFIE Strategy’s independent submission to the European Commission’s renewed hydrogen strategy consultation on November 11. A reproducible Python model compares domestic production, imported industrial products and competing technologies across selected industrial and transport markets. An evidence workbook and interactive dashboard show how hydrogen requirements change when import capacity, electricity costs and production routes change. The submission asks planners to test proposed infrastructure against that demand, rather than assuming demand to justify the infrastructure.

#5551. Antihypertensives Still Worth It for the Healthiest 10%, Large Study Suggests

— Drop in major cardiovascular events evident across spectrum of predicted risk

Across hypertensive individuals with varying predicted cardiovascular risk, blood pressure (BP) reduction was associated with a lower occurrence of real major cardiovascular events, according to a meta-analysis.

Using individual participant data from randomized trials, investigators found that major cardiovascular events were significantly less likely with every 5-mm Hg reduction in systolic BP from pharmacotherapy over 5 years (11.4% vs 13.0% with placebo or other control; HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.88-0.92).

This arguably covered people across the whole spectrum of cardiovascular health, as indicated by a study-specific risk model that put people with 5-year predicted risk <4% in the lowest decile and those with estimated risk >27% in the highest decile, reported Kazem Rahimi, DM, MSc, of the University of Oxford in England, and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine.

"BP lowering was associated with a decreased risk of major cardiovascular events across the risk spectrum, including a predicted 5-year risk below 4%," the researchers concluded.

The study adds to the limited literature on BP-lowering treatment in low-risk populations. Without better evidence, guideline recommendations for BP reduction in these individuals had been based on the assumption that the observed benefits of BP-lowering therapy in higher-risk individuals may be extrapolated to peers at lower risk.

"Many of the hypertensive trials, such as the SPRINT trial, have noted cardiovascular risk reduction in a high-risk group of patients with antihypertensive therapy. This meta-analysis shows that antihypertensive therapy reduces cardiovascular events across the risk spectrum and notably low-risk patients have a similar relative risk reduction as higher-risk patients," commented Matthew Sorrentino, MD, of University of Chicago Medicine.

Nevertheless, Rahimi's team found that the greatest absolute reduction in cardiovascular events occurred in the highest-risk group. The number needed to treat to prevent one major cardiovascular event over 5 years was 38 in the highest decile of predicted risk versus 255 in the lowest decile.

This is to be expected, according to Sorrentino. "The number needed to treat in a low-risk population will be significantly higher than in a high-risk cohort because of a lower incidence of events in the low-risk group, but the important finding is that risk reduction can be demonstrated in the low-risk cohort."

"Antihypertensive therapy will benefit anyone with consistently elevated BP regardless of calculated risk," he stressed.

Sorrentino said that the study supports the American Heart Association and the American College of Cardiology guideline on BP treatment, which does not suggest holding treatment in lower-risk individuals unable to achieve BP target with a lifestyle program.

Starting in 2025, the American groups said that low-risk individuals with an estimated 10-year cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk <7.5% (based on the PREVENT-CVD calculator) should initiate antihypertensives if average systolic BP remains at least 130 mm Hg (or average diastolic BP remains at least 80 mm Hg) after 3-6 months of lifestyle intervention, a class I recommendation.

Of note, Rahimi's team had an internal risk estimator for the meta-analysis, not PREVENT or another calculator used in clinical practice.

"This study is helpful to help us understand how BP lowering can be important even in lower-risk groups. While not all risk calculators are comparable, the overarching message is the same," maintained Sadiya Khan, MD, MSc, of Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago.

"The key thing we know is that treating BP may be one of the most important things we can do to prevent cardiovascular disease even if someone may be at lower risk," she told MedPage Today. "If they are at higher risk, they will get much more absolute benefit from the treatment, so for individuals who have already had a heart attack or stroke, this could not be more important."

For their meta-analysis, Rahimi and colleagues relied on individual participant data from 51 randomized trials comparing antihypertensive treatment with placebo, an active comparator, or usual care.

The 357,440-person cohort had a mean age of 65 years and was 42% women. Mean baseline BP was 152.4/87.3 mm Hg, and the median predicted 5-year risk of a major cardiovascular event was 12.3%.

The primary outcome of interest was a first major cardiovascular event (i.e., stroke, ischemic heart disease, or heart failure resulting in death or hospitalization). Studies reached a median follow-up of 4.2 years in this report.

As for safety, the investigators opted for a narrower evidence base of 19 trials that compared antihypertensive treatment with placebo or usual care. The three prespecified safety outcomes consistently trended higher with the former:

Patients of all predicted risk levels shared an increase in the risk of safety events with antihypertensive treatment.

"Because the absolute reduction in the 5-year cumulative incidence of a major cardiovascular event in lower deciles was smaller than in higher deciles and the relative risk of adverse events was similar across the risk spectrum, the balance between benefit and harm narrowed as the predicted risk decreased and is unlikely to be captured by any single risk or BP threshold," Rahimi and colleagues noted.

"Quantifying this balance would require methods that account for differences in the severity, duration, and irreversibility of the outcomes concerned, which was beyond the scope of this analysis," they cautioned.

Rahimi's group also acknowledged that event counts under trial conditions may differ from those in routine practice, where the duration of treatment is often shorter and typically characterized by lower adherence and less protocolized care.

#5550. HLTH 2026: Elsevier upgrades ClinicalKey AI with full patient EHR context

HLTH 2026: Elsevier upgrades ClinicalKey AI with full patient EHR context" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Elsevier unveiled this week a major upgrade to ClinicalKey AI, enabling the AI-powered clinical decision support tool to access a patient’s full electronic health record and evaluate treatment plans against the company’s evidence-based medical library.

As AI advances, Elsevier has strategically shifted from a traditional academic publisher—it’s one of the world's largest publishers of scientific, technical and medical content—to an AI-driven analytics information company, incorporating generative and agentic AI into its healthcare and academic research.

ClinicalKey AI is a HIPAA-ready point-of-care decision support tool that draws answers from articles sourced from approximately 1,000 world-leading journals. Elsevier’s upgraded ClinicalKey AI is already deployed at more than 1,200 hospitals, and the company says the solution integrates with all EHR providers. Elsevier recently struck a content agreement with the JAMA Network that brings full-text content and visuals from the JAMA Network Family of Journals to ClinicalKey AI.

ClinicalKey AI was originally co-developed through a strategic partnership between Elsevier and OpenEvidence. An Elsevier spokesperson said the company's collaboration with OpenEvidence on ClinicalKey AI has concluded.

The company has rapidly expanded its AI capabilities and features, including ClinicalKey Nursing AI, an AI-powered tool built specifically for nurses and nursing workflows. Elsevier has also developed specialized AI assistants, such as LeapSpace, an AI-assisted workspace for researchers that’s built on 15+ million peer-reviewed articles and book content and 100 million Scopus records, according to the company.

Three months ago, the company rolled out its "Ask AI" feature across more than 1,500 U.S. hospital sites using its flagship ClinicalKey platform. With the generative AI feature, clinicians can ask conversational clinical questions and receive direct, cited answers drawn from evidence-based sources, including premium journals and content from leading medical organizations, the company said. Unlike general-purpose chatbots, Ask AI does not pull from the open web and does not store, process or retain patient-identifiable information, according to the company.

In a move to develop context-aware AI, the company acquired Wellsheet in June. The health technology company aggregates and synthesizes patient chart data—including notes, labs, imaging and medication orders—from EHRs to provide relevant clinical intelligence at the bedside.

“The problem we’re trying to solve here is that physicians are challenged by so many things when they’re taking care of patients; top among them is patient complexity. Patients have more and more conditions, and they’re taking more and more medications. It can be hard to really understand the full picture and determine how to proceed,” Dr. Claudine Lott, physician executive for clinical solutions at Elsevier, told Fierce Healthcare during the HLTH conference this week.

“Our original ClinicalKey AI tool has been a place where the clinician can go, and they can ask a question, and it searches this curated database of evidence-based content we’ve given it and gives them an answer. But there was a bit of a missing piece in that it wasn’t capturing that patient context. If you wanted to get an answer, that’s really tailored to a patient, it was limited to what you can type in,” she said.

She added, “Wellsheet has 10 years of experience with looking at the entirety of the patient chart and helping to surface that to the clinician.”

There is a growing market for AI-powered clinical decision support products, but Elsevier contends its advantage lies in its depth of patient context and its large, curated content base, with a wholly owned, large proprietary library of peer-reviewed STM literature, including content from millions of articles, journals and books.

San Juan Regional Medical Center in Farmington, New Mexico, is using ClinicalKey AI’s new patient context functionality to provide quality care with fewer resources. With smaller clinical and quality teams than large academic health systems, and in a state where nearly 40% of residents rely on Medicaid, the medical center, which serves the Four Corners area, has found this support especially valuable, according to Carlo Hallak, M.D., physician executive, information services, at San Juan Regional Medical Center.

A non-profit, community-owned acute care hospital and Level III trauma center, San Juan Regional Medical Center operates outpatient and specialty clinics alongside its main hospital campus, San Juan Regional Rehabilitation Hospital and San Juan Health Partners clinics.

Hallak emphasized that Elsevier is a primary source of medical knowledge rather than a “wrapper” for other AI platforms, and that was a key distinction for the organization, he said. And ClinicalKey AI is designed for the entire care team. “The hospital is run by nurses, mid-level providers, other caregiver teams,” he told Fierce Healthcare at the HLTH conference.

The medical center aims to move clinicians to enterprise LLMs integrated with the electronic health record that can provide the full patient context, Hallak said.

"We're already seeing how ClinicalKey AI can be instrumental at the bedside and help improve care for our patients. As a rural healthcare center, we are proud to say that by using ClinicalKey AI to check each patient’s care against the same evidence base that major health systems rely on, we’re able to deliver the standard of care patients expect in any major city or leading academic center," Hallak said.

He added, "ClinicalKey AI reads the whole chart, checks it against the evidence and shows exactly where each finding comes from. That support is invaluable for a hospital like ours, and we’re already seeing strong adoption of ClinicalKey AI among our clinicians."

Hallak cited an example of a physician who used ClinicalKey AI to correctly identify viral meningitis, preventing an aggressive and unnecessary treatment course for bacterial meningitis.

ClinicalKey AI supports the physician’s judgment rather than replacing it, helping the clinician get to relevant evidence faster, he said, noting that, in the case of the viral meningitis patient, the physician’s clinical judgment was critical in recognizing that something was unusual and then consulting colleagues. The AI tool then helped accelerate the next step by quickly surfacing information the clinician otherwise would have found by searching the medical literature.

Physicians also use the tool during weekly complex case discussions to quickly review trending medications, images and test results in one summarized sheet, he noted.

“It’s going to expedite a lot of the work they do when it comes to these complex cases,” he said.

The AI solution can quickly summarize a complex patient history at the point of care, and this can help care teams in the emergency department understand a frequent ED patient, Hallak said.

One patient has visited their emergency department 95 times in less than a year, in addition to making numerous visits to neighboring health systems, Hallak said. When that patient arrives, clinicians who aren't familiar with him would traditionally have to dig through the chart to understand his history. With Elsevier's ClinicalKey AI tool, they can ask for a summary of the patient's recent visits and care and get that information within seconds, he noted.

Because patients who frequently visit hospital EDs typically receive care at multiple organizations, San Juan Regional Medical Center is also working with other local health systems on interoperability efforts so clinicians can get a more complete picture of what happened during the patient's visits across different facilities.

As a rural hospital with staffing constraints, technology is essential to filling workforce gaps and supporting care delivery, Hallak contends.

"We don't have enough physicians, enough nurses, enough transporters, enough caregivers. We will never be able to have enough of those," he said.

Hallak envisions ClinicalKey AI will be particularly valuable for discharging patients from the hospital faster.

Generative AI tools can help speed up patient discharges by identifying barriers, assessing patients’ care needs and providing relevant information from both structured and unstructured data. Because the platform is designed for the broader care team, case managers and physicians can access the same information, while push notifications can alert clinicians when test results are available so they can act quickly, Hallak said.

"From an operational perspective, it allows for this care team coordination of care, and also from a physician perspective, it provides the context whenever there's something hanging and they're trying to understand more what's happening with the patient['s] discharge. You could be a hospitalist, and you've been off shift for like seven days, and then you come to the hospital and now the patient is on their tenth day, but you inherit that discharge. Going through, reading every progress note for every single day, reading every consult for every subspecialty that looked at this patient usually would take two to three days to actually get the patient out of the building safely," he said.

Rather than manually compiling information for a discharge summary, clinicians can use ClinicalKey AI to aggregate relevant information from across the patient’s record, trace it back to its source and review the AI-generated summary before signing off on the discharge, according to Hallak.

"It is a game changer, in my opinion. One of our hospitals said it used to take me three days to discharge a patient; now it takes me less than three hours," he said.

Going forward, the system expects to measure operational outcomes such as length of stay, safe discharge and multidisciplinary-rounds use, according to Hallak. The medical center also plans to evaluate clinicians' use of the tool and how it changes care decisions.

The medical center has also deployed other AI tools such as Oracle Health's clinical AI agent for ambient documentation.

"These things are crucial. We're hoping to bring in a clinical AI agent for nurses as well to help the whole care team be able to eliminate the noise, the friction that typically EHRs or IT would bring to the conversation," Hallak said.

The medical center is taking a risk-based approach to AI governance, using source verification and peer review for AI-generated summaries while applying greater scrutiny to tools that are predictive or suggestive, Hallak noted. That oversight involves clinical experts as well as compliance, legal and cybersecurity teams along with traditional vendor security and product-vetting requirements.

AI governance should become stricter as the technology moves from summarizing information to recommending or taking actions, he said.

Elsevier designed ClinicalKey AI with security and trust in mind, including HIPAA compliance, citations that show where information comes from and safeguards that keep the tool from prescribing what clinicians should do. Instead, it surfaces relevant information to help clinicians make their own decisions, Lott said.

"Health systems tell us two things stand in the way of adopting AI: tools that don’t work with their existing EHR partners, and concerns about security, compliance and responsible use," Omry Bigger, president of Clinical Solutions at Elsevier, said. "ClinicalKey AI was designed to address both. As an EHR-supported and HIPAA-compliant ready solution, ClinicalKey AI integrates seamlessly across health systems to provide clinicians with trusted evidence and patient context that gives them tailored clinical insights for each patient at the point of care."

#5549. Flock Cameras And Their Contracts Can (And Do) Have State-Specific Provisions

Lately, and far too often, we seem to ask, "What the Flock?" You tired yet? Private citizens across the country are, and interestingly, so are the cities, counties, and towns that hired the Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) company in the first place. Because, (no) thanks to Flock's contracts and a lack of state statutes, breaking up with Flock Safety can be as frustrating as finding bird poop on your freshly washed car.

For example, Flock's Evidence Policy states that customers, who are usually police departments, wholly own and control the data its cameras collect. Except when they don't. Per the company's retention policy, said data is also kept for only seven days by default before being wiped from the cloud server. Except when it isn't: state laws can allow longer retention.

A growing number of cities are dropping Flock camera contracts, but that doesn't mean the data is gone or that the recordings have stopped. Even if garbage bags are thrown over a Flock camera's prying eyes, the police are still watching every move you make. Ostensibly, they're not doing it on purpose, but the rotten apples using ALPR systems for unprofessional reasons get plenty of attention, like the "good cop" who stalked his wife and the bad cops who conducted unlawful data searches. A silver lining is that sharing between agencies, particularly those out of state, is already restricted or outright illegal in some states.

Flock's blanket policy allows customers, whoever they may be, to share data as they see fit to "help solve crime." Where states have stepped in, though, the protections on the use of that data are clarified and far stricter, and any mishandling of it can be subject to penalties.

This isn't the first time a state's provisions have the final say. Look at seat belts. While federal law requires a manufacturer-provided safety belt installed for every seat in a passenger vehicle, states determine whether wearing seat belts is required. For example, even though death is on the line, New Hampshire adults needn't buckle up. Click it or ticket is the rule of thumb everywhere else.

That level of engagement isn't the same with ALPRs, though. What seemed like a good idea at the time has converged into a rare consensus of everyone united in their dislike of Flock cameras, and politicos are just playing catch-up.

According to the National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL), as of September 2026, there are 27 states with ALPR statutes in place with regard to government and law enforcement use. Indiana's rule applies only to homeowners' associations. In that state, the law says HOAs can host ALPRs only if they're installed on behalf of law enforcement, and HOAs cannot access the data. But that's the only specificity, meaning Indiana sets no deadline for deleting plate data. That isn't the case elsewhere.

Connecticut, Maine, Virginia, and Washington have a 21-day deletion deadline. Iowa, Missouri (by executive order), and Oregon have a maximum 30-day window while California (Highway Patrol only) and Minnesota opt for 60 days. Then you've got 90-day limits in Kentucky, Montana, North Carolina, and Tennessee; 120 days in Illinois (in select areas); and 180 days in Nebraska. These are limits for routine data, though. Data tied to an ongoing investigation or court case can generally be stored longer.

California isn't an anomaly (for once): other states are also locking out federal agencies, like ICE, from accessing ALPR data. Connecticut, Illinois, New Jersey, New Mexico, and Washington expressly outlaw sharing of information for immigration enforcement purposes. In some states, the ban also extends to investigations related to receiving health-related care across state lines. Statutes for Connecticut, Illinois, New Mexico, and Washington explicitly state that obtaining certain health services is a protected activity. We already know the government can track supposed abortion travel through your cell phone, but potential prosecution is more difficult without visual evidence of your vehicle near a clinic.

But there remain too many states without additional protections for their constituents, leaving cities fending for themselves if Flock isn't playing fair. That being said, the pushback is bipartisan, with the Flock-Off Act introduced to Congress in September 2026, a positive step toward reversing the now-rampant abuse of the massive surveillance network. In hopes of spinning some positive public relations, Flock Safety provided law enforcement with a guidebook on building trust with cities but also on how to "own the narrative before someone else does." Villains gonna villain.

#5547. Most Lupus Patients in Remission Can Safely Stop Steroids, Study Finds

— No increase in flare risk after stopping, although certain patients may benefit from continuing

For patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in remission, flare risk was not increased after stopping all glucocorticoids in a small Italian study.

Among 480 SLE patients in a prospectively followed cohort achieving remission, of whom 75% had steroids withdrawn, rates of disease flares were actually a bit lower in the off-steroids group compared with a propensity-matched group on low-dose maintenance (2.07 vs 3.44 per 100 patient-years), according to Margherita Zen, MD, PhD, of the University of Padua in Italy, and colleagues.

A propensity-matching analysis confirmed that the rates didn't differ substantially, with a hazard ratio of 0.767 numerically favoring the off-steroids group (P=0.45), the researchers reported in Rheumatology.

But this overall similarity didn't apply to certain subgroups. Zen and colleagues found that patients with cutaneous features, arthritis or myositis, leukopenia, or vasculitis faced statistically significant increases in flare risk with steroid withdrawal versus maintenance, with hazard ratios ranging from 1.9 to 3.5.

These results are potentially important insofar as they can inform clinical decision-making on whether patients with SLE in remission should try having steroids withdrawn. Long-term use, of course, comes with a raft of adverse effects that would be best to avoid. But clinicians have had to balance that with the risks from SLE flares, which can lead to irreversible organ damage along with the pain and discomfort associated with active lupus.

Zen and colleagues cited several previous studies that also found no increase in flare risk with steroid discontinuation, but a 124-patient randomized trial published in 2020 found a fivefold increase in flares with discontinuation. However, Zen's group also pointed out that, in this trial, steroids were not tapered but halted abruptly, which isn't normally done in routine practice. This conflicting evidence suggested another study is needed to provide clear direction.

Theirs isn't exactly that study -- it was not randomized but rather compared patients whose clinicians decided on their own judgment whether to withdraw steroids for SLE patients in remission. Propensity matching certainly helps make the comparison meaningful, but the observational design remains an important limitation.

Patients in the study were members of the prospectively assembled Padua Lupus Cohort, which had enrolled 541 SLE patients as of 2023. The group focused on the 480 who had achieved remission, defined as a SLE Disease Activity Index-2000 (SLEDAI-2K) score of zero on stable drug therapy including steroid doses no greater than 5 mg/day in prednisone equivalents. Any increase in SLEDAI-2K score or change in background medication during follow-up, including restarting steroids, was considered a flare. A total of 358 remitted patients had their steroids tapered, with no prespecified schedule; the other 122 remained on low-dose steroids.

On average, patients taken off steroids differed in a few ways from those chosen to remain on maintenance: they were somewhat younger (mean age 41 vs 46) and had shorter disease duration (mean 12 vs 15 years). Also, leukopenia was more common among those on maintenance (prevalence 49% vs 35%), as was a standard overall measure of organ damage accrual. To make the groups more properly comparable, the propensity-matched analysis winnowed them down to 314 in the withdrawal group and 114 on maintenance.

Flares were relatively uncommon: across 3,423 patient-years of follow-up for the 480 participants in remission, just 86 flares occurred, more often in the maintenance group.

A key concern with flares is the extent to which they cause new organ damage. In the withdrawal group, Zen and colleagues found a numerical association between flares and damage accrual that fell short of statistical significance (incidence rate ratio 1.598 comparing flared vs nonflared patients, P=0.227), and thus not entirely reassuring. But damage accrual was worse in the maintenance group, at an annual rate of 7.14 units per 100 patient-years, versus 3.89 per 100 patient-years after withdrawal -- not unexpected given the higher numerical flare rate with maintenance.

Notably, about half the maintenance group attempted tapering unsuccessfully. Among those who did succeed, the median tapering duration was 17 months (IQR 8-35), suggesting the process was not always easy.

Besides the nonrandomized study design and small numbers of events, other limitations included the lack of prespecified tapering schedules or characteristics of patients for whom to attempt steroid withdrawal. In addition, most patients were white. Zen's group also noted that the baseline for organ damage accrual was set well before tapering attempts began.

#5545. Are People Who Drive Exotics And Luxury Cars Really More Attractive?

Let's face it, cars have never been mere transportation. A Ferrari in the driveway makes a statement. So does a hand-me-down hatchback — just a very different one. Some cars cost millions and are built by the handful, while others are cheap and are built by the millions. For one buyer, a $3.8-million Bugatti Chiron is an acceptable indulgence. For another, spending a cent beyond what it takes to get from A to B makes no sense, even if they can afford it.

Income, culture, personality, and upbringing all pull buyers in different directions, and appearances matter more to some people than others. So does an exotic or luxury car actually make its owner more attractive? The short answer: it's complicated. When women rate a man's attractiveness, a prestige car can sometimes help, but the evidence is thinner than the stereotype suggests.

For example, in a 2010 study published in the British Journal of Psychology, women used a one-to-ten scale to rate the attractiveness of the same man, photographed in either a fancy Bentley Continental GT or a Ford Fiesta ST. They rated the man significantly higher in the Bentley, while men's ratings of a woman didn't change with the car she sat in. However, this is just one study.

A 2025 study published in Evolution and Human Behavior ran four experiments with heterosexual women to test whether luxury cars increased men's attractiveness, and its title says it all: "No evidence for relationships between conspicuous consumption and male attractiveness." So the real answer depends on who's looking, what they're looking for, and how the question itself is phrased.

A 2010 study published in the American Journal of Psychological Research used the rating site HotOrNot. The same man appeared in four photos: by himself, then touching a worn-out Dodge Neon, a Ford Focus, and a Mercedes C300. His average score climbed from 5.36 to 6.17 with the Mercedes, and only the Mercedes photo scored significantly higher than the solo shot.

The type of attention may matter more than the amount. A 2011 Journal of Personality and Social Psychology study gave 408 students a written profile of a 32-year-old analyst who had just bought either a Honda Civic or a Porsche Boxster. As a date, the Porsche owner gained a small edge with women (d = 0.29, where 0.2 counts as small). As a potential husband, his edge was negligible (0.02). The biggest shift (0.71) was in how open to casual sex women assumed he was.

Meanwhile, a 2018 Evolutionary Psychological Science study had undergraduates compare two men buying cars on the same budget. The result: the one who chose reliability over flash was rated more attractive for a long-term relationship. And in a 2016 Evolutionary Psychology study, 405 German men gave a luxury-car owner higher marks for status, ambition, intelligence, and looks, while viewing him as a bigger threat to their relationships.

The 2025 Evolution and Human Behavior study is the only one here to use a true exotic, pitting a Lamborghini against a Fiat Uno, and it found no boost to men's attractiveness. So the jury's still out on the driver, but when it comes to the cars themselves, your favorite Lamborghinis make a pretty convincing case on their own.

#5544. Consumers believe AI will be key in making healthcare simpler: survey

Consumers believe AI will be key in making healthcare simpler: survey" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Americans want a healthcare experience that's simpler and easier to understand, and artificial intelligence may be the key to getting there, a new survey shows.

The poll, conducted by the Harris Poll and commissioned by Elevance Health, found that 82% of American patients view at least some part of healthcare information as a "foreign language," and close to half (45%) said they made a healthcare decision they later regretted due to a lack of understanding.

The survey was conducted among 2,0001 adults in mid-July, and 74% said they have encountered a key barrier, such as understanding their health insurance or a medical bill. And only a quarter (27%) said they completely understand their own health coverage.

That said, most (79%) of those surveyed said they believe AI can help to improve the healthcare experience overall.

Ratnakar Lavu, chief digital information officer at Elevance Health, told Fierce in an email that because the tech has the ability to quickly surface and parse key data about a member or health need, it can serve as a central piece of the puzzle in making a more personalized experience.

"AI-enabled tools give us the ability to create a unique member context," he said. "Because of this digital technology, we can now truly 'know the person' and proactively work with them to help them manage their healthcare needs."

For example, 82% of those surveyed said they would like to receive answers about healthcare as quickly as they can use an app to order a food delivery, and 83% would like to easily access recommendations that pull from their health coverage, individual health needs and financial situation.

Seventy-two percent said they would trust AI for accuracy on at least one type of information, such as an explanation of benefits, cost estimates or details on medication.

However, while many Americans believe AI can play a leading role in driving a better health experience, just 20% said they currently use the tech regularly as a source of information. And while 72% said they trusted the tech to surface key health information, 33% said they would trust an AI platform to translate their insurance benefits, and 30% said they trust the tech to estimate care costs.

Just 13% said they would trust AI to make diagnoses.

Lavu said that healthcare organizations looking to roll out new tools need to avoid simply embedding AI into programs for the sake of it, and be transparent about both the use case as well as the role of the human in the loop.

The study also found that women were less likely than men to trust AI, and younger generations were more likely to use it as a source of healthcare information than older groups.

"We have to implement AI at the speed of trust, which means being thoughtful about where AI adds value, not just delivering technology for technology’s sake," he said. "Trust is also earned when AI-enabled programs truly make things easier for the consumer. "

For example, Elevance Health has deployed an AI-powered program to support utilization management reviews and help drive faster approvals where possible, though AI is not used to make claims denials. It is also leaning on AI for more proactive member engagement initiatives through its digital channels, identifying individuals that would benefit from extra support or who may face gaps in care.

"We start by listening to members and identifying where healthcare is creating the most confusion or friction," Lavu said. "From there, we determine the right solution, which may or may not involve AI. When AI is the right tool, it should fit naturally into familiar interactions and make it easier for members to get an answer or take the next step."

#5542. Our Patients May Already Be Using Peptides. Counseling Matters.

In October, HHS issued a policy under which licensed pharmacies can prepare compounded medications using six unapproved peptides: BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500. Social media has been abuzz ever since, as these products are increasingly marketed for injury recovery, metabolism, cognitive performance, and longevity. However, there's one major problem: these peptides have not been deemed safe or effective and are not approved by FDA. Under the interim policy, HHS will refrain from enforcing certain restrictions while the FDA evaluates their safety and suitability for compounding.

The policy follows the July 2026 meeting of the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee. Just before the meeting, FDA scientists recommended against adding any of the seven peptides under consideration, citing insufficient evidence for safety and effectiveness and concerns about peptide identity, characterization, and quality. Despite these concerns, the committee voted to recommend six of the seven peptides be added to the list of substances eligible for compounding -- without undergoing the premarket safety, efficacy, and quality review required for approved drugs. This creates a different regulatory pathway from the one followed by the many other FDA-approved peptide-based therapeutics, and the composition of the committee raised questions about potential conflicts of interest.

News of the announcement quickly spread, prompting some to wrongly interpret the decision as a sign that FDA approved these peptides. To be clear, this policy bypasses premarket safety, efficacy, and quality review required under FDA.

Drawing on our respective backgrounds in research and clinical medicine, we recently came together to discuss these concerns. Our complementary perspectives underscore an important challenge for physicians: understanding what the scientific evidence tells us about these substances while navigating the questions and misconceptions patients may bring into the exam room.

Peptide-based medicines are already used to treat a range of conditions, such as diabetes and weight management. But all peptide-based medications are different, and the success of approved treatments (such as certain GLP-1s) doesn't mean other peptides are safe or effective. Many of these "wellness" substances are deceptively marketed as "natural alternatives," but that doesn't make them natural or harmless, as they are still pharmaceuticals with unknown human dosing, safety, or efficacy data to guide prescribing.

Consider BPC-157, widely promoted for injury recovery and tissue repair. It has been marketed as a "natural" peptide found in our bodies, yet it has never actually been identified in a human body. Much of the enthusiasm stems from laboratory and animal research suggesting potential health benefits. But these preliminary findings cannot establish whether BPC-157 improves recovery in humans or what risks it may pose. Researchers have raised questions about its ability to simulate the growth of new blood vessels, a process that can support tumor growth and spreading. Encouraging people to take BPC-157 when we are lacking critical preclinical and clinical data is both irresponsible and potentially dangerous.

Even claims of clinical research can create a false sense of reassurance. Consider a TB-500 study listed on ClinicalTrials.gov that explicitly described itself as "fictional" up until November 7, 2026. (Note we're currently investigating why a trial with a "fictional" designation would be published on ClinicalTrials.gov.) There are, in fact, no human clinical trials on TB-500. There are some studies of the parent peptide thymosin beta-4 but you cannot extrapolate biology from a peptide fragment to its parent peptide.

The same scrutiny must apply to safety. FDA scientists have flagged serious concerns as have the American Medical Association, the Economic Cycle Research Institute, and the Institute for Safe Medication Practices. Drug development involves more than identifying a potentially promising biological effect. Researchers must identify the target of the molecule, understand the biological pathways it promotes, establish appropriate dosing, investigate toxicity, and understand the consequences of repeated exposure all in preclinical studies before even considering human testing, let alone concluding that it is safe and effective in humans.

Some potential harms may not become apparent for months or years. Without adequate long-term studies or any tracking systems for those using these drugs now, or planning to obtain them through compounding, even identifying a connection between a later health problem and earlier peptide exposure may prove difficult.

FDA-approved treatments backed by rigorous evidence should always be the standard for patient care. Physicians have a responsibility to thoroughly counsel patients about the risks and limitations of unapproved treatments, including peptides, ensuring they have the information needed to make informed decisions. For patients interested in experimental treatments, legitimate clinical trials offer a pathway under appropriate safeguards.

But clinicians must also recognize that patients may already be using these substances, often obtained outside their regular medical care and, in some cases, without any physician involvement. During routine exams and medication reviews, physicians should ask directly about peptides and other unapproved drugs, particularly those obtained through wellness clinics or online providers. Understanding what patients are taking, where they obtained it, and at what doses is essential to identifying potential adverse effects and drug interactions.

For patients already using these products, clinicians should document their use, evaluate possible adverse effects, and report suspected reactions through FDA's MedWatch program. For BPC-157 and many other experimental peptides, there are no adequate studies establishing how these products interact with commonly prescribed medications, and their long-term risks remain largely unknown, particularly for older patients managing multiple chronic conditions.

There are also plausible, largely unstudied concerns about peptides that stimulate growth-related pathways or promote new blood vessel formation in patients with active or prior cancer. Compounded and gray-market products introduce further uncertainty, including contamination, inconsistent potency, and, particularly in illicit products, substituted ingredients. Clinicians may not even know what substance a patient has taken, making potential drug interactions harder to identify. Until better evidence is available, clinicians should routinely ask about peptide use, review these products alongside each patient's medical conditions and medications, and report suspected adverse reactions to FDA's MedWatch, even when causality is uncertain.

The HHS policy has brought renewed attention to a much larger problem: the growing promotion and use of unapproved and untested products before their benefits and risks are understood. Physicians should not recommend these unknown substances as established treatments or allow the politicization of policy to be mistaken for scientific endorsement. Our responsibility is to uphold the standards of evidence that protect patients, not normalize the use of treatments that have yet to meet them.

#5540. There's Evidence That Road Sign Fatigue Can Cause Drivers To Ignore The Rules

Road signs only work if drivers notice them, and plenty of people say they've stopped. A Signs.com survey of 1,000 U.S. adults found that 34% of people say that there are so many signs that they're less likely to notice or follow them. That 34% skews young — 40% each of Gen Z and millennials reported sign fatigue versus 19% of baby boomers, with men (39%) reporting it more than women (27%).

Behavior echoes the attitude. Of those thousand participants, 25% ignored a road sign in the past month. Three-quarters of drivers admitted to speeding, while 43% said they rolled through stop signs and 41% ran yellow lights instead of slowing to a stop. By those numbers, speed limit signs are the ones drivers disregard most — adding to the debate over speed limits and how much they improve safety.

The most common excuse was confusing wording or signage. In the survey, 61% said they'll ignore a sign that's unclear, ahead of judging a situation low-risk (55%). Half even said they'd brushed off a rule because they assumed it existed mainly for liability reasons. Meanwhile, 42% of respondents said they comply most when a sign is clear, 33% when the sign is relevant to their safety, and 28% when it's backed by enforcement they can see. Keep the caveats in mind, though. Signs.com sells road signs, and the figures are self-reported online answers.

The Federal Highway Administration defines driver information overload as giving motorists more information than they can perceive and act on in time. It lists possible consequences from earlier research, including sharp slowdowns, late or erratic maneuvers, wrong turns, long glances away from the road, and disregarding critical information.

A 2022 simulator study of 30 drivers published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health found visual workload was lowest at about 30 bits of sign information per kilometer and rose when signage got either denser or sparser. Its authors note the results apply only to Chinese highways since the signs followed Chinese standards, but the broader pattern can still be considered for American drivers.

Confusion is measurable too. In a 2022 MyVision.org survey of about 1,060 drivers, roughly two in five couldn't identify the "divided highway ends" and "railroad after turn" signs, and about one in five mistook a text-free road construction sign for another sign.

So is sign fatigue real? FHWA notes there's little hard evidence, but people say it is, and the lab data shows too much signage raises drivers' visual workload. As for signs that do come down, retired road signs can sometimes be bought legally.

#5539. Scientists Report Strong Evidence That Specially Bred Mosquitoes Can Fend Off Dengue

— The new research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus

Children who lived in Brazilian neighborhoods buzzing with a special kind of mosquito were far less likely to catch dengue or another worrisome virus, chikungunya, researchers reported.

The major study of more than 5,700 children in one of the world's dengue hot spots offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit these viruses can be a viable strategy rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten.

In neighborhoods populated by these so-called Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, researchers found about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections in schoolchildren compared to similar neighborhoods -- an effect sustained even during Brazil's severe 2024 dengue outbreak, said Sri Edupuganti, MD, MPH, of Emory University, part of the international research team.

The researchers reported the findings at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene.

"This is really exciting," said David Hamer, MD, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn't involved with the Brazilian study. He predicts that pairing more use of these Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing steps to fight mosquito-borne disease could "knock dengue down to much lower levels" in many places.

The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s.

Usually in the continental U.S., dengue is found mostly in people who traveled internationally. But as of Friday, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa.

Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy.

How it works: Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. It is harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The bacteria dramatically reduce the mosquitoes' ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects -- males and females -- into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population.

Field trials and other studies in Indonesia and elsewhere have shown the strategy can significantly lower dengue diagnoses. But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya, or the Zika virus.

The 4-year study compared children living in neighborhoods that all got the same pesticide and other mosquito-control interventions, but half were randomly assigned to have Wolbachia mosquitoes released into the area. There were too few cases of Zika to calculate if the special mosquitoes had any effect on that disease.

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA plan Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth said in its complaint that it is bringing the lawsuit to ensure "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations."

The star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage plans and listed on the Medicare plan finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

"The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A plan’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive."

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The company sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the company said that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

"Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination."

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the company said.

In addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the company said.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the plans available to them," Elevance said.

"An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the company continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing plans."

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

The court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

The company said that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement."

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the company's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

"The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like."

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

In a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the company argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene says that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

The use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the company, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in plans with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the company said in the lawsuit.

CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the company estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 plan year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene said.

"Beyond the financial impact to the company and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company said in the complaint

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer says that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, plans, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The company argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to plan payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment said in the lawsuit.

The company adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

"Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about plan enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the company said. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute."

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

In addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the company tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

"Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment said in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings."

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the company said.
