#5478. Opinion: Montana’s ‘right to try’ law makes patients responsible for bearing costs — and risks

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Miner is a behavioral and social scientist at RAND. James is an associate policy researcher at RAND.

In July, Montana became the first state to license clinics to offer patients who are not terminally ill drugs and devices that the Food and Drug Administration has not approved. Supporters call state Senate bill 535 a first-in-the-nation expansion of the “right to try.” Critics say it lets patients, including medical tourists from other states, pay out of pocket for unproven therapies. They are both right, in different ways. While the expansion of access to experimental treatments may provide patients with hope, the risks that patients may pay high costs for ineffective and even unsafe treatments remain high.

The goal is to expand access to experimental therapies, with stem cell, anti-aging therapies, and biologics being likely use cases. But the law leaves major questions unanswered: How much will patients pay? Who will bear the cost if complications arise later? And, because these therapies are being used outside a rigorous research setting, how will anyone know whether they actually work?For patients, a primary concern is likely to be cost. SB535 makes patients financially responsible for the experimental treatment — with the price set by the company supplying the drug or device. The required patient agreement must describe “all the anticipated costs” of the treatment itself. But patients will likely face additional costs, including travel to Montana for those out of state, and follow-up care.

Patients are also, in theory, responsible to pay out of pocket for medical care related to any complications — they are not supposed to go through their insurance companies. But how will insurers determine if a medical problem stems from an experimental treatment? That’s left ambiguous by the law. Long-term medical effects will be particularly hard to trace, especially if a product hasn’t yet had robust safety testing and documentation of its long-term side effects. Thus, care for complications may fall on patients, or it may be paid by insurers who had no say in the use of an experimental treatment.

And how are people to judge whether a treatment is worth its price? For approved therapies, there’s trial data on survival rates, plus continued post-market study. These data help clarify the expected benefits for specific patients. SB535 does not require companies to conduct comparable analyses, nor are companies bound to set prices with any value framework in mind.

Proponents of SB535 argue that skipping costly trials will lower development costs and, eventually, prices. However, if companies wish to generate evidence for conventional FDA approval, they will need to go beyond the requirements in SB535. If they fail to collect detailed patient characteristics such as history of disease and patient demographics, it will be hard to determine how the drug might work in a larger patient population. Supporters say the data will resemble real-world evidence, but the validity of real-world evidence still depends on clear study methods and consistent data collection and reporting.

It’s also possible that SB535 could undermine the rigorous testing needed for FDA approval. That’s because SB535 does not require the same patient protections, data collection requirements, or oversight that the FDA requires. Some companies may forgo the clinical trial FDA pathway entirely, while others may find that direct access disincentivizes patients from enrolling in trials.

None of this means patients with few options for treatment should be dismissed or ignored. But they can make an informed decision about how much to pay for treatment only if the true costs and risks are visible. Montana currently has no systematic way to assess how patients interpret costs, what they actually incur and pay, or how those costs relate to short- and long-term outcomes.

If other states want to expand access to experimental treatment, there are other models they could look to, such as CMS’s Coverage with Evidence Development. It requires systematic collection and reporting of data on clinical effectiveness and short- and long-term harms.

States could also require companies to collect data on outcomes for 15 years, just like the FDA does for cell and gene therapies. These types of data can enable transparency and may help patients make informed decisions about potential treatments in consultation with their care team.

Montana can still move in that direction by requiring standardized cost disclosure before consent, a registry with defined long-term follow-up, and independent evaluation of financial and clinical outcomes.

Without those steps, we will not know whether state right to try laws can be a cost-effective way to generate evidence and access to emerging therapeutics. Patients who try may be left physically and financially vulnerable, with little knowledge gained from their risk.

Skye A. Miner is a behavioral and social scientist at RAND, a nonprofit, nonpartisan research institution. She specializes in the ethics of emerging technologies. Hannah O. James is an associate policy researcher at RAND who researches the value of U.S. health care spending and state-level health policies.

#5477. Rural communities face heavier chronic disease burden, increasing pressure on PCPs: athenaInstitute

Rural communities face heavier chronic disease burden, increasing pressure on PCPs: athenaInstitute" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Millennials living in rural areas have 42% more documented chronic conditions on average compared to those in other environments, a new report from athenaInstitute found.

And, millennials in rural communities are 47% more likely to have at least two chronic conditions. This heavier chronic disease burden extends to other generations as well, analysts note.

Half of Baby Boomers (50.4%) in rural areas have three or more documented conditions, which the report says is “on par” with non-rural individuals in the Silent and Greatest generations.

The 2026 Rural Ambulatory Care Report (PDF) analyzed athenahealth network data from 12.3 million rural patients between 2021 and 2025, along with more than 30,000 clinicians and 1,861 rural practices across the U.S. It examined factors such as appointment activity, workforce composition, payments, and more.

Athenahealth CMO and athenaInstitute co-chair Nele Jessel, M.D., said in a statement the findings show that while rural practices are not “standing still in the face of enormous challenges,” there are “limits to how much more they can absorb as patient needs continue to grow.”

“They are adapting how they deliver care and finding ways to keep patients connected to the care they need,” Jessel said. “With renewed focus on rural healthcare, there is a real opportunity to build on what is working by investing in the workforce, technology and models of care that can help these practices continue serving the communities that depend on them.”

Primary care physicians in rural areas have to wear multiple hats, as specialty care needs at practices are higher in rural communities.

The report found that primary care handles 68.7% of visits involving anxiety or depression diagnoses versus 55.1% in non-rural areas. Moreover, 25% of rural patients with documented anxiety or depression had a substance use disorder—up from 19.8% in non-rural communities.

Data shows rural and non-rural healthcare practices collected roughly the same share of what they were owed by insurers in 2025, but analysts note a difference in patient balances.

Rural practices collected about $70 of every $100 owed, while non-rural practices collected about $78—which analysts say is about a 10% gap.

Another potential source of financial vulnerability for rural practices is Medicaid. Medicaid covered 27.5% of rural visits, which analysts note leaves these practices more exposed to eligibility changes set to begin in 2027.

#5476. Pregnancy is the ‘perfect storm’ for eating disorders, but doctors keep missing them

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Reporting for this story was supported by the Pulitzer Center.

REISTERSTOWN, Md. — Katye Jorgensen had been fighting anorexia and bulimia for years when she got pregnant at 25. Weigh-ins at prenatal appointments filled her with dread and certain foods terrified her, but she powered through for her baby’s sake. Then she struggled to breastfeed her son and lose weight after giving birth, and her mental health deteriorated.

After her second pregnancy two years later, Jorgensen became obsessive about exercise and fixated on comments about how well she was “bouncing back.” At her husband’s urging, she started seeing a therapist and a dietitian. Eventually, they staged an intervention and she agreed to enter intensive treatment, which she said saved her life.

“I went to my postpartum appointment, I mentioned a lot of this, and even though I really liked those doctors, it still didn’t set off any red alarms for anybody,” said Jorgensen, who is now 37.

Jorgensen is one of many women who struggle with eating disorders before and after childbirth but slip through the cracks of the U.S. health care system. Research suggests about 4.3% of pregnant women and more than 9% of new mothers experience eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, or binge eating disorder, though research is limited and no one knows their exact toll.

Those rates are on par with national averages: an estimated 2.6% to 8.4% of women will experience an eating disorder over their lifetimes — that’s up to 14.6 million women and girls in the United States.

Eating disorders have been linked to health issues for pregnant women — including miscarriage, high blood pressure, anemia, and bleeding — and complications for their developing babies, including small head circumference, low birthweight, autism, and asthma. After birth, women with a history of eating disorders appear more likely to experience postpartum depression and anxiety and to report problems feeding their newborns.

The risks vary by eating disorder. Studies don’t prove that eating disorders directly cause these issues and not everyone with a perinatal eating disorder will experience them. Still, the evidence is enough to worry clinicians.

“If we don’t treat these disorders … there are risks involved there. This isn’t a neutral situation,” said Leah Graves, a registered dietitian and a clinical adviser at the National Eating Disorders Association.

Few screening tools have been validated for eating disorders in pregnancy, and none are widely used. Obstetricians typically receive very little training about these conditions, leaving them unequipped to identify or manage eating disorders. And even with a diagnosis, many pregnant women and new mothers don’t receive timely treatment due to spotty insurance coverage and a shortage of local specialists, according to research and interviews with more than a dozen eating disorder researchers, doctors, dietitians, therapists, policy advocates, and mothers.

“It’s been a huge gap,” said Elizabeth Claydon, an associate professor at West Virginia University who researches eating disorders. “People have had this; they’ve lived with eating disorders during pregnancy. We just haven’t caught them and been able to help.”

Eating disorders usually develop in adolescence or young adulthood, but they can also emerge around pregnancy, menopause, or other periods of profound physical and life change.

Several factors can raise the risks in pregnancy: the feeling of a lack of control, rapid physical and hormonal changes, negative body image, scrutiny of the pregnant person’s diet and weight for medical reasons, the need to consume extra calories to breastfeed, a new identity and family role, and societal pressure to return to pre-pregnancy weight and succeed at motherhood.

Many women struggle with body image issues or unhealthy thoughts or behaviors around food, weight, or exercise that don’t meet the criteria for a clinical diagnosis. Pregnancy can tip the scales into an active eating disorder.

Pregnancy can also hide symptoms that overlap with eating disorders, such as nausea, vomiting, appetite changes or pumping breast milk specifically to burn calories, said Christine Call, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the University of Pittsburgh.

But many women hide their symptoms, making it difficult for doctors, or even family members, to know when someone needs help.

There’s no single trajectory in the perinatal period. Some women with eating disorders fare better during pregnancy and sustain that recovery, while others relapse once their child is born. Other women, years into recovery, see their eating disorders come roaring back in pregnancy or postpartum. Some struggle throughout pregnancy, with no respite. And others develop an eating disorder for the first time in the perinatal period.

“There’s so much shame and guilt about eating and doing things right, taking care of yourself for your baby during this period,” Call said.

Jennifer Kreatsoulas was diagnosed with anorexia 15 years before her first pregnancy, but her eating disorder “came back with a vengeance” after her second child was born, alongside postpartum depression. She decided to seek treatment when she realized she was too weak to push a stroller while out on a Mother’s Day walk with her husband and 1-year-old daughter.

“It’s destructive, but I was really trying to cope, and my brain just switched back to what it knew how to do from all those years previous,” said Kreatsoulas, now 50 and living in Pennsylvania. She attributes her relapse to “hormones, lack of sleep, complete overwhelm, your identity becoming something that you don’t know — you lose yourself in it, just because that’s what’s demanded as a mother.”

In a recommendation buried in a 2019 opinion on obesity bias, the ethics committee of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists suggests that OB-GYNs assess all their patients, pregnant or not, for eating disorders. And it recommends that all pregnant and postpartum patients be screened for anxiety and depression — as does the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force.

But ACOG’s clinical guidance on perinatal mental health doesn’t cover eating disorders, and the organization has no guidance on how to screen for or manage them during pregnancy and after birth.

“Providers don’t see it because we’re not looking for it,” said Danielle Prentice, a maternal-fetal medicine specialist at Oregon Health & Science University and a member of ACOG’s nutrition expert group.

Some states have expanded maternal mental health screening in recent years, but without a clinical standard on perinatal eating disorders, policymakers have had little to go on. In Massachusetts — where Lindsay Clancy’s high-profile murder trial drew public outrage over the inadequacy of postpartum mental health care in the U.S. — state officials recently said they would increase screening and support for depression, anxiety, bipolar spectrum disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and postpartum psychosis.

Eating disorders were excluded because the state followed ACOG’s published guidance to decide which perinatal mental health conditions to include, according to a spokesperson for the Massachusetts Executive Office of Health and Human Services.

“Providers who have concerns about a patient’s eating behaviors, nutrition, body image, weight-related behaviors, or history of an eating disorder should use their clinical judgment and conduct or refer for further assessment as appropriate,” the spokesperson said via email.

Existing eating disorder screening tools may not be suitable for pregnant or postpartum patients. The most common one, known as the SCOFF (“Sick-Control-One Stone-Fat-Food”), has five questions, including: “Have you recently lost more than 14 pounds in a 3-month period?”

Researchers have also warned that eating disorder screening tools tend to be centered on white body ideals, suggesting they may miss women of color and feed into biases about who is at risk. Studies indicate Black women experience eating disorders, particularly binge eating, at rates similar to white women, but are less likely to be diagnosed or treated. Eating disorder experts say the “SWAG” stereotype — skinny, white, affluent girl — of eating disorder patients prevents clinicians from recognizing eating disorders in anyone who doesn’t fit that mold.

“People of color [and] trans people are not seen as having an eating disorder as an option, especially in pregnancy,” said Jessica Wilson, a registered dietitian in California.

Ideally, West Virginia University’s Claydon said, screening for eating disorders should become a standard part of perinatal health care. If the screener flags a potential eating disorder or worrisome symptoms, the patient could be referred to an expert for a final diagnosis.

Yet persuading obstetricians to adopt another screening tool could be a challenge. Screening at the six-week postpartum checkup can feel like a perfunctory exercise, though maternal mental health issues can emerge or linger much longer.

“They give you the questionnaire, which is really more like, ‘Do you want to hurt yourself or somebody else? No? OK, cool, bye.’ That’s it,” Jorgensen said.

Screening may identify a patient in need of support, but that doesn’t mean resources or specialists are available.

“Universal screening is only effective if there’s treatment,” said Marianna Thomeczek, a researcher at the University of Kansas who is developing a postpartum screening tool for Black women.

Women with an active or recent eating disorder can have complex medical needs during pregnancy, Prentice said. They may need supplementation to address nutritional deficiencies, preconception folic acid to support fetal development and prevent birth defects, and extra ultrasounds to monitor the baby’s growth, she said.

Pregnancy may also prompt women to seek eating disorder treatment, which typically calls for therapy paired with care from a doctor and dietitian, according to the American Psychiatric Association. It ranges from regular appointments to intensive day programs, residential treatment, or hospitalization, depending on how sick a patient is and her specific condition.

Health coverage can be a major barrier. Many private insurers cover visits with dietitians for patients with eating disorders, but dietitians say claims are often denied, and plans may limit the number of visits or require copays patients can’t afford, especially while preparing for a new baby. Specialized eating disorder dietitians may be out-of-network.

To get more intensive care, women often have to prove medical necessity, said Ashley Moser, a clinical education specialist at The Renfrew Center, one of the country’s oldest eating disorder treatment facilities. Pregnancy can help make the case, but it’s still difficult.

Access to care is even more difficult for low-income women who rely on Medicaid. Only 22 state Medicaid programs allow registered dietitian-nutritionists to bill independently for adult medical nutrition therapy. And while there are 384 eating disorder centers offering intensive treatment in the U.S., only about 25% accept Medicaid coverage, according to a study published earlier this year. Five states have no treatment centers at all.

There’s very little evidence about what works to prevent eating disorders or their relapse during pregnancy. Researchers in Massachusetts are currently testing whether peer group support and cognitive dissonance exercises can help, modeled on a longstanding program for teenage girls and young women called The Body Project. Early results, published this month, are promising, but bigger studies are needed to prove it actually works.

Pregnant women can also ask their doctors to adjust routine practices they find triggering. During Jorgensen’s third and final pregnancy, she pushed for blind weigh-ins and asked doctors not to relay her blood sugar levels unless there was a problem.

Overall, clinicians, researchers, and mothers said that as maternal mental health receives more national attention, perinatal eating disorders should as well. Partners and families should know the risks, they said, to help ensure women feel safe speaking up rather than suffering alone.

“We need to change the system, we need to change the policies, but women also need to know that they’re not alone in experiencing this,” Claydon said. “It’s not an unusual thing to occur during pregnancy, because it is that perfect storm.”

Gabriela Galvin is a freelance journalist in London who covers health and social policy. In 2025, she was awarded a European Press Prize.

#5475. AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis

Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult. Its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions, including kidney stones, allowing warning signs to go unnoticed.

Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis. In some patients, the technology detected subtle warning signals dating back as far as five years.

The new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked. By recognizing these patterns, researchers hope to make bladder cancer screening more accurate and help doctors find the disease when treatment is most likely to succeed.

AI Finds Hidden Bladder Cancer Clues in Medical Records

Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs of bladder cancer is visible blood in the urine (hematuria). However, blood in the urine can also result from noncancerous problems, including kidney stones and prostate conditions. This overlap makes it difficult to determine which patients need further investigation and contributes to missed cases.

Confirming bladder cancer currently requires a procedure called cystoscopy (where a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder). Although effective, the examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients who are most likely to have the disease.

To explore a possible solution, a team led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients. The records covered a 25-year period, from 1995 through 2020.

The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators (from smoking and exercise habits to medication use). From this enormous collection of information, the system narrowed the list to 38 features that were especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk.

AI Identifies 85% of Bladder Cancer Cases

The results suggest that AI could substantially improve the way patients are assessed for bladder cancer.

The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not have the disease. It also performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.

Importantly, the system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis. Some of the warning signals it recognized could be traced back up to five years, suggesting that valuable clues may exist in medical records long before cancer is discovered.

The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors, including smoking and blood in the urine. However, it also uncovered unexpected associations that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to detect.

For example, patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared to have a lower risk of bladder cancer. Meanwhile, long-term use of tamoxifen (a breast cancer medication) was associated with a higher risk.

These findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it. Instead, they raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms that researchers believe deserve closer examination.

Another surprising finding involved blood in the urine. Although this symptom is often considered a major warning sign, its significance appears to depend partly on a patient's other medical conditions. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, for instance, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk.

Understanding these relationships more fully could eventually help doctors distinguish patients who need urgent investigation from those who may not require invasive testing.

Beyond identifying warning signs, the AI system could also divide patients into three groups according to their estimated likelihood of having bladder cancer: low-risk (below 7% probability), uncertain (grey zone: 7-55%), and high-risk (above 55%).

This approach could help healthcare providers decide which patients need immediate attention and which may benefit from additional monitoring.

For example, patients in the uncertain category might be monitored before undergoing procedures such as cystoscopy. If further research confirms the system's reliability, this could reduce unnecessary examinations while allowing doctors to concentrate resources on people at greatest risk.

PhD student Xu Wang, who led the data analysis, said: "Bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022."

"Despite its prevalence, no routine screening program exists for the general population, and - following symptoms - detection relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Our system goes far beyond traditional symptoms, and it's great to have uncovered the results that we have. The research shows that the combination of multiple factors - from medication histories to seemingly unrelated conditions - can reveal patterns invisible to conventional screening methods."

Could AI Help Doctors Catch Bladder Cancer Earlier?

The potential benefits extend beyond improving diagnostic accuracy. Detecting bladder cancer earlier could mean more treatment options, better survival outcomes, and fewer patients undergoing invasive procedures unnecessarily.

Dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, emphasized the importance of developing better screening methods.

"Bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families.

"It could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier, when survival outcomes and quality of life can be dramatically improved."

Professor Shang-Ming Zhou believes the findings point toward a more individualized approach to cancer screening, in which AI helps doctors interpret a patient's broader medical history rather than relying primarily on individual symptoms.

"This work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.

"By harnessing the power of interpretable machine learning and comprehensive health records, we're moving closer to detecting this disease at its earliest, most treatable stages."

Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.

All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Before the model can be introduced into other healthcare settings, researchers will need to determine whether it performs equally well with different patient populations and medical record systems.

Professor Zhou explained why broader testing is essential.

"It's important to emphasize that further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely - for example, all of the data analyzed came from the SAIL database in Wales, so we'd want to investigate other datasets too.

"But it's a very exciting early study. Additional studies would also be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions."

The findings offer an encouraging glimpse of how artificial intelligence might improve cancer screening by uncovering patterns hidden within years of routine medical information. With further validation, such tools could help doctors recognize bladder cancer sooner, prioritize patients who need testing, and potentially improve outcomes.

The study, "Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs," was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering.

The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

#5473. The stories we’re grateful for this year

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Disability in Health Care Reporting Fellow

Rose covers disability and mental health, and she helps write STAT’s daily Morning Rounds newsletter. Confidential tips can be sent to Rose on Signal at rosebroderick.11.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Hope everyone is enjoying their food coma after yesterday. What was your favorite dish? I am still thinking about my friend’s pumpkin pie.

Speaking of the holiday, STAT staffers have put together a list of the stories we’re thankful for this year. Scroll down to see our favorites.

Anorexia, binge eating, and other disorders can emerge before and after childbirth, but the women who struggle with them often slip through the cracks of the U.S. health care system.

Research is limited, but we do know a few things: About 4.3% of pregnant women and more than 9% of new mothers experience eating disorders. Women with a history of eating disorders appear more likely to experience postpartum depression and anxiety and to report problems feeding their newborns. And obstetricians typically receive very little training about these conditions or how to use the few screening tools we have validated for eating disorders in pregnancy.

Read more about the gap in this research.

In the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ recent update to how Medicare pays physicians, the agency cut the payment rate for certain services provided on the same day by 20% when the services are provided by the same physician or practice.

A bit wonky, I know, but it’s part of the agency’s broader shift away from specialist care and the fee-for-service model, and one of many reimbursement challenges that specialists are contending with.

What does this mean? Opponents say the policy change will force patients to return for separate appointments and increase out-of-pocket costs and wait times. People with Parkinson’s disease, for example, could struggle  to get outpatient Botox injections that are critical for relieving pain. Read more.

We asked STAT staffers to share some of their favorite stories — the pieces they loved reading, or ones they’re still thinking about. Here’s what they said:

I’m grateful for this dispatch from a big conference of people who want to live forever, or at least create a lot of shareholder value before they die. I’m guilty of gawking at the loudest voices in the longevity movement and occasionally dismissing them as men who say alarming things while being weird with their fluids. Sarah Todd, being a good journalist, meets them where they are (the Bay Area, obviously) and finds that whether they’re pitching full-body scans or plotting to reenact ” Never Let Me Go,” most longevity enthusiasts are just like the rest of us: scared to death of inevitably dying. — Damian Garde, STAT reporter at large, live and feature journalism

“Thankful” is not exactly the best word for how I feel about Megan’s story about scientist Brian Donovan; it’s actually pretty depressing. But it’s stayed with me since April because it so well captured the broad impact of federal grant cancellations, the specific challenges interdisciplinary academic researchers face, and the important work that gets left behind as a result. — Andrew Joseph, STAT Europe correspondent

Great journalism doesn’t only uncover secret injustices or corruption. It also reveals the scourges that are hiding in plain sight. Alcohol is so embedded in our culture and consciousness that we may not realize how harmful it has been and could be. This amazing series doesn’t exist to ban drinks from our family Thanksgivings. But it does a great public service of explaining the scope of alcohol addiction, the influence of the industry, and the failures that got us to this point. — Bob Herman, STAT business of health care reporter

Not a story per se, but I loved getting to debrief the Elizabeth Holmes documentary with my fellow STAT reporters. — Margaret Manto, STAT Washington correspondent

I’m especially thankful for Tara Bannow’s tour-de-force investigation of HaloMD. This was especially gutsy reporting because it didn’t stop at the doors of HaloMD. It dug deeper into the lives and motivations of the people leading the company. The reporting led the way in scrutinizing how profiteers have taken advantage of a well-intended policy to ban surprise bills. It was followed by many other outlets and again showed why STAT’s agenda-setting coverage is so vital. — Casey Ross, STAT chief investigative reporter, data and technology

It’s easy to feel pessimistic about what technology is doing to our brains and those of future generations. Which is why I’m grateful for this story from Isa Cueto, which explores creative ways people are working to reclaim kids’ attention spans from compulsive social media scrolling. Rich with rigorous science and insights gleaned from time spent with real teenagers, it offers a welcome antidote to the notion that the attention crisis is a foregone facet of modern life. — Megan Molteni, STAT science writer

We think of human anatomy — organs, muscles, nerves, bones — as a conquered science. Medical students master its intricacies, layer by layer. We can scan the body, palpate it, examine its cells. But anatomy is not history. Subramaniam Krishnan, a cardiac electrophysiologist in California, reminded me that the architecture of our bodies still contains mysteries. Krishnan discovered a pouch within the atrial septum of one of the most studied organs in medical history. He described his finding in his First Opinion essay, “I discovered a new structure in the heart — just by looking closely.” Scientific insight, he wrote, is often limited by “our own assumptions about where to stop looking.” Krishnan nudges us to remember that the frontiers of medicine don’t lie only in AI or genomics — and that curiosity and observation can still spark discovery. — Kathy Burge, STAT contributing editor

#5472. AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.

For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.

But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?

"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."

A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI

The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.

If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.

"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.

The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.

Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.

AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story

The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.

AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.

This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.

"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.

The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.

Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.

That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.

"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.

Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior

The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.

If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.

"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.

Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.

The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.

Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain

Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.

By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.

"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline."

A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.

To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.

Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.

The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.

#5470. Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis

A deadly form of blood cancer may begin taking shape more than 50 years before a person is diagnosed, according to new research revealing the surprisingly long and predictable path to leukemia.

Scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over a lifetime, discovering that in two-thirds of the cases studied, the first genetic mutation that helped drive the cancer appeared before age 20. These early changes could remain largely unnoticed for decades before eventually contributing to the disease.

The findings suggest that doctors may one day be able to identify people at risk of developing leukemia years or even decades before symptoms appear. They also raise the possibility of preventing the cancer by slowing the growth of abnormal blood cells long before the disease takes hold.

Blood Samples Reveal Leukemia's Hidden History

Published in Nature, the study was conducted by researchers at the University of Cambridge and University College London (UCL). By examining blood samples collected over many years, including some obtained as long as 15 years before diagnosis, the team pieced together a detailed history of how leukemia develops.

The scientists treated these stored samples as a kind of genetic fossil record. Using highly sensitive DNA sequencing and mathematical models, they worked backward to estimate when cancer-related mutations first appeared, how quickly the affected cells multiplied, and how they competed with other blood cells as the disease approached.

AML is an aggressive blood cancer that affects approximately 2,700 people in the UK annually. Its outlook is often poor, with only about one in six patients surviving at least five years after diagnosis.

Scientists have long known that many otherwise healthy older adults carry blood cells with mutations associated with leukemia. This condition, called clonal hematopoiesis, does not necessarily lead to cancer. In fact, most people with these mutations never develop AML. Until now, researchers have struggled to understand why some individuals progress to leukemia while others do not, partly because they lacked a detailed record of the genetic changes occurring in the years before diagnosis.

To investigate, the team turned to samples from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS). That project involved approximately 50,000 women who provided blood samples annually for as long as 11 years.

For the new analysis, researchers examined samples from 47 women who eventually developed AML, with an average age at diagnosis of 72. They compared these findings with samples from 46 similar women who remained free of blood cancer.

Cancer Mutations Can Remain Hidden for Decades

The results revealed an extraordinary timeline. In two-thirds of the women who developed AML, the earliest mutation contributing to the disease was estimated to have occurred before their 20th birthday.

At first, the altered blood cells multiplied extremely slowly, sometimes taking several years just to double in number. But as additional cancer-driving mutations accumulated, their growth accelerated dramatically.

Each new mutation typically increased the rate of growth by roughly two to three times. By the time cells had acquired four mutations capable of driving cancer, their populations could double within weeks instead of years.

Perhaps even more surprising was how consistently these populations behaved.

Researchers found that groups of genetically related blood cells, known as clones, generally expanded at predictable rates once they became established. Their growth tended to slow only when they faced limited space or competition from another clone that was multiplying more quickly.

This consistency could have important medical implications. By measuring the growth of a particular clone using just a few blood samples, scientists may be able to estimate how large that population will become many years into the future, potentially even decades later.

The researchers also identified a striking pattern that appeared in some patients well before leukemia was diagnosed.

In at least one-third of AML cases, a single population of mutated blood cells had grown so extensively that it dominated the blood years before diagnosis. Scientists call this process a "somatic sweep."

None of the women in the comparison group who remained free of blood cancer showed the same pattern.

The researchers then examined data from the UK Biobank and confirmed that people showing evidence of these sweeps faced a substantially greater risk of developing AML.

This finding suggests that somatic sweeps could serve as an important early warning sign. However, conventional genetic testing can miss them because the mutations involved are sometimes incorrectly classified as inherited genetic variations.

Professor Jamie Blundell, who led the research at the University of Cambridge's Early Cancer Institute, explained how the team reconstructed the disease's history.

"Serial blood samples are a fossil record of the blood's evolution. They let us go back in time and reconstruct when each mutation arose and how fast it grew. What surprised us most is how predictable the growth of these clones is. Once a clone is established, its growth rate today tells you where it will be years, even decades, from now."

He added: "Because the growth is exponential, even modestly slowing a high-risk clone over the decade or more before diagnosis could substantially reduce the chance it becomes leukemia. This opens up strategies we can exploit to prevent these clones ever becoming leukemia."

Could Leukemia Be Prevented Before It Develops?

The discovery could change how doctors approach a disease that often appears to develop with little warning.

Dr. Caroline Watson, the study's first author and a researcher at the Early Cancer Institute, emphasized the contrast between the sudden impact of a leukemia diagnosis and the decades of biological changes that may precede it.

"As a hematologist, I've seen how suddenly AML can change someone's life. This study shows that the changes leading to AML can build over decades, with the affected cells growing in surprisingly predictable ways."

Watson is also an Honorary Consultant Haematologist who treats patients at the Cambridge Clonal Haematopoiesis Clinic at Addenbrooke's Hospital. The clinic is the first in Europe dedicated to leukemia prevention and already monitors people whose blood cell mutations place them at increased risk of developing the disease.

She added: "At our clinic, we already assess and monitor people who carry blood-cell mutations that increase their risk of leukemia. Today's findings give us real hope of improving how we identify which of them are at greatest risk and point to a window in which prevention could one day be possible."

Years of Blood Samples Unlock New Cancer Clues

A major reason the researchers could reconstruct leukemia's development was the availability of blood samples collected repeatedly from the same individuals over many years.

Professor Usha Menon of the UCL Institute of Clinical Trials and Methodology, who led the original UKCTOCS project, highlighted the unexpected scientific value of those samples.

"While UKCTOCS was designed to assess ovarian cancer screening, a key outcome was the establishment of a unique bioresource of serial serum samples. This resource has provided unprecedented opportunities to study how cancers develop over time and to discover and validate biomarkers for earlier detection. We owe an enormous debt of gratitude to the participants whose willingness to contribute their samples and data over many years made this possible. Their generosity is the foundation of this achievement."

The women who developed AML received their diagnoses between ages 53 and 83. Because the researchers did not have blood samples taken at the time of diagnosis, they could not directly examine the final stage of the disease's development in those patients.

The findings also showed that not every case followed the same extended timeline of detectable changes. In approximately one in five cases, growing populations of mutated blood cells became detectable only one to two years before diagnosis. This suggests that some patients may have a much shorter opportunity for early intervention.

Despite these limitations, the results offer an encouraging possibility: leukemia risk might be reduced by intervening long before the disease develops.

According to the researchers' mathematical models, even a modest reduction in the growth of high-risk blood cell clones could have a substantial effect over time. Because these cells multiply exponentially, slowing their expansion across the ten or more years between a second cancer-driving mutation and diagnosis could significantly reduce the likelihood that they eventually progress to leukemia.

This raises the prospect of preventive treatments designed to restrain dangerous cell populations rather than waiting until they have developed into cancer.

The next challenge is determining whether such an approach can be used safely and effectively in people identified as having an elevated risk of AML. Although the research provides a promising framework for earlier detection and prevention, clinical studies will be needed to establish whether slowing these abnormal cells actually prevents leukemia in humans.

The research was primarily supported by UK Research & Innovation and Cancer Research UK.

#5469. Mastering Digital Marketing - How to Grow Your Business Online

Having a solid digital marketing strategy is essential if you want to succeed as a business owner in the modern day. Effective digital marketing lets you get more eyes on your business and ensure consistent growth.

Because digital marketing trends are forever changing, it’s important to stay on top of your brand’s strategy. Doing so ensures that you stand out above your competitors and gain the recognition that your brand deserves.

If you’re unsure how to master your digital marketing strategy, consider working with an expert company that can help you figure out which direction to go. A professional agency, such as Scorpion Digital Marketing Agency, can support your online efforts to maximize your success.

If you don’t want to outsource your digital marketing processes, try these top tips below to maintain an effective digital marketing strategy and boost your business growth.

Your website is where most of your new audience will find your business and your existing customers will shop for your new products and services. If you create a strong first impression through your website, you can gain credibility and authority in your industry.

Make sure to regularly update your website content so it’s accurate and on-trend. Doing so also signals to Google that your website is authoritative and credible, increasing your rankings on search engine results pages (SERPs).

The higher your rankings, the higher your visibility, meaning you can expand your reach with minimal effort. When updating your content, use plenty of industry-relevant keywords and key phrases to ensure your target audience finds your site.

With a strong social media strategy, you can significantly expand your reach and gain recognition as a trustworthy brand. Regularly posting content enables you to provide consistent value to your audience while displaying your expertise.

You can create posts highlighting the benefits of your products or the quality of your services. You can share positive testimonials and reviews from happy customers to build your credibility.

Social media platforms allow you to connect directly with your target audience too. You can answer queries and concerns in your DMs and show the human side of your brand.

Video marketing is becoming increasingly effective. Over four-fifths of consumer internet traffic comes from videos, so it's the perfect way to expand your reach and drive more traffic to your website.

Whether you use live or pre-filmed video content, you can capture your target audience's attention and provide helpful information in an engaging way. You can share demonstrations of how to use your products or explain your services in more detail to persuade consumers to check out your brand.

Optimize your videos for search engines by including keywords and phrases in your video titles and descriptions. Doing so increases your rankings on SERPs and puts your brand in front of as many people as possible.

#5468. Industrial internet of things satellite platform Myriota raises $40M to scale its constellation and expand

Australia-based Myriota Pty. Ltd., a global satellite platform for the industrial internet of things, today announced it has raised $40 million in the first portion of its Series C to launch next-generation satellites and accelerate customer adoption across international markets.

Main Sequence Ventures, Hostplus and Australia’s National Reconstruction Fund Corporation co-led the round. Funds SA joined as a new investor. The round raised the company’s total funding to more than $107.5 million, and is expected to close in early 2027.

Founded in 2015, Myriota’s platform makes satellite connectivity commercially viable for large-scale industrial IoT, using the same core technology to track mining equipment and trailers to also monitor fuel tanks, livestock water supplies and off-grid solar.

The company’s platform combines satellite connectivity, low-power devices, field installation tools and fleet management software to support existing infrastructure. The objective is to provide access to communication tools that connect what is in place with turnkey service, so a company can connect devices, machines and smart sensors no matter how remote they are.

“We’re at the beginning of a fundamental shift in industrial IoT,” Chief Executive Ben Cade said. “Industries increasingly rely on data from the field to make decisions about their operations, assets and resources, and as AI moves into the physical world, that data becomes even more essential.”

The company expanded its platform over the past 12 months with the launch of HyperPulse, a global 5G non-terrestrial network, or NTN, and terrestrial service, and AssetHawk, a rugged, long-life asset tracker designed to make it economical to track industrial objects.

Alongside the expansion, it also grew into new verticals such as industrial fuels. It monitors and tracks fuel deployments across North America and Latin America, with EMEA and Asia Pacific to follow.

Myriota competes in a sector led by established operators such as Iridium Communications Inc., Orbcomm Inc. and Viasat Inc., alongside a growing field of providers pursuing cheaper, standards-based connections for industrial sensors and trackers.

The company said it intends to use the funds to expand its space infrastructure, including developing and launching its next-generation satellites.

#5467. Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds

A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. The findings provide a clearer picture of the connection between diabetes and Alzheimer's, including how much the risk increases and how frequently new cases occur.

Researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis. They estimated that for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes, approximately 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease over the course of one year.

A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.

Understanding the Link Between Diabetes and Alzheimer's

Study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, explained that the findings offer a more precise understanding of Alzheimer's risk among people with type 2 diabetes.

Unlike previous research reviews that often examined multiple forms of diabetes or dementia together, this analysis concentrated specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. It also measured how frequently people with diabetes developed Alzheimer's, providing an additional perspective on the connection between the two conditions.

"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," Dr. Adewuyi said.

"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes."

The study, "Incidence and risk of Alzheimer's disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis," was published in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy.

#5466. Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging

Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than previously understood. A new study from Johns Hopkins University found that people with lower bone density in their spine experienced faster cognitive decline and more rapid deterioration of the brain's white matter as they aged.

The findings, published in Radiology, a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), suggest that bone health and brain aging may be more closely connected than scientists once realized.

Bone mineral density reflects how much mineral material, including calcium, is present in a given volume of bone. Lower density makes bones more fragile and increases the likelihood of fractures. Although the effects of bone loss on skeletal health are well established, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how declining bone density might relate to changes in the brain.

Using AI to Investigate Bone Density and Brain Health

To explore this connection, a research team led by Sara Momtazmanesh, M.D., a postdoctoral research fellow in the Department of Radiology and Radiological Sciences at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, examined existing data from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). The analysis included information from participants who had undergone chest CT scans without contrast dye, multiple types of brain MRI examinations, and tests measuring cognitive performance.

The researchers applied a deep learning algorithm developed in the laboratory of Shadpour Demehri, M.D., a Johns Hopkins professor of radiology. The AI system analyzed non-contrast chest CT images from 2,086 MESA participants to determine their initial thoracic vertebral volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), a measurement of bone density in the spine.

Of those participants, 715 had the required bone density measurements along with brain MRI results and cognitive testing, making them eligible for the final study group.

The researchers examined the MRI scans for two indicators of changes in the brain's white matter. The first was white matter hyperintensities, areas of abnormal tissue that appear unusually bright on certain MRI images. The second was reduced fractional anisotropy, a measurement that can indicate deterioration in the microscopic organization of white matter. Both types of changes have been associated with cognitive decline and a greater risk of dementia.

Follow-up imaging data were available for 408 participants for white matter hyperintensities and 405 participants for fractional anisotropy, allowing researchers to examine how these brain changes progressed over time.

Lower Bone Density Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline

The analysis revealed a notable pattern: participants with lower spinal bone density at the beginning of the study tended to experience a faster decline in overall cognitive performance.

The researchers also identified changes in specific brain regions that are important for thinking and memory. Lower bone density was associated with greater accumulation of white matter hyperintensities in the corpus callosum, a structure that supports executive function, working memory, and attention.

Another connection emerged in the anterior limb of the internal capsule, a brain region involved in executive function. Participants with lower bone density showed a more pronounced decline in fractional anisotropy in this area, suggesting worsening white matter integrity.

"This study is the first longitudinal secondary analysis linking baseline vertebral bone mineral density to changes in white matter structure, white matter hyperintensity progression and cognition," Dr. Demehri said. "This comprehensive study using both imaging and clinical assessments sends a clear signal that bone density at baseline is associated with both functional and imaging measures of age-related brain degeneration."

Despite the connection between weaker bones and declining brain health, the researchers emphasized that their findings do not establish that osteoporosis causes dementia.

Instead, bone deterioration and brain degeneration may be consequences of some of the same biological changes that occur with aging.

"This study is not about cause and effect, but rather the observation of a metabolic syndrome that may cause both bone and brain degeneration," Dr. Demehri said. "The co-occurrence observed in the study may reflect shared metabolic drivers of aging, including insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and menopausal change, rather than a direct bone-to-brain effect."

These findings raise the possibility that identifying people with reduced bone density could also help recognize those at greater risk of neurological decline. Earlier identification might create opportunities for additional screening and better management of risk factors that affect both skeletal and brain health.

Routine CT Scans Could Reveal Hidden Signs of Brain Aging

One potentially valuable implication of the research is that doctors may be able to obtain useful information about bone density from CT scans that patients have already received for unrelated medical reasons.

"Chest CT is done for lung cancer screening, calcium scoring, nodule follow-up, and many other indications," Dr. Momtazmanesh said. "These scans could provide an opportunistic measurement of bone density from the thoracic spine that is associated with a loss of cognitive function."

By using AI to analyze existing medical images, researchers may be able to identify patterns of age-related disease that would otherwise go unnoticed. This approach could also help scientists investigate why conditions affecting different parts of the body often develop together.

Dr. Demehri concurred: "Diagnostic images contain an immense amount of data that AI can now synthesize at scale across multiple organ systems. This creates a robust, newly feasible opportunity to interconnect co-existing age-related pathologies that have traditionally been studied in isolation and to identify shared biological pathways and potential common causal mechanisms."

The study highlights a potentially important connection between bone health and cognitive function, while also demonstrating how AI could make routine medical imaging more informative. Although further research is needed to understand the biological mechanisms involved, the findings suggest that measurements taken from the spine may provide valuable clues about changes occurring in the aging brain.

The study, "Deep Learning-derived Bone Mineral Density and Longitudinal White Matter Microstructure and Cognitive Decline: Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis," also included Quincy A. #5465. Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease

Changes in mood later in life may offer important clues about what is happening inside the brain, even before problems with memory or thinking become noticeable. New research suggests that the buildup of tau, a protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease, may contribute to worsening depressive symptoms in older adults.

The study, published in JNeurosci, was conducted by Teodora Markova of Brandeis University and her colleagues. The team investigated how tau levels relate to depression during normal aging and in people experiencing the cognitive (memory, attention, and thinking) difficulties associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Protein Linked to Worsening Depression

To investigate this connection, researchers analyzed information from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, a research project that tracks changes in brain health over time. The data included older men and women, some with cognitive difficulties and others whose memory and thinking abilities remained intact.

Participants underwent multiple brain scans designed to detect tau accumulation and completed questionnaires assessing depressive symptoms at different points during the study. This allowed researchers to examine how changes in tau levels corresponded with changes in mood over time.

Among participants with normal cognitive abilities, the researchers discovered a striking pattern. Those whose tau levels increased more rapidly also tended to experience a faster rise in depressive symptoms. Higher tau levels also helped predict more severe depressive symptoms in these individuals.

The results suggest that tau may begin influencing mood before measurable cognitive problems emerge. However, the same relationships were not observed among participants who already had mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease.

Could Depression Reveal Early Brain Changes?

The findings suggest that tau accumulation during the early stages of brain aging may contribute to the development or worsening of depression. They also raise the possibility that changes in mood could provide useful information about brain health before memory loss becomes apparent.

Researchers believe that following depressive symptoms over time, alongside other assessments, could eventually help identify older adults who may be at greater risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases. However, additional research is needed to establish whether these early changes in mood can reliably predict future cognitive decline.

Markova emphasized the importance of studying these relationships over longer periods, particularly as some participants develop more noticeable depression or begin experiencing cognitive difficulties.

"Future work can continue to track how participants' tau levels and depression symptoms evolve over longer periods of time, particularly as some develop cognitive impairment or more clinically significant levels of depression. Continuing to follow these trajectories, observing how early mood changes relate to later clinical outcomes, and establishing relationships with other methods tracking the development of Alzheimer's disease will provide more clarity on methods to determine which individuals may be at an increased risk."

#5464. Key insights from HPE’s Q4 earnings report

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally. The selloff suggests Wall Street still prices HPE as a low-margin server vendor, even though the results describe a networking and artificial intelligence infrastructure company with demand exceeding its ability to ship.

Fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance. HPE now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 27% to 35%, with adjusted earnings of $5.05 to $5.35 per share, according to its earnings release.

I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out. Here are my four takeaways for investors and information technology leaders:

Neri explained that networking orders grew more than 4.5 times faster than networking revenue in the quarter, up from 3.5 times the quarter before, and HPE exited the year with $10.5 billion in AI backlog.

HPE doubled its networking purchase commitments over the summer and raised them again in the fourth quarter, but those components carry lead times of 28 to 40-plus weeks, so Neri expects networking conversion to pick up starting in the second quarter. Supply constraints are a better problem to have than weak demand, but they mean fiscal 2027 hinges on converting orders rather than winning them.

The Juniper Networks integration is complete, and the annual cost-synergy target has risen to $800 million, but the bigger story remains the profit mix. Chief Financial Officer Marie Myers said networking will account for more than 40% of HPE’s operating profit by the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, up from less than a quarter of revenue. AI is a major driver, with routing orders growing by triple digits as customers connect AI data centers to one another.

Security was the soft spot, which Neri called “just timing.” When I asked whether the security portfolio is where he wants it as the industry consolidates around big platforms, he argued for a different path.

“Fortinet and we have a different strategy — the convergence of security and networking — and we are taking it all the way down to the silicon level,” he said. The convergence of networking and security is underway but will take time to execute, as a considerable amount of technical debt must go through its depreciation cycle. In a greenfield situation, organizations can easily deploy a converged solution, but in a brownfield environment, it requires much more work. This is the right strategy, but it remains a “prove-it” business for HPE.

Many neoclouds rely on vendor financing and chip-backed debt, raising real concerns about who is left exposed if the buildout slows. HPE says it has stayed out, and Neri was quite emphatic about it on the briefing.

“I want to be clear: We have not financed any neocloud through HPFS, our financing arm,” he said. “We have zero exposure to any AI financing for neocloud.” HPE has likely left some revenue on the table, but it drew the line in the right place. It will sell to neoclouds, as its $1.2 billion Vultr order shows, without acting as their bank. Enterprise and sovereign customers account for the majority of its cumulative AI orders, and if the neocloud financing chain breaks, HPE’s financing arm won’t be the one holding the paper.

Training built the first phase of AI infrastructure, and Neri believes inference will build the next and will dominate demand for AI infrastructure. “I believe by the end of the decade, 80% will be in AI inferencing,” he said. “Much of that will land on-prem. Much of that will be distributed, for sure. That’s why the server business is structurally well-positioned.”

Once agents are in production, token costs become a recurring bill, and companies will want inference running alongside their own data. Those servers require far more memory and pull in storage and services, which is better business than racking graphics processing units for a hyperscaler.

Evidence of this is the interest in Helios, the Advanced Microdevices Inc. rack that uses HPE’s Ethernet switching rather than Nvidia’s proprietary interconnect. I asked Neri whether Jensen Huang’s brief departure from Nvidia Corp. had opened that door. He said interest was building before then, as customers look to diversify.

HPE shares jumped 17% on Monday ahead of the report as part of a broader AI rally, then fell about 13% in early trading on Tuesday, ending near where they started the week. I see three reasons for this.

The first is margins. Cloud & AI operating margin was 18.4% in the quarter, and HPE guided to about 14% for fiscal 2027. Reuters reported that JPMorgan analysts called margin mix the key debate for investors.

The second is pricing. Myers said higher selling prices have been the biggest driver of server growth, and she expects gross margin to moderate in the second half as AI server volumes ramp and costs rise faster than pricing.

The third is timing. HPE expects about 54% of revenue in the second half, with the ramp tied to Helios shipments, the Oracle Corp. deal, customer data center readiness and component supply. Those are fair execution questions, but they miss the shift in where HPE’s profit comes from.

On the topic of margins, the 18.4% came off an unusual stretch of favorable pricing that should not have been modeled as permanent. Neri argued the guide is still “significantly higher than any historical margin we have had in this business,” and he’s right outside the past year. A year ago, the segment’s margin was 9.3%. Margin rate also isn’t margin dollars. At 30% to 40% revenue growth, my math shows Cloud & AI adding well over $1 billion in operating profit at the midpoint.

The bears are right that price-driven server growth doesn’t warrant a premium multiple, which is why the mix matters more. The market is fixated on the segment whose margins are normalizing and ignoring the one whose margins are expanding. Adjusted earnings per share are still guided to grow by 27% to 35%, in line with revenue growth. That’s far from the margin doom-and-gloom narrative on the stock.

The back-half concern is real but manageable. Myers described the pipeline as multiples of the backlog, and Neri said the guide assumes only historical win rates against it.

Then there’s quality. HPE is guiding to about 30% growth and at least $5.5 billion in free cash flow, has no neocloud financing exposure and has already brought leverage below its target. It trades at about eight times the midpoint of its adjusted earnings guidance. “I don’t see us at a multiple that is 8 to 9x; it makes no sense whatsoever,” Neri said on the earnings call.

For old HPE, that’s true, as it’s a server vendor, but HPE is increasingly a network vendor each quarter. In fact, during our pre-call with Neri, he led with networking and spoke at length about the business before pivoting to the server business. Expect networking to continue to drive a larger share of profits.

Fiscal 2027 is an execution year. HPE must convert purchase commitments into shipments, ramp Helios and prove that networking margins can climb even as cloud and AI margins settle. I’ll be watching networking order conversion more closely than server margins. If HPE executes, today’s multiple will prove to be too low.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.
